entries.title: The Love Hierarchy
entries.synopsis: A three-tier funnel governing qualification for any relationship — short or long term. Every tier must be passed in sequence. Failure at any level is disqualifying for that tier and everything above it.
phrases: each tier must be passed in sequence
boundaryConditions: The hierarchy describes a qualification sequence within each stated perspective; it is not one universal ranking shared by every person.
commonMisreadings: Passing a person's listed factors does not create attraction, consent, compatibility, or entitlement to a relationship.
pressureTests: Would the same candidate pass short-term primary factors but fail long-term secondary or tertiary factors?

entries.title: Jason's Hierarchy
entries.synopsis: Tier 1 Primary Factors Physical attractiveness · Classiness · Attraction towards me Tier 2 Secondary Factors Fun & Easygoing · Assertiveness / Initiative · Purity / Lack of Baggage Tier 3 Tertiary Factors Alignment in values · Common interests · Availability
phrases: Tier 1 Primary Factors Physical attractiveness · Classiness · Attraction towards me
Tier 2 Secondary Factors Fun & Easygoing · Assertiveness / Initiative · Purity / Lack of Baggage
Tier 3 Tertiary Factors Alignment in values · Common interests · Availability
boundaryConditions: This is one named person's stated preference ordering, published so it can be argued with; it is not a claim about what men in general rank first.
commonMisreadings: A woman who passes every tier in Jason's hierarchy has earned a relationship with him.

entries.title: Physical attractiveness
entries.synopsis: Face, body, and overall physical appeal — what registers first, before anything else.
boundaryConditions: Any single factor unmet → immediate disqualification. No exceptions, short- or long-term.
Tier 1 holds three factors that must all clear, so ranking looks first does not make looks sufficient.
commonMisreadings: Physical attractiveness alone carries a woman through the primary tier, with classiness and attraction optional.

entries.title: Classiness
entries.synopsis: Carries herself with grace and refinement — dignified, not crude or attention-seeking.
boundaryConditions: Any single factor unmet → immediate disqualification. No exceptions, short- or long-term.
Classiness here is bearing and self-presentation; sexual history sits in the separate secondary factor for baggage.
commonMisreadings: Classiness means a man wants a woman who is sexually inexperienced rather than dignified in bearing.

entries.title: Attraction towards me
entries.synopsis: The pull runs both ways — she's visibly drawn to me, not just tolerating interest.
boundaryConditions: Any single factor unmet → immediate disqualification. No exceptions, short- or long-term.
The factor asks for visible mutual pull, which means it cannot be satisfied by a woman's willingness to be pursued.
commonMisreadings: A woman tolerating his interest counts as attraction towards him at the primary tier.

entries.title: Fun & Easygoing
entries.synopsis: Light, playful, low-maintenance company — easy to be around, not tense or high-friction.
boundaryConditions: All three met → long-term eligible. Partial → short-term only.
Low-friction company is about temperament, not compliance; a woman who argues well can still be easy to be around.
commonMisreadings: Men want an easygoing woman who agrees with him and avoids every disagreement.

entries.title: Assertiveness / Initiative
entries.synopsis: Meets me halfway — initiates and contributes instead of leaving me to carry everything.
boundaryConditions: All three met → long-term eligible. Partial → short-term only.
The factor asks her to carry a share, not to lead; it is a complaint about one-sided effort rather than a preference for being led.
commonMisreadings: Assertiveness in a woman means she leads the relationship while he follows her plans.

entries.title: Purity / Lack of Baggage
entries.synopsis: Little heavy history or unresolved damage; not dragging a chaotic past into the present.
boundaryConditions: All three met → long-term eligible. Partial → short-term only.
The factor is about unresolved damage and ongoing chaos, which a partner count measures only loosely and sometimes not at all.
commonMisreadings: A woman's partner count is the whole of purity, so a low number clears this factor.

entries.title: Alignment in values
entries.synopsis: Agrees on the things that decide a shared life — how to live and where it's headed.
boundaryConditions: Assumed in a long-term context — these factors sustain the relationship.
Tertiary placement records what gets evaluated last, not what matters least once a relationship is actually running.
commonMisreadings: Shared values matter more to him than physical attraction, so alignment outranks the primary tier.

entries.title: Common interests
entries.synopsis: Enough overlap in how we like to spend time that the relationship has its own texture.
boundaryConditions: Assumed in a long-term context — these factors sustain the relationship.
Shared interests give a relationship texture; they are placed third because overlap can be built where attraction cannot.
commonMisreadings: A couple with the same hobbies has the compatibility that decides whether the relationship lasts.

entries.title: Availability
entries.synopsis: Actually free to invest — emotionally, practically, and in timing.
boundaryConditions: Assumed in a long-term context — these factors sustain the relationship.
Availability covers emotional and practical capacity as well as timing, so being unattached does not establish it.
commonMisreadings: A single woman with free time is available, whatever she is still emotionally carrying.

entries.title: A generic male
entries.synopsis: A synthesis of two blind AI proposals (Claude + ChatGPT), arbitrated. The male asymmetry: status, income, and achievement — near the gate for women — rarely create desire on their own here. The male gate is blunter: do I want her, does she want me back, and is it safe to invest?
phrases: Gate 1 Desire Physical attractiveness & vitality · Sexual receptivity · Low-friction presence
Gate 2 Attachment Warmth & kindness · Loyalty & exclusivity · Respect & admiration
Gate 3 Life Fit Shared values & family · Emotional stability · Practical compatibility
boundaryConditions: This is a synthesis of two AI proposals about central tendency, arbitrated by hand; it describes an average gate and no individual man's.
commonMisreadings: A man wants a woman for her status, income and achievement, exactly as women weigh his.

entries.title: Physical attractiveness & vitality
entries.synopsis: Face, body, femininity, grooming, and style — plus youth, health, and energy. The immediate "do I want her?" signal.
boundaryConditions: Fail any one and she never enters the frame — desire is the gate, and warmth, values, or loyalty can't manufacture it.
Vitality is part of this factor rather than a separate one, which is why the gate is written as appeal plus energy.
commonMisreadings: A woman's face and body decide his desire, so youth, health and energy add little.

entries.title: Sexual receptivity
entries.synopsis: She shows real attraction back — warmth, flirtation, touch, openness — not cold tolerance or passive evaluation.
boundaryConditions: Fail any one and she never enters the frame — desire is the gate, and warmth, values, or loyalty can't manufacture it.
Receptivity means warmth actually returned; passive evaluation reads as absence of it, not a quieter version of it.
commonMisreadings: A man desires a woman who politely tolerates his attention, since tolerance reads as receptivity.

entries.title: Low-friction presence
entries.synopsis: Pleasant to be around: not combative, chaotic, contemptuous, or emotionally punishing from the start.
boundaryConditions: Fail any one and she never enters the frame — desire is the gate, and warmth, values, or loyalty can't manufacture it.
Low friction sits at the desire gate rather than the attachment gate, which is the claim that attraction can be extinguished early.
commonMisreadings: A woman's combative and chaotic streak stops mattering once a man finds her attractive enough.

entries.title: Warmth & kindness
entries.synopsis: Affectionate, appreciative, gentle in tone; makes his life feel lighter rather than heavier.
boundaryConditions: Clear it and he can attach. Fail it and she stays attractive but short-term — unsafe to invest in.
Warmth is what the attachment gate weighs on the way to commitment; placing it after commitment inverts the sequence.
commonMisreadings: A woman's warmth toward a man matters only after he has committed to the relationship.

entries.title: Loyalty & exclusivity
entries.synopsis: Not advertising constant availability or playing him against other men; no reason to doubt commitment.
boundaryConditions: Clear it and he can attach. Fail it and she stays attractive but short-term — unsafe to invest in.
This factor is about the absence of reasons to doubt, so manufactured competition works against it rather than for it.
commonMisreadings: A woman playing a man against other suitors deepens his attachment and his desire for exclusivity.

entries.title: Respect & admiration
entries.synopsis: Genuinely likes him and values his effort; doesn't treat him as a utility, placeholder, or status accessory.
boundaryConditions: Clear it and he can attach. Fail it and she stays attractive but short-term — unsafe to invest in.
Admiration here means valuing his effort as his; being useful to her ambitions is the failure mode the factor names.
commonMisreadings: A woman can want a man as a status accessory and still genuinely admire him.

entries.title: Shared values & family
entries.subcategory: A generic male · Gate 3 · Life Fit
entries.synopsis: Aligned on commitment, children, domestic life, culture if relevant, and what a good life is for.
boundaryConditions: Where a life holds together — values, stability, and daily compatibility decide whether it lasts.
Gate 3 is the last gate, not an optional one; alignment is evaluated late and still has to hold.
commonMisreadings: A man can marry a woman who wants a completely different domestic life and still fit.

entries.title: Emotional stability
entries.subcategory: A generic male · Gate 3 · Life Fit
entries.synopsis: Conflict doesn't curdle into cruelty, volatility, or endless drama; she repairs instead of escalating.
boundaryConditions: Where a life holds together — values, stability, and daily compatibility decide whether it lasts.
The factor is about repair after conflict, not the absence of conflict, so a couple who fight and reconcile clear it.
commonMisreadings: Constant drama makes a man desire a woman more, so volatility signals passion rather than misfit.

entries.title: Practical compatibility
entries.subcategory: A generic male · Gate 3 · Life Fit
entries.synopsis: Lifestyle, habits, money behavior, social rhythm, and daily routines can actually coexist.
boundaryConditions: Where a life holds together — values, stability, and daily compatibility decide whether it lasts.
Practical fit is placed last because it is negotiable, which is different from being automatic.
commonMisreadings: Two partners with incompatible money habits and daily routines will settle it once love is strong.

entries.title: A generic female · Claude's take
entries.synopsis: Synthesized from mate-preference research — central tendency, not any one person. Note the diagonal: status sits at her gate, and provision/commitment ride higher than they do on the male side.
phrases: Tier 1 Primary Factors Confidence & frame · Status & ambition · Physical attractiveness
Tier 2 Secondary Factors Spark & chemistry · Leadership & pursuit · Stability & treatment
Tier 3 Tertiary Factors Provision & stability · Commitment & loyalty · Shared values & goals
boundaryConditions: This is a central tendency synthesized from mate-preference research; individual variation around it is wide enough that the ordering will be wrong for many women.
commonMisreadings: Every woman ranks confidence, status and physical attractiveness the same way this central tendency does.

entries.title: Confidence & frame
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Primary factors
entries.synopsis: Self-assured and non-needy; holds his own center instead of leaning on her for it.
boundaryConditions: Any single factor unmet → no real attraction. Disqualifying, short- or long-term.
Frame here means holding his own centre, which is compatible with vulnerability and distinct from suppressing feeling.
commonMisreadings: Women want a man who leans on them for reassurance, since dependence signals confident frame.

entries.title: Status & ambition
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Primary factors
entries.synopsis: Direction and drive — competent, going somewhere, commands a room without trying.
boundaryConditions: Any single factor unmet → no real attraction. Disqualifying, short- or long-term.
Status in this tier is read off competence and trajectory; measured income sits lower, in the tertiary provision factor.
commonMisreadings: Women want a man's income rather than his direction, so drive without earnings weighs little.

entries.title: Physical attractiveness
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Primary factors
entries.synopsis: Genuinely attractive to her — looks, grooming, the masculine presence she wants.
boundaryConditions: Any single factor unmet → no real attraction. Disqualifying, short- or long-term.
Attractiveness is stated as attractiveness to her, which makes it a fit question rather than a universal ranking of male faces.
commonMisreadings: Women want a man's looks least, so grooming and masculine presence stay optional for him.

entries.title: Spark & chemistry
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Secondary factors
entries.synopsis: That hard-to-fake electric pull — humor, tension, the feeling of being drawn in.
boundaryConditions: All three met → long-term eligible. Partial → short-term / situationship only.
The factor is named hard-to-fake for a reason; it is the one item on this list that resists deliberate construction.
commonMisreadings: Chemistry between a man and a woman can be manufactured by following the right routine.

entries.title: Leadership & pursuit
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Secondary factors
entries.synopsis: Leads and pursues decisively; makes plans and makes her feel chosen, not kept waiting.
boundaryConditions: All three met → long-term eligible. Partial → short-term / situationship only.
Leadership here is about making plans and making her feel chosen, which is a claim about initiative and not about authority over her.
commonMisreadings: A man who waits for a woman to make the plans is leading the courtship well.

entries.title: Stability & treatment
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Secondary factors
entries.synopsis: Emotionally steady and kind in how he treats her — safe, consistent, no games.
boundaryConditions: All three met → long-term eligible. Partial → short-term / situationship only.
Steadiness is placed second, behind desire factors — which says it rarely creates attraction on its own, not that it costs him any.
commonMisreadings: A woman wants a man's unpredictability, so steady kind treatment lowers her attraction to him.

entries.title: Provision & stability
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Tertiary factors
entries.synopsis: Materially reliable — can build and hold down a life, and provide if needed.
boundaryConditions: Weighted toward provision & commitment for the long haul — these sustain the relationship.
Provision is tertiary in this reading, which is the diagonal the page is built to show: status opens the gate, measured provision does not.
commonMisreadings: A man's ability to provide is what first makes a woman want him, ahead of everything.

entries.title: Commitment & loyalty
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Tertiary factors
entries.synopsis: Wants to commit and stays faithful — in it for real, not keeping options open.
boundaryConditions: Weighted toward provision & commitment for the long haul — these sustain the relationship.
Commitment is evaluated once desire and trust are established; its low placement is about sequence, not about how much it matters.
commonMisreadings: A man's willingness to commit is what creates a woman's attraction rather than following it.

entries.title: Shared values & goals
entries.subcategory: A generic female · Claude's take · Tertiary factors
entries.synopsis: Aligned on the big questions — kids, lifestyle, where the relationship is going.
boundaryConditions: Weighted toward provision & commitment for the long haul — these sustain the relationship.
Alignment is a filter applied to people already wanted, so it can end a relationship without ever having started one.
commonMisreadings: A couple aligned on children and lifestyle will feel attraction because the big questions match.

entries.title: A generic female · ChatGPT's take
entries.synopsis: ChatGPT's framing: attraction opens the door, competence keeps the frame romantic, consistency lets her relax, stability makes him future-shaped. The asymmetry: kindness, loyalty, and emotional availability are real but rarely Gate-1 — they gain power only after attraction and competence clear the first filter.
phrases: Gate 1 Desire Attraction · Masculine competence · Safety & calibration
Gate 2 Trust Consistency · Emotional attunement · Selective investment
Gate 3 Fit Provision capacity · Shared values & lifestyle · Character under pressure
boundaryConditions: The claim is about ordering, not worth: kindness and loyalty are described as real and powerful once the first filter has cleared.
commonMisreadings: Kindness and loyalty put a man through her first gate, before attraction and masculine competence.

entries.title: Attraction
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 1 · Desire
entries.synopsis: Face, body, height, style, voice, smell, physical presence — the first filter, even when softened into "vibe."
boundaryConditions: Fail any one and he never enters the frame. Attraction opens the door, competence keeps it romantic, safety lets her stay in it.
The factor names the physical channel plainly, including voice and presence, because softer language for it tends to hide rather than replace it.
commonMisreadings: Calling it a vibe means women want personality first, with physical presence a later filter.

entries.title: Masculine competence
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 1 · Desire
entries.synopsis: Confidence, social ease, decisiveness, status signals, self-command — does he seem like a capable man?
boundaryConditions: Fail any one and he never enters the frame. Attraction opens the door, competence keeps it romantic, safety lets her stay in it.
Competence sits at the desire gate as a read taken early from bearing and social ease, not as a verified record of achievement.
commonMisreadings: Women want a capable-seeming man only after trust is already fully established between them.

entries.title: Safety & calibration
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 1 · Desire
entries.synopsis: Not creepy, not chaotic, not socially blind; shows interest without making her feel trapped or embarrassed.
boundaryConditions: Fail any one and he never enters the frame. Attraction opens the door, competence keeps it romantic, safety lets her stay in it.
Calibration is about reading the room while still showing interest; the factor rules out neither pursuit nor directness.
commonMisreadings: Women want a man whose interest arrives intensely and fast, so feeling trapped is her problem.

entries.title: Consistency
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 2 · Trust
entries.synopsis: Follows through and communicates clearly; doesn't vanish and reappear or make her feel disposable.
boundaryConditions: Clear all three and she relaxes into the risk. Gaps here keep him at arm's length, however attractive.
Consistency is a trust-gate factor, which means it is what converts early interest into something durable rather than what creates the interest.
commonMisreadings: Women want a man who vanishes and reappears, so steady follow-through weakens her trust.

entries.title: Emotional attunement
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 2 · Trust
entries.synopsis: Notices her, reads tone, makes her feel chosen — warm without becoming needy.
boundaryConditions: Clear all three and she relaxes into the risk. Gaps here keep him at arm's length, however attractive.
The factor explicitly pairs warmth with non-neediness, so it treats the two as separable rather than as points on one dial.
commonMisreadings: Women reject a man attuned to their feelings, because noticing her reads as neediness.

entries.title: Selective investment
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 2 · Trust
entries.synopsis: Not just chasing access to any woman; he makes her feel specifically valued.
boundaryConditions: Clear all three and she relaxes into the risk. Gaps here keep him at arm's length, however attractive.
Selectivity is about being chosen specifically; it is a claim about how investment is read, not an instruction to withhold it.
commonMisreadings: Women want a man who pursues every available woman, since volume signals high value.

entries.title: Provision capacity
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 3 · Fit
entries.synopsis: Not just rich, but functional: direction, discipline, earning potential, handles adult life.
boundaryConditions: Where a life is built — values, provision capacity, and who he becomes under pressure decide whether it lasts.
The factor is written as functional rather than rich, which makes it a read on how he handles adult life at any income.
commonMisreadings: Women want a man's wealth alone, so discipline and direction count for little.

entries.title: Shared values & lifestyle
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 3 · Fit
entries.synopsis: Family plans, social rhythm, religion/politics if relevant, ambition, long-term expectations.
boundaryConditions: Where a life is built — values, provision capacity, and who he becomes under pressure decide whether it lasts.
Which values are load-bearing varies by couple; the factor names the categories to check and does not rank them.
commonMisreadings: A man can marry a woman with opposite family plans and ambitions and still fit.

entries.title: Character under pressure
entries.subcategory: A generic female · ChatGPT's take · Gate 3 · Fit
entries.synopsis: Conflict style, loyalty, honesty, patience — does he turn cruel, weak, or reckless when things get hard?
boundaryConditions: Where a life is built — values, provision capacity, and who he becomes under pressure decide whether it lasts.
This factor is placed last because pressure is what reveals it, which means it is usually observed after the earlier gates have already cleared.
commonMisreadings: Women choose a man on his courtship behaviour, so conduct under pressure reveals less.

entries.title: The Five Levers of SMV
entries.synopsis: Most "SMV" talk collapses a person into a single score and then argues about the decimal. The useful version is structural: your standing is built from five movable factors, then scaled by forces you mostly don't control — the clock, the market you're in, and what's actually being selected for. Raise the levers. Respect the multipliers.
phrases: Looks + Money + Status + Charm + Exposure × Clock × Market × Context
boundaryConditions: Not a real equation — a map. The "+" hides the fact that one weak factor can quietly cap the others, and the weights themselves shift with context. The arithmetic is illustrative; the structure is the point.
SMV is contextual, market-relative, and time-sensitive rather than a fixed trait.
The five levers model dating-market response, not human worth or moral worth.
commonMisreadings: A composite market estimate is not a clinical score, a universal rank, or a promise of any individual's response.
pressureTests: Does the conclusion survive a change of age band, location, platform, relationship goal, or available pool?

entries.title: Looks
entries.synopsis: The visual packet the market reads in milliseconds — and the one place a stranger’s snap judgment is, statistically, doing real work. This isn’t vanity. It’s triage: looks decide who gets considered at all, before any other factor gets a vote.
phrases: The signal that fires before you say a word.

Stop fighting the parts you can’t move and max the ones you can. Lean, groomed, well-dressed, and well-photographed beats "good bones, no effort" in the only arena that scores you: the first three seconds.
boundaryConditions: Bone structure, height, base face. Past a point, genetics set the ceiling, and pretending otherwise just sells you surgery and serums.
Looks act as a high-leverage first gate but do not by themselves supply compatibility, availability, or retention.
commonMisreadings: Looksmaxxing into paralysis. When "I’m not attractive enough" becomes the reason to never enter the market, Looks has stopped being a lever and become an alibi for staying out of the game entirely.
High looks are not equivalent to high total SMV in every market or to long-term relationship quality.
pressureTests: Is the claimed effect still present after separating initial attention from being chosen and kept?

entries.title: Face
entries.synopsis: Averageness, symmetry, and sexual dimorphism. "Average" here means mathematically composite, not forgettable — blended faces read as more attractive (Langlois & Roggman, 1990).
boundaryConditions: The face does the most work in the opening seconds and progressively less once someone actually knows you; the shared score dissolves as acquaintance grows.
Averageness and symmetry are population-level rater agreements, not per-feature scores that can be summed into an individual's rating — single bones explain little alone.
commonMisreadings: An average face is a plain forgettable face, so averageness makes women reject a man.
Men reject a woman on her face in the first second, and that snap read holds forever.
pressureTests: Is the claim about the first-impression read, or has it been extended to who gets chosen and kept after that?

entries.title: Body
entries.synopsis: Composition and shape carry more signal than raw weight. The female hourglass (waist-to-hip ~0.7) and the male V-taper (shoulder-to-hip ratio) are the dimorphic cues the eye is tuned to.
boundaryConditions: The dimorphic shape cues are read differently by sex and by ecology; hunter-gatherer samples prefer higher ratios than the Western samples the 0.7 figure came from.
Body composition is among the most movable slices of Looks, so a reading of it is a snapshot of a current state rather than a fixed trait.
commonMisreadings: A 0.7 waist-to-hip ratio is the universal ideal, so men in every culture prefer exactly that.
pressureTests: Is the claim about shape and composition, or has it quietly become a claim about a number on a scale?

entries.title: Height
entries.synopsis: A near one-directional lever for men: women’s preference for taller partners is stronger than men’s preference for shorter ones — but it’s a window, not a ladder. Very large gaps get dispreferred too.
boundaryConditions: A preference measured on stated rankings and a preference acted on in real pairings are separate measurements.
commonMisreadings: Every woman rejects a man under six feet, so height alone settles who she dates.

entries.title: Grooming & style
entries.synopsis: The most malleable slice of Looks. Skin, hair, fit, scent, posture — the part you can move in weeks, not generations.
boundaryConditions: Grooming moves in weeks, not generations, and cannot substitute for the layer LE classifies as fixed: bone structure, height, and base face.
Grooming improves the first-three-seconds read; it does not supply Charm, Exposure, or anything that happens after the door opens.
commonMisreadings: Good grooming and style make up for the face underneath, so any man can attract women.
pressureTests: Is the improvement being counted against the movable slice, or is it being asked to fix something the model classifies as fixed?

entries.title: Voice
entries.synopsis: An overlooked cue. Lower-pitched male voices and higher-pitched female voices read as more attractive, signaling body size and dimorphism (Puts; Feinberg).
boundaryConditions: The pitch findings are rating-study effects on perceived attractiveness; they do not describe how a voice performs across a whole conversation, where Charm takes over.
LE states a perceptual effect only; it makes no claim that pitch is trainable or that performing a lower voice reproduces the effect.
commonMisreadings: A deeper voice is more attractive for everyone, so women with lower voices attract more men.
pressureTests: Is the pitch claim being applied to the correct sex, and is it about perception or about outcomes?

entries.title: Age
entries.synopsis: Looks are time-stamped. This is where the Clock multiplier bites hardest — and the reason "start now" beats "start perfect."
boundaryConditions: The Clock scales each factor differently — Looks and fertility cues are front-loaded while money, status, and prestige accrue with age — so one age number does not move total SMV in a single direction.
LE grades the peak-age story as Contested: a soft, averaged slope built on stated preferences and fertility cues, not a personal deadline.
commonMisreadings: Women peak at twenty-two and hit a wall, so after that age men stop wanting them.
Men date younger women because a woman's age is the only number that prices her in the market.
pressureTests: Is age being used as a population slope, an individual verdict, or a stand-in for an unstated relationship goal?

entries.title: Money
entries.synopsis: Not the number in your account — the signal that you can provide, that your life is under control, and that the arrow points up. Money buys options and quietly raises the floor under every other factor.
phrases: Resources, stability, and the direction of both.
Fix the floor before chasing the ceiling. Stable, low-debt, and clearly-rising reads better than a leased flex on a fragile base. Then treat earning power as a multi-year build, not a weekend hack.
boundaryConditions: Where you start: family money, the local economy, your field’s ceiling. The opening hand is luck.
Money is one lever whose salience varies with life stage, market, and relationship goal.
commonMisreadings: Two failure modes, opposite directions. The wallet-as-personality flex — and the inverse cope that "she only wants money," a story that conveniently excuses building any.
Resources cannot be assumed to manufacture attraction or erase failures in every other lever.
pressureTests: Would the same result hold when income is visible but status, generosity, debt, and lifestyle fit differ?

entries.title: Income
entries.synopsis: Current earning power — the visible, askable number. Matters, but reads as less attractive than people fear when the rest is stable.
boundaryConditions: The cross-cultural sex difference in weighting financial prospects is a stated preference and shrinks in live, face-to-face settings; stated and revealed diverge here.
Money's weight rises sharply for long-term mating and falls for short-term, and LE treats the floor — assets and stability — as doing more work than the headline number.
commonMisreadings: Women care most about income, so a bigger salary is what makes women want a man.
pressureTests: Is the claim resting on what people said they wanted, or on who they actually picked?

entries.title: Assets & stability
entries.synopsis: The floor: savings, low debt, no money panic. Quietly more attractive than flash, because it signals a life someone could join without rescuing.
boundaryConditions: Where you start — family money, the local economy, your field's ceiling — is the opening hand, which LE classifies as luck rather than discipline.
Money's weight is context-dependent and rises for long-term mating, so a profile tuned for stability can underperform on short-term metrics.
commonMisreadings: Savings and low debt are boring, so women want visible flash and big spending instead.
pressureTests: Is the signal being read as financial security, or as a moral claim about who deserves a partner?

entries.title: Trajectory
entries.synopsis: The market prices direction, not just position. "Building" and "accelerating" often beat "arrived but stalled."
boundaryConditions: Trajectory sits under Money, whose whole weight rises for long-term mating and falls for short-term.
LE puts the floor ahead of the slope and frames earning power as a multi-year build rather than a weekend hack.
commonMisreadings: A rising trajectory is enough on its own, so women want potential more than an actual floor.
pressureTests: Is the trajectory claim backed by a moved floor, or is potential being asked to stand in for one?

entries.title: Provisioning signal
entries.synopsis: Whether a partner reads you as a stable life to join or a project to fix. This is the part Money is really standing in for.
boundaryConditions: Reading as stable and reading as wealthy are different judgments, and only the first is what this factor tracks.
commonMisreadings: A woman commits to whichever man earns most, so income settles who she will marry.

entries.title: Spending freedom
entries.synopsis: The ability to create experiences without strain — taste, generosity, logistics. Not flexing; just not flinching.
boundaryConditions: LE defines this as creating experiences without strain — not flexing, just not flinching — and names the wallet-as-personality flex as where the factor curdles.
It describes capacity, not obligation; LE counts both the flex and its mirror-image cope, "she only wants money", as failures of the same factor.
commonMisreadings: Spending big on dates and gifts is what makes money attractive, so women want a flashy man.
pressureTests: Is the claim about strain-free capacity, or has it become a claim about visible spend?

entries.title: Status
entries.synopsis: Where you sit in the eyes of others, and the route you took to get there. Status is the most socially-read factor: you see it less in the person than in how the room reacts to them.
phrases: Your rank — and crucially, how you got it.

Chase prestige, not dominance theater. Get good at something people value, get vouched for, and let preselection talk for you. Borrowed dominance — the manufactured alpha act — reads as exactly the tell it is.
boundaryConditions: Inherited status and the prestige of where you already stand. Slow to inherit; instant to squander.
Status is audience- and context-dependent; recognition in one circle may not transfer to another.
commonMisreadings: Status-chasing that eats the self. When rank becomes the entire personality — performative dominance, status anxiety, treating people as audience — you’ve polished the signal and hollowed out the thing it was supposed to signal.
Status is not the same as virtue, intimacy, or broad public fame.
pressureTests: Does the claimed status advantage persist outside the network that recognizes it?

entries.title: Dominance
entries.synopsis: Rank through assertiveness, presence, and willingness to take space. One of two real routes to status (Henrich & Gil-White, 2001) — potent, but read warily for the long term.
boundaryConditions: Dominance is one of two separable, measurable routes to rank; prestige is the other, and LE calls it the more durable one.
Women tend to favor dominance cues more for short-term partners and prestige more for long-term ones, so the lever's value is goal-dependent.
commonMisreadings: Dominance is what status means, so a man acting alpha outranks everyone and women want him most.
pressureTests: Is the dominance read being scored for a short-term or a long-term goal, and does the answer change the verdict?

entries.title: Prestige
entries.synopsis: Rank through competence and freely-given respect: being genuinely good at something people value. The other route, and the more durable one.
boundaryConditions: Prestige is conferred by people who value the thing you are good at, which means it cannot be self-declared.
Prestige is weighted more heavily for long-term partners than short-term, and the inherited portion is slow to accrue and instant to squander.
commonMisreadings: Prestige is just your job title and salary, so women want the man with the best title.
pressureTests: Is the respect being described freely given, or is it deference extracted by position?

entries.title: Reputation
entries.synopsis: What gets said about you when you’re not in the room. Compounds slowly, forfeits fast.
boundaryConditions: Reputation is what gets said about you when you are not in the room, not the impression you manage while present.
Reputation is scoped to the network that carries it and supplies no Exposure of its own: a good name in rooms you are never in scores nothing.
commonMisreadings: A wrecked reputation rebuilds as fast as it was lost, so women want him again quickly.
pressureTests: Is the reputation claim scoped to a specific network, and is the person actually in front of that network?

entries.title: Preselection
entries.synopsis: Visible evidence that others already chose you. Being wanted makes you more wanted — humans copy observed mate choices (Place et al., 2010).
boundaryConditions: Copying an observed choice shifts how existing value gets read, which is a smaller effect than creating value.
commonMisreadings: Being visibly wanted creates attraction from nothing, so a man with dates needs nothing else.

entries.title: Leadership & network
entries.synopsis: Whether you shape rooms or just fill them, and the quality of the people who vouch for you.
boundaryConditions: LE reads this as the quality of the people who vouch for you and whether you shape rooms or just fill them, not as list size or attendance.
Who vouches for you is a Status signal, not an Exposure one — a strong network never converted into qualified encounters does not move the denominator.
commonMisreadings: More contacts means more status, so a man with a bigger network meets more women to date.
pressureTests: Is the claim about the quality of the people vouching, or about how many of them there are?

entries.title: Charm
entries.synopsis: The live layer. Looks open the door; Charm decides whether you’re invited back through it. Presence, wit, warmth, calibration, and the ability to make another person actually feel something in your company.
phrases: What you do with the attention once you have it.

Get live reps. Charm does not improve in your head — it improves in real conversations where you can be misread, recover, and recalibrate. For most introverted, principled men this is the single highest-return factor, because it’s pure skill and almost nobody trains it on purpose.
boundaryConditions: Baseline temperament, social wiring, neurodivergence. Some people genuinely start with a steeper hill, and that’s worth naming honestly.
Charm can improve conversion after interaction but cannot reliably rescue a profile that never reaches interaction.
commonMisreadings: Charm weaponized into manipulation — "game" that treats people as locks to be picked. The moment technique loses warmth it reads as exactly what it is, and it stops working on anyone worth keeping.
Social skill is neither irrelevant nor an unlimited substitute for all threshold traits.
pressureTests: Did the source observe an actual interaction, or infer charm's power from profiles that never met?

entries.title: Conversation & wit
entries.synopsis: Making time spent with you better than time without you. Humor does more work here than almost anything else.
boundaryConditions: LE grades humor as Mixed and the fitness-indicator mechanism as Contested: a speed-dating test failed to support it and the male humor-production edge is smaller than first claimed.
Charm operates after Looks have opened the door; conversation does not substitute for the first filter or for Exposure.
commonMisreadings: Being funny is a proven fitness signal, so a man who makes women laugh reliably wins attraction.
pressureTests: Does the humor claim survive the replication failure LE cites, or does it depend on the original fitness-indicator framing?

entries.title: Calibration
entries.synopsis: Reading signals and escalating at the right speed. The gap between "smooth" and "creepy" is almost entirely timing, not content.
boundaryConditions: LE grades Charm as the most trainable factor but marks that grading a Lens — a framing, not a measured finding — and says it improves only in live conversation, not rehearsal.
Baseline temperament, social wiring, and neurodivergence mean some people start with a genuinely steeper hill here, which LE names rather than papers over.
commonMisreadings: Creepiness is about the words a man picks, so a woman rejects him for content alone.
pressureTests: Is the failure being described a content problem or a timing problem, and does that change the fix?

entries.title: Emotional steadiness
entries.synopsis: Not leaking neediness under ambiguity. Calm is attractive precisely because it’s rare and hard to fake.
boundaryConditions: LE defines this as not leaking neediness under ambiguity, and grounds it in calm being rare and hard to fake — which is a claim about the difficulty of faking it.
Baseline temperament, social wiring, and neurodivergence set a genuinely steeper hill for some people, and steadiness sits inside Charm, which operates after Looks open the door.
commonMisreadings: Staying calm means hiding every feeling and acting indifferent, so a woman wants you and chases.
pressureTests: Is the calm being described real regulation under ambiguity, or disengagement wearing the same face?

entries.title: Warmth
entries.synopsis: The capacity to make someone feel safe, seen, and at ease — the half of Charm the strategy crowd keeps forgetting.
boundaryConditions: The Context multiplier reweights toward stability, prestige, warmth, and reliability for long-term goals and away from them for short-term; warmth's weight moves with the game being played.
LE indexes warmth as the half of Charm the strategy crowd forgets, and grades Charm's trainability as a Lens rather than an evidence-backed effect size.
commonMisreadings: Being warm and kind is enough by itself, so a woman desires any man who is nice.
pressureTests: Is the claim about making someone feel safe and seen, or about being agreeable enough to be chosen?

entries.title: Presence
entries.synopsis: Whether people remember the feeling of being around you after you’ve left the room.
boundaryConditions: LE defines presence as whether people remember the feeling of being around you after you have left — a claim about residue, not about the room while you are in it.
Charm operates after Looks have opened the door, and LE grades its trainability as a Lens rather than a single measured finding.
commonMisreadings: Presence means commanding the room and being the loudest man there, which is what women want.
pressureTests: Is the presence being described what people felt afterwards, or only what they noticed at the time?

entries.title: Exposure
entries.synopsis: The factor nobody romantic wants to admit is decisive: surface area. The best profile in the world scores nothing if it’s never seen. Exposure is the denominator sitting under every other factor — and usually the most neglected.
phrases: How many qualified people actually encounter you.

Increase qualified surface area and then act on it. Better photos, the right channels, recurring social environments, consistent initiative. For most people who feel stuck, the bottleneck isn’t their score — it’s that almost no one is seeing it.
boundaryConditions: The market you’re physically in right now — its size, age pool, and ratio. Real constraints, not excuses, but constraints.
Exposure multiplies opportunities to be evaluated; it does not guarantee favorable evaluation.
commonMisreadings: Spray-and-pray volume with zero standards — or its mirror image: treating low exposure as proof the market is rigged, rather than the one variable most under your own control.
A lack of outcomes under very low exposure is not clean evidence of low desirability.
pressureTests: How many relevant people could actually encounter and evaluate the person under study?

entries.title: Geography & sex ratio
entries.synopsis: The local supply and demand you’re embedded in. Your value is relative to the ratio around you — though in the US that ratio sorts far harder by credential than by city (Angrist, 2002; ACS).
boundaryConditions: The ratio evidence is graded Mixed: it describes population-level shifts in commitment norms and bargaining power, not a per-person adjustment factor.
A brutal local market is data, not a verdict — LE classifies the market you are physically in as fixed while classifying which rooms and channels you use as movable.
commonMisreadings: The sex ratio here is brutal, so the dating market is rigged and every approach fails.
pressureTests: Is the ratio being used to explain the market's terms, or to explain away one person's outcomes?

entries.title: Volume of contact
entries.synopsis: How many plausible, available people you actually cross paths with — qualified encounters, not raw foot traffic.
boundaryConditions: LE counts qualified encounters — plausible, available people — not raw foot traffic, and names spray-and-pray volume with zero standards as where Exposure curdles.
Exposure is the denominator under every other factor, not a replacement for them; more encounters do not raise Looks, Money, Status, or Charm.
commonMisreadings: Raw volume of contact fixes exposure, so a man who meets more single women will win.
pressureTests: Are the encounters being counted actually plausible and available, or is the raw number doing the work?

entries.title: The online funnel
entries.synopsis: Apps as a high-volume, brutally-sorted channel: effective, and merciless about the desirability hierarchy.
boundaryConditions: Volume and sorting are distinct: a channel can raise how many people see you while narrowing who replies.
commonMisreadings: Apps rank every man honestly, so a woman who rejects him there would reject him anywhere.

entries.title: Recurring environments
entries.synopsis: Repeated contact beats one-off events. Propinquity and mere exposure quietly manufacture attraction over time.
boundaryConditions: Propinquity and mere exposure work slowly and quietly over time; LE frames the lever as being consistently around, which a single encounter cannot invoke.
Recurring environments raise the odds of being seen; they do not change how the market prices what it sees.
commonMisreadings: Repeated exposure builds attraction, so a man should keep showing up until the woman wants him.
pressureTests: Is the environment actually recurring with the same people, or is it a series of one-off rooms?

entries.title: Initiative
entries.synopsis: The multiplier on everything above. Surface area you never act on is just scenery.
boundaryConditions: Initiative multiplies what exists and cannot manufacture a pool the local market, ratio, and age band do not contain.
LE calls Exposure the most movable factor for anyone willing to act, which makes low initiative a diagnosis rather than a verdict on the market.
commonMisreadings: Initiative is the whole game, so enough approaches will eventually make some woman want you.
pressureTests: Is the bottleneck the score being offered, or that almost nobody is seeing it?

entries.title: The Clock
entries.synopsis: Every factor is time-stamped. Looks and fertility cues are front-loaded; money, status, and prestige accrue with age. Your score isn't a fixed point — it's a trajectory, and the slope can matter as much as the height.
phrases: SMV is a curve, not a constant.
boundaryConditions: Use it to respect timing, not to panic. The clock rewards starting now over starting "when you're finally ready."
Age effects vary by sex, goal, fertility plans, cohort, and market; they are slopes and trade-offs, not one cliff.
commonMisreadings: A man's dating value peaks young and falls, on the same curve women walk after thirty.
pressureTests: Is age being used as a population trend, an individual destiny, or a proxy for an unstated goal?

entries.title: The Market
entries.synopsis: There is no absolute SMV. The same profile is a 6 in one city and an 8 in another, depending on the sex ratio, the age pool, and the competition around it. The market sets the exchange rate; you just hold the currency.
boundaryConditions: A brutal local market is data, not a verdict — but the exit is narrower than it looks. Across US metros the ratio barely moves (roughly 5 points either side of parity), and moving has been tested directly against marriage outcomes and came back null.
The same profile can face different scarcity, competition, and norms in different markets.
commonMisreadings: A man rated six in one city is rated six in every city he dates in.
pressureTests: Would the claim reverse in a market with a different sex ratio, geography, app mix, or relationship norm?

entries.title: The Context
entries.synopsis: The five factors aren't weighted the same in every situation. For short-term attraction, Looks, dominance, and immediacy spike. For long-term, stability, prestige, warmth, and reliability take over. A profile tuned for one can underperform in the other.
boundaryConditions: Know which game you're playing. Optimizing your whole self for short-term metrics, then wondering why long-term keeps failing, is a category error.
Traits are weighted differently in stranger markets, social circles, apps, hookups, and long-term selection.
commonMisreadings: The five factors carry identical weight whether a woman wants a fling or wants marriage.
pressureTests: Which stage and venue produced the observed response, and is the source generalizing beyond it?

entries.title: The Conversion Ladder
entries.synopsis: A stage model for separating attention, desire, choice, and durability — the lens the rest of this page sits inside. It is not a universal love equation; it is a debugging tool. A person can win one rung and fail the next, which is why app attention, sexual interest, commitment, and relationship stability should never be treated as the same signal.
boundaryConditions: The ladder distinguishes stages analytically; real relationships can loop, stall, regress, or skip observable steps.
commonMisreadings: Being seen or receiving messages is not proof of desire, selection, compatibility, or durable commitment.
pressureTests: At exactly which transition did the evidence occur, and what evidence shows movement to the next stage?

entries.title: The Calibration Error
entries.synopsis: Every score on this site is an estimate of an estimate. The ratings that feed the curves, the gates and the calculators are overwhelmingly self-assessments — and self-assessed looks track how strangers actually rate you at about r ≈ 0.24. That is not a rounding problem.
boundaryConditions: The error measured is self-about-self on physical attractiveness; ratings of third parties are a different and more reliable instrument.
A weak correlation with observer ratings does not make self-rating useless as a predictor of the rater's own behaviour.
A correlation of this kind does not convert into a point-scale margin of error, and no source here supplies one.
The overestimation was measured on people grouped by stranger-rated looks, not on people who report a low score for themselves.
commonMisreadings: In dating, a self-rated looks score is accurate enough to fix your matching-curve position.
Women in dating overestimate their looks, and men rate themselves accurately.

sourceLinks.label: Feingold (1992), Psychological Bulletin 111(2):304–341
Greitemeyer (2020), Scandinavian Journal of Psychology 61(4)

pressureTests: Is the difference being argued about larger than the instrument's own error bar?

entries.title: The Interaction Gate
entries.synopsis: Profiles, checklists, and calculators can reject a known mismatch. In the available speed-dating evidence, pre-date traits and preferences did not reliably rank pair-specific desire. The operating distinction is simple: pre-contact evidence may screen out; richer interaction must select in.
boundaryConditions: Profiles and calculators can reject known mismatches, but positive compatibility remains indeterminate until live interaction.
commonMisreadings: A high profile score or checklist match cannot establish chemistry, felt safety, or mutual ease.

sourceLinks.label: Joel, Eastwick & Finkel (2017), Psychological Science
Baxter et al. (2022), PNAS

pressureTests: What changed after voice, timing, mannerisms, conflict style, and reciprocal interest became observable?

entries.title: The Readiness Gate
entries.synopsis: A good candidate and an available candidate are not the same state. For a commitment goal, pair-specific interest must clear one gate and present willingness and capacity to build must clear another. Chemistry without readiness is not a delayed yes or a renovation project.
boundaryConditions: A viable match can still fail when one or both people lack availability, intention, capacity, or timing.
commonMisreadings: Readiness failure does not prove either person is defective, nor does potential override a present no.

sourceLinks.label: Hadden, Agnew & Tan (2018), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
Pew Research Center (2019), “Why people get married or move in with a partner”
Smock, Manning & Porter (2005), “Everything’s There Except Money,” JMF
Ishizuka (2018), Demography
Kearney & Wilson (2018), REStat

pressureTests: If attraction and compatibility are held constant, is there evidence of present capacity and reciprocal intent?

entries.title: The Marriage Bar
entries.synopsis: The parent entry separates interest from willingness. This entry names a third gate that neither of those measures: a socially defined economic-readiness threshold for marriage specifically. A couple can want each other, want marriage, and already share a household — while the wedding waits on savings, debt, stable work, or the ability to stage a milestone.
boundaryConditions: All core evidence is U.S.-specific; the bar's level and contents vary by class, culture, cohort, race, prior marriage, parenthood, housing market and legal regime.
Stated reasons are self-reports and can rationalize after the fact; the SIPP analysis is prospective but observational.
Economic readiness bundles earnings, assets, debt, housing and wedding affordability; they are empirically separable and not reducible to income.
The bar belongs to the couple and its context, not to one partner's earnings.
commonMisreadings: Living with a partner means the relationship will naturally become marriage once love is strong.
Couples delay marriage because they want expensive weddings, while ordinary finances play little role.
An unemployed man is automatically unready for marriage regardless of his partner's resources.

sourceLinks.label: Pew Research Center (2019), “Why people get married or move in with a partner”
Smock, Manning & Porter (2005), “Everything’s There Except Money,” JMF
Ishizuka (2018), Demography
Kearney & Wilson (2018), REStat

pressureTests: Is a stalled cohabitation being read against the willingness gate when it sits below the economic bar?
Would the claim survive the boom-town result, where earnings rose and marriage did not?

entries.title: The 7–7 Rule
entries.synopsis: A binary qualification gate for serious long-term candidates: physical attractiveness ≥ 7 and the personality composite ≥ 7. The two sides are scored independently — a high score on one never compensates for a low score on the other. The personality side is an aggregate, not a single trait, so one charming quality can’t carry a weak overall composite.
boundaryConditions: The thresholds are a practical LE heuristic, not a population law or guarantee of a successful relationship.
commonMisreadings: Two sufficient scores do not bypass consent, timing, attraction asymmetry, or the Interaction Gate.
pressureTests: Can a candidate clear both model thresholds yet fail because the measured dimensions omit a decisive live factor?

entries.title: Sub-5 Auto Disqualification
entries.synopsis: A score below 5 in any single important component — a load-bearing sub-factor of the looks or personality composite — signals active incompatibility, not just weakness. It catches what an average launders: a 7 composite can be hiding a 3 underneath. It doesn’t matter how strong everything else is — one important component under 5 trips the floor.
boundaryConditions: The rule represents hard personal minimums inside LE's scoring model, not a moral judgment or a universal cutoff.
commonMisreadings: A below-threshold model result does not make a person lesser or predict every evaluator's decision.
pressureTests: Is the disqualifying dimension truly non-negotiable for this evaluator, or an averaged preference treated as absolute?

entries.title: Treatment Markup System
entries.synopsis: A dual-use model. First it scores: each person’s base is looks + treatment, and whoever brings the stronger treatment earns a markup on top — behavior is a real value-add, not décor. Then it pairs: read Person A and Person B as a couple and ask whether they actually match.
boundaryConditions: Differential effort can reveal perceived leverage, but context, personality, resources, safety, and strategy can also affect treatment.
commonMisreadings: Money spent, pursuit intensity, or politeness alone is not a clean meter of attraction.
pressureTests: Does the treatment difference persist across comparable contexts and costs, or is one anecdote carrying the inference?

entries.title: Looks Rating Evaluation System
entries.synopsis: A looks score is not static, but it is not infinitely fluid either. Every rating carries a support floor and a resistance ceiling that bound how perception drifts over time. Initial evaluations are highly accurate — but bias, familiarity, and behavior all apply pressure within the band.
boundaryConditions: The scale is an anchor for disciplined comparison, not an objective biometric truth or universal verdict.
commonMisreadings: A numeric looks estimate should not be presented as more precise than the inputs or evaluator agreement allow.
pressureTests: How much does the rating move across evaluators, styling, photos, age, and in-person presentation?

entries.title: The Parity Rule
entries.synopsis: The 7–7 tells you what a top long-term partner has to clear; it doesn’t tell you who you get. The Parity Rule does: your realistic ideal is your own coordinates. A 6–6 (looks-6, personality-6) pairs with a 6–6, a 4–4 with a 4–4, down the ladder to 1–1. The 7–7 is the universal aspiration; parity is the attainable one. You don’t marry the gate — you marry your tier.
boundaryConditions: Assortative matching is a distributional tendency with exceptions, trade-offs, and measurement error.
commonMisreadings: Population clustering near parity does not decree who any individual may attract or retain.
pressureTests: What compensating lever, selection channel, or measurement error explains stable off-parity couples?

entries.title: The Spiderman Effect
entries.synopsis: The Parity Rule says you can’t objectively attain a 7–7 as a 6–6. The Spiderman Effect says you can attain one subjectively: to another 6–6 you read as their 7–7, and they read as yours. Two equals, each pointing at the other as the special one — the meme made literal. As long as both believe it, it functions as real, because attraction runs partly on perception, not only on the consensus score.
boundaryConditions: Repeated exposure and social context can change evaluation only when real contact occurs; proximity is not entitlement.
commonMisreadings: Familiarity does not guarantee attraction and must not be used to excuse persistence after rejection.
pressureTests: Would the outcome survive without repeated low-pressure contact, community trust, or constrained alternatives?

entries.title: SMV Matching
entries.synopsis: How attractiveness sorts the market. Score looks as a within-sex percentile — a 7 is the 70th percentile of one’s own sex, not an absolute. Across already-paired couples, partners’ rated looks correlate at r ≈ 0.4 — moderate, real matching.
boundaryConditions: The five layers organize recurring patterns; they do not collapse into one deterministic equation for every pair.
commonMisreadings: Market leverage, attention, and partner quality are distinct outcomes and cannot be substituted for one another.
pressureTests: Which layer actually explains the case, and what observed exception would the layer fail to explain?

entries.title: The Matching Curve
entries.synopsis: Within-sex looks matching among already-paired couples. One curve — it applies identically to men and women.
boundaryConditions: Regression toward the middle describes the average partner, and the spread around that average stays wide.
commonMisreadings: Couples who date pair at identical looks ratings, so the curve predicts each partner's score.

entries.title: The Attention Market
entries.synopsis: Who gets noticed before anyone pairs. Attention is not the same thing as commitment.
boundaryConditions: Online attention distributions depend on platform mechanics and do not directly measure desire, selection, or offline pairing.
commonMisreadings: Message or swipe concentration is not proof that the same minority monopolizes relationships.
pressureTests: Does the pattern persist in actual dates and relationships after platform sorting and inactive accounts are removed?

entries.title: The Option Pool
entries.synopsis: Who can be converted from attention into realistic dates or commitment. Options and pairings are different things.
boundaryConditions: Visible options are not equivalent to viable, reciprocal, available, or compatible options.
commonMisreadings: A large inbox or local population should not be counted as a large pool of relationship candidates.
pressureTests: After reciprocity, goal, location, attraction, readiness, and compatibility filters, how many options remain?

entries.title: The Charm Ceiling
entries.synopsis: How far can game / charm actually carry you, and where does it cap? Part 1 takes a Blackpill creator’s looks-vs-game model at face value; Part 2 draws the research model on its own axes. The source is strictly male-perspective (the man judged, women as acceptors), so Part 1 follows that; Part 2 is tabbable to either the male or female view.
phrases: Right about the stranger-market arena it maps — apps, cold approach — but false generalized to all of dating. Charm is access-gated, not value-gated.
boundaryConditions: Charm matters most after interaction and has limits when a hard attraction or safety threshold is not met.
commonMisreadings: The ceiling does not mean personality is irrelevant; it distinguishes access to interaction from conversion within it.
pressureTests: Is charm being credited for creating access, or for improving outcomes among people who already had access?

entries.title: The Status Trade
entries.synopsis: Beyond looks and charm, overall mate value is a blend — and this is where the framework’s opening promise pays off: the “trading up” people notice enters through status. We take the canonical Red Pill hypergamy claim, then check it.
phrases: A real status tilt treated as an innate, immutable iron law. Women do weight status more — but educational hypergamy has reversed and the provider norm is halving, so it is fading, not hardening.
boundaryConditions: Cross-lever compensation is partial and context-specific; no lever universally purchases another person's desire.
commonMisreadings: A statistical pairing trade-off is not a transactional entitlement.
pressureTests: Does the apparent trade remain after age, network, shared goals, and direct attraction are considered?

entries.title: The Men’s Strike
entries.synopsis: The hypothetical that haunts the manosphere: if men acted in coordination and simply stopped — stopped approaching, asking, initiating — the market would seize, women would feel the absence, and the terms would reset in men’s favor. It is a real question with a measurable spine, because initiation is overwhelmingly male — so withdrawal is, in principle, men’s to attempt.
boundaryConditions: A coordinated refusal and an uncoordinated drift produce similar counts from different causes, and only the second is observed.
commonMisreadings: Men have already coordinated a withdrawal, so women now compete for the few who date.

entries.title: The Abundance Trap
entries.synopsis: The apps’ founding promise was that more options would make finding a partner easier. The trap is that visible abundance changes the chooser: with the whole distribution on screen, evaluation replaces connection, the next profile taxes the current one, and standards drift upward without the underlying market moving at all. Both sexes run this loop — whoever holds the fatter option stack runs it harder.
boundaryConditions: Choice overload survives replication as a conditional effect, so the conditions have to be present before it is invoked.
commonMisreadings: More visible options make a woman choose faster, so abundance helps her find a partner.

sourceLinks.label: Iyengar & Lepper (2000), JPSP
Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd (2010), J. Consumer Research
Chernev, Böckenholt & Goodman (2015), J. Consumer Psychology
D’Angelo & Toma (2017), Media Psychology
Pronk & Denissen (2020), Social Psychological and Personality Science
Pew Research Center (2023)

entries.title: The Operative Frame
entries.synopsis: The claim, drawn from red-pill primary literature, that a culture’s default — what counts as normal, fair, or past arguing about — is not neutrally negotiated between the sexes. It is set by whichever side’s imperative currently holds more reproductive and social leverage.
boundaryConditions: Era- and lever-specific: it describes the post-1960 window in which one contraceptive technology existed asymmetrically, and makes no claim about any individual couple.
The model predicts its own weakening if male-controlled contraception reaches parity.
commonMisreadings: The feminine imperative is a coordinated plan women organise deliberately.
The feminine imperative describes what individual women intend.
The 1960 birth control history and its causal weight are equally settled.
pressureTests: Is the claim the historical asymmetry, which is documented, or the causal weight assigned to it, which is not?

entries.title: The Search Cost
entries.synopsis: Everything above this entry prices people. Nothing above it prices the search. Being in the market costs time, money, attention and a running dose of rejection — and that meter is a live input to how a search ends, alongside everything the rest of this page already models. The claim here is not that budgets explain settling.
boundaryConditions: Burdett and Coles shows only that a taste for similarity is unnecessary; it still requires a shared desirability ranking and mutual acceptance, and yields discrete classes rather than a smooth matching curve.
In that model cheaper search makes people pickier and the classes finer, so lowering search cost is not predicted to blur the bands.
The Pew figures measure user sentiment, not a search budget; no study has instrumented a dating search budget directly.
commonMisreadings: People who settle in dating stopped wanting anyone better than the partner they accepted.
Quitting the dating apps after long searching proves a person had unrealistic standards.

sourceLinks.label: Burdett & Coles (1997), “Marriage and Class,” Quarterly Journal of Economics 112(1):141–168
Pew Research Center (Feb 2020)
Pew Research Center (Feb 2023)
Rosenfeld, Thomas & Hausen (2019), “Disintermediating your friends,” PNAS 116(36):17753–17758
Ofcom, Online Nation 2024
Groundwork Collaborative (Feb 2026), “Swipe Right to Pay” (DiVito, Chokrane & Abdelhamid)

pressureTests: Did this person's standards change, or did the search budget they had left change?

entries.title: The Meeting Channel
entries.synopsis: The Search Cost prices the looking. This entry prices where the looking happens. A meeting channel — the apps, friends, work, school, a bar, a congregation, a hobby — is not a neutral pipe: each channel draws a different pool, runs a different screening order, and bills a different cost.
boundaryConditions: The Ofcom reach decline is UK adults over a single year; reach is not engagement and the UK is not the US.
The channel screening-order comparison is LE's model and no study has tested per-contact outcomes across channels directly.
Commercial burnout percentages from opt-in industry panels are excluded as evidence throughout.
Channel shares describe where existing couples met, which lags where current searchers are searching.
commonMisreadings: Dating apps are the only way anyone meets a partner anymore.
Deleting the dating apps means a man has given up on finding a relationship.
Everyone agrees the dating apps are dead and people all meet in person again.

sourceLinks.label: Rosenfeld, Thomas & Hausen (2019), “Disintermediating your friends,” PNAS 116(36):17753–17758
Pew Research Center (Feb 2023), n = 6,034
Ofcom, Online Nation 2024

pressureTests: Is a channel-share statistic being read as a verdict on a channel's quality?
Does the claim separate the pool a channel draws from the order in which it screens?

entries.title: The Market-Maker’s Cut
entries.synopsis: The parent entry prices the search and 15.1 prices where it happens. This entry prices the fact that the dominant venue is a business, and the business is paid by the search, not the match. A subscription market-maker collects for every month a search continues and collects nothing extra when it succeeds.
phrases: apps profit from keeping you searching
pay to see who liked you
boundaryConditions: The Groundwork report is advocacy work: its documentation of practices is cited, its policy conclusions are not.
The incentive misalignment is structural and one-directional, but whether it dominates feature design over churn pressure is unmeasured.
Opt-in burnout and exhaustion percentages are excluded as evidence, consistent with the Search Cost's standing refusal.
Pricing audits cover specific apps, tiers, countries and years; practices change under litigation and regulation.
commonMisreadings: Dating apps deliberately keep every paying user single forever so the monthly subscription revenue continues.
Paying for the premium tier guarantees matching with a genuinely better class of partner.
Seeing few matches on a dating app proves your own market value is hopelessly low.

sourceLinks.label: Groundwork Collaborative (Feb 2026), “Swipe Right to Pay” (DiVito, Chokrane & Abdelhamid)

pressureTests: Is a feature being read as a market verdict when it is a revenue decision?
Would this claim survive at a venue paid per success instead of per month?

entries.title: The Signal Cost Rule
entries.synopsis: Every profile is a set of claims, and the market has no referee. The working rule this site proposes is neither honesty nor intuition: ask what a claim would have cost the sender if it were false. A physique costs two years and is hard to send falsely at all.
boundaryConditions: The rule ranks the cost of the display, not the price of the object: a rented car is expensive to own and cheap to show.
Signalling theory requires a cost that differs across sender types; proportionality to absolute faking cost is this site's heuristic rather than the theorem.
Only height, weight and age were checked against ground truth; the photograph and relationship-status ordering rests on daters rating their own accuracy.
The ground-truth deception study covers 80 daters in one metropolitan area before swipe apps, so its magnitudes are historical rather than current.
commonMisreadings: Online dating profiles are mostly fabrications, so the person who arrives is a stranger.
In dating, any profile claim that happens to be true is reliable evidence about someone.

sourceLinks.label: Toma, Hancock & Ellison (2008), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 34(8):1023–1036

pressureTests: What would this signal have cost the sender if it were false?

entries.title: The Third-Party Layer
entries.synopsis: Every model on this page treats pairing as a transaction between two people. It is not. Friends and family supply introductions, information, approval, veto and enforcement — and how much approval a relationship has predicts whether it survives. This site has charted the collapse of the venues and the channels where that layer used to operate without ever naming what the layer was doing.
boundaryConditions: The approval evidence is correlational and mostly measures perceived approval reported by one partner, so the causal direction stays open.
A failed replication of the forbidden-love effect removes its support without establishing that opposition corrodes a relationship.
Network power that stabilises a good pairing also enforces a bad one and gates partners on class, caste, race or religion.
commonMisreadings: Family disapproval of a romance makes couples fight harder and bond more tightly together.
Friends and family approving of a romance is what causes couples to stay together.

sourceLinks.label: Sinclair, Hood & Wright (2014), Social Psychology 45(3):170–178
Freedman, Powell, Le & Williams (2019), Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
