entries.title: The Costless Exit
entries.synopsis: The parent entry says it in one line: ghosting is nearly free in a market of strangers and was expensive in a market of neighbours. This entry gives that line its own ledger. When two people share no network, ending contact carries no reputational bill — and the same accounting that makes exit without notice (ghosting) nearly free also makes retention without intent (breadcrumbing: sporadic signals that keep an…
phrases: keeping you on the back burner
boundaryConditions: The ghosting null on life satisfaction, loneliness and helplessness is one cross-sectional Spanish sample's null, not an established absence of harm.
Prevalence figures come from convenience and single-country samples; none is a population estimate.
The shared-network price mechanism is LE's synthesis; the channel comparison it predicts has not been tested directly.
Harassment, stalking and abuse contexts are outside scope and change every calculus in the entry.
commonMisreadings: Getting ghosted after a promising few weeks proves the other person was a heartless narcissist.
Sporadic flirty texts from a match mean the relationship is slowly moving toward real commitment.
Ghosting is harmless etiquette now because every online dater fully expects sudden silent disappearance.

sourceLinks.label: Freedman, Powell, Le & Williams (2019), Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
Navarro, Larrañaga, Yubero & Víllora (2020), IJERPH 17(3):1116

pressureTests: Is a price change in exit conduct being read as a character change in the people?
Which side of the ledger is the claim on: the silent exit, or the option held open?

entries.title: The Support Portfolio
entries.synopsis: The parent entry prices what the network does to a pairing — verification, approval, enforcement. This entry prices what it provides for each partner: emotional support and social connection, held as a portfolio across a partner, friends, family, and community.
phrases: my partner is my best friend
women do the emotional labor of friendship
boundaryConditions: Channel count, support quality, concentration, reciprocity and coordination labor are separate measurements; ordinary partner care satisfies none of the burden mechanism by itself.
The mankeeping scale rests on same-reporter, cross-sectional samples of partnered women in the U.S. and U.K.; it validates a measurement, not a prevalence, a cause, or a general fact about men.
The friendship surveys establish sex differences in specific channels under specific wordings and recall windows; they do not measure a sole channel or show women repairing men's networks.
The peer-network and best-friend-label studies are observational and cross-sectional; relationship quality can drive friendship investment as readily as the reverse.
commonMisreadings: A man's partner naturally becomes his whole support system once the relationship turns serious.
Women lose interest in dating because every man expects one partner to manage his friendships.
More friends always improve a man's relationship because outside support removes pressure from his partner.

sourceLinks.label: Survey Center on American Life (2021), The State of American Friendship
Pew Research Center (2025), Where men and women turn for emotional support
Marabel-Whitburn et al. (2023), JSPR
Pennington et al. (2025), JSPR
Ferrara & Vergara (2024), Psychology of Men & Masculinities
Mancini et al. (2026), Sex Roles

pressureTests: Is one couple's support split being read as a fact about all men?
Does the claim separate having few channels from burdening the one that remains?

entries.title: The Delegation Boundary
entries.synopsis: The parent prices the third parties around a couple; the Costless Exit priced leaving; the Support Portfolio priced the load. This entry prices being represented. Courtship assistance transfers different amounts of agency: feedback leaves the seeker authoring and deciding; co-authorship shares the presentation; substitution lets a proxy present, screen, select, or converse as the seeker.
boundaryConditions: Proofreading, accessibility support, advice, collaborative drafting, undisclosed impersonation, and autonomous selection transfer different decisions and stay distinct.

Platform ranking, seeker-set filters, and shortlists the seeker still reviews remain Meeting Channel mechanics; delegation begins when an assistant applies or invents preferences without the seeker's review.
The evidence base is descriptive and qualitative — no population prevalence, causal harm estimate, success rate, or human-versus-AI ranking exists.
commonMisreadings: A polished profile proves the seeker will hold a first date conversation equally well.
Using any assistant makes every courtship deceptive from the first message onward.
An intermediary who finds a match can guarantee chemistry once the relationship moves offline.

sourceLinks.label: Rochadiat, Tong, Hancock & Stuart-Ulin (2020), “The Outsourcing of Online Dating,” Social Media + Society
CBS News
The Guardian (2025)
AP
The Guardian (2026)

pressureTests: Which decision was transferred here — the wording, the screening, or the seeker's own judgment?
Would the assisted performance survive the first unassisted conversation?

entries.title: The Good-News Rule
entries.synopsis: Relationship quality is not expressed only in how partners handle bad news. What happens when one person brings home a win is another diagnostic channel. Celebrate before you evaluate: let the good event land as a shared gain before adding cautions, comparisons, logistics, or a story about yourself.
boundaryConditions: The cited relationship-quality finding applies inside an existing relationship and does not erase selection-stage constraints.
commonMisreadings: Evidence that relationship experience predicts satisfaction is not proof that attraction, matching, or outside stressors never matter.

sourceLinks.label: Gable et al. (2004), JPSP
Gable, Gonzaga & Strachman (2006), JPSP

pressureTests: Is the source applying an in-relationship association to initial partner selection or treating association as causation?

entries.title: The Sham Relationship
entries.synopsis: A diagnostic lens for relationships that persist without the thing they appear to be about. A sham isn’t merely a bad relationship — it is one whose existence the attraction model can’t account for. It comes in two layers that fail for different reasons and live in different spaces: a hard sham built on motive, and a soft sham built on mismatch or a broken floor.
boundaryConditions: Motive holding a pairing up and an unnamed mismatch are different diagnoses, and they call for different remedies.
commonMisreadings: A couple who stay together without attraction or desire are simply dating badly.

entries.title: The Replaceability Asymmetry
entries.synopsis: What keeps you satisfied with the partner you already have? Not how well they match your stated ideals — across three studies, ideal-partner fulfilment barely moved satisfaction once one other variable entered the model. What moved it was mate value discrepancy, and it moved conditionally: people whose partner outranks them stay satisfied regardless of who else is available.
boundaryConditions: The conditional runs through mate value discrepancy, not preference fulfilment; the weak Study 3 preference effect is unreplicated.
All three samples are partnered heterosexual convenience-panel adults, correlational, from one lab.
commonMisreadings: Higher mate value than your partner leads to dissatisfaction.

sourceLinks.label: Conroy-Beam, Goetz & Buss (2016), Evolution and Human Behavior 37(6):440–448

pressureTests: Does the claimed dissatisfaction survive when better alternatives are scarce? The source indicates it does not.

entries.title: Attention to Alternatives
entries.synopsis: Interdependence theory named the quantity decades ago: a comparison level for alternatives — your running estimate of how you’d do if you left. The addition here is treating attention to that comparison as its own variable: how much a person notices, seeks out and gets distracted by other candidates.
boundaryConditions: The source is an unpublished draft chapter from a single research programme with small samples and no located independent replication.
The breakup-prediction result is one undergraduate sample over eight weeks and says nothing about established relationships.
commonMisreadings: Noticing that a stranger is attractive puts a relationship at risk.

sourceLinks.label: Miller (2007), 10th Sydney Symposium of Social Psychology chapter

pressureTests: Is the attentiveness chronic and trait-like, or situational and downstream of existing dissatisfaction?

entries.title: Mate Retention Intensity
entries.synopsis: Satisfaction is an input to behaviour, not just a mood. When mate value discrepancies pushed satisfaction up or down, that change predicted how much retention behaviour people reported deploying — the range of tactics from compliments and attention through vigilance and guarding.
boundaryConditions: The satisfaction and trust pathways run in opposite directions in the same dataset; collapsing them into one quality-drives-effort story erases the finding.
One correlational path model on a convenience sample, with no located replication of the mediation.
commonMisreadings: More retention behaviour means a more committed or healthier relationship.

sourceLinks.label: Conroy-Beam, Goetz & Buss (2016), Evolution and Human Behavior 37(6):440–448

pressureTests: Is the retention behaviour in question devotion or control? The score alone cannot tell you.

entries.title: The Desire-Maintenance Split
entries.synopsis: “Desire fades with familiarity” is said as one claim. It is three, and they are not equally supported. (a) Desire, sexual satisfaction and frequency decline over relationship duration — real prospective support, plus separate cross-sectional support that cannot rule out age or cohort.
boundaryConditions: The prospective leg covers newlyweds in the first four to five years only; nothing here speaks to decades-long relationships.
The cross-sectional leg cannot separate relationship duration from age or cohort, by its own authors' statement.
commonMisreadings: Anxious attachment suppresses sexual desire.
Desire declines with familiarity, and that is one settled finding.
Attraction fades once a couple gets comfortable, so a long relationship needs constant novelty to stay alive.

sourceLinks.label: McNulty, Wenner & Fisher (2016), Archives of Sexual Behavior 45(1):85–97
van Lankveld, Dewitte, Verboon & van Hooren (2021), Frontiers in Psychology 12

pressureTests: Which of the three sub-claims is being asserted, and does the citation offered actually test that one?

entries.title: The Desire-State Split
entries.synopsis: Desire has more than one sequence. Spontaneous desire arrives before an erotic context; responsive desire can emerge after willingness, attention and rewarding stimulation have already begun. That is a difference in timing, not a diagnosis of the lower-desire partner. And when partners want sex at different levels, the discrepancy belongs to the pair: neither person carries it alone.
boundaryConditions: Responsive desire begins from genuine willingness and must leave room to stop; it is not consent created by persistence.
Basson's response cycle centres women, and the stress diary centres couples coping with sexual interest/arousal disorder; neither licenses a universal sequence or prevalence claim.
Desire discrepancy predicts distress in observational dyadic data; the lower-desire partner is not thereby identified as its cause.
commonMisreadings: Responsive desire means a reluctant partner should agree to sex and wait for desire to appear.
The lower-desire partner causes a couple's desire discrepancy and needs to be fixed.

sourceLinks.label: Basson (2002), Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy 28(sup1):17–28
Jodouin, Rosen, Merwin & Bergeron (2021), Archives of Sexual Behavior 50(8):3637–3649
Girouard et al. (2025), International Journal of Clinical and Health Psychology 25(2):100582

pressureTests: Is there present willingness and a live option to stop, or is responsive desire being used to launder pressure?
Is the claim about one person's level of desire or the distance between two partners' levels?

entries.title: The Ownership Load
entries.synopsis: Household work has two ledgers: execution and ownership. Doing a task records the visible minutes. Owning it means anticipating the need, deciding the standard and timing, arranging the work, remembering it and checking that it is complete. If one partner must still notice, assign and audit, the hands may have changed while the cognitive load did not.
boundaryConditions: The supporting studies are self-report and non-experimental, so unequal ownership is associated with satisfaction and desire rather than proven to cause either.
The samples are concentrated in different-gender parents and heterosexual cohabitors; the mechanism is not yet population-universal.
The 2026 dyadic study is published in an unedited early-access version and may change during final production.
Fairness and equality are not synonyms: a deliberately uneven arrangement can be experienced as fair when ownership is visible and agreed.
commonMisreadings: A partner who completes assigned chores owns an equal share of the household work.
Every household task must be divided exactly fifty-fifty for a relationship to be fair.

sourceLinks.label: Petts, Carlson & Wong (2025), “Cognitive Housework and Parents’ Relationship Satisfaction,” Journal of Marriage and Family
Coundouris & Henry (2026), Scientific Reports
Harris, Gormezano & van Anders (2022), Archives of Sexual Behavior 51(8):3847–3870

pressureTests: Who notices, decides, remembers and checks the task when nobody sends a reminder?

entries.title: The Satisfaction Flywheel
entries.synopsis: The best-designed study in this group: eight waves across the first four to five years of 207 marriages. Sexual satisfaction predicts changes in relationship satisfaction, and relationship satisfaction predicts changes in sexual satisfaction, at roughly equal strength — a real two-way loop, not one domain quietly driving the other. Frequency of sex sits inside the same loop.
boundaryConditions: Demonstrated in newlywed couples in the first four to five years; the one located longer-marriage comparison found only one of the two directions.
The partner effects are exploratory secondary analyses, not the study's confirmatory hypotheses.
commonMisreadings: Good sex causes a good relationship.

sourceLinks.label: McNulty, Wenner & Fisher (2016), Archives of Sexual Behavior 45(1):85–97

pressureTests: Is the claimed direction the only one tested, or has the reverse path been modelled in the same data?

entries.title: The Agreement Surface
entries.synopsis: A relationship label names a category, not its operating contract. “Monogamous,” “open,” and “polyamorous” leave material questions unanswered: what counts as sex or romance, what is disclosed and when, whether any bond has priority, how time and money are allocated, which health practices apply, and how an agreement can be revised.
boundaryConditions: A relationship label is useful shorthand but does not specify every boundary concerning sex, romance, disclosure, hierarchy, time, resources, health or revision.
Changed boundaries apply prospectively and require genuine freedom to decline; they do not retroactively authorize a breach.
Agreement can still be coerced, and the framework does not require advance authorization for every ordinary act.
The satisfaction meta-analysis compares self-selected relationship structures and does not establish equivalence in causality, durability, coordination cost, parenting or health outcomes.
commonMisreadings: Agreeing to an open or monogamous relationship gives blanket consent to every act normally associated with that label.
Monogamy is intrinsically more satisfying than consensual non-monogamy.
If a partner dislikes an act afterward, that retroactively makes the act a boundary violation.

sourceLinks.label: Anderson et al. (2025), Journal of Sex Research
Stewart, Stults & Ristuccia (2021), Archives of Sexual Behavior
Mogilski et al. (2026)

pressureTests: Which actual agreement was mutually legible before the act, and is a category label being substituted for it?
Is a structural comparison being turned into a claim about what causes satisfaction?

entries.title: The Financial Architecture Split
entries.synopsis: A couple’s account topology and its financial fidelity are separate variables. Joint, separate and hybrid accounts describe where money sits. Fidelity describes whether conduct stays inside the couple’s disclosed and accepted financial rules. Separate accounts can be transparent and agreed; a joint account can coexist with hidden debt, income, spending or transfers.
boundaryConditions: The pooling trial sampled willing, mostly White, different-sex engaged or newlywed couples entering first marriages; it does not generalize to every couple or relationship stage.
Differential attrition was substantial, especially in the assigned-joint condition, and the outcome was self-reported relationship quality.
Separate, joint and hybrid accounts are topologies rather than fidelity grades; disclosure and compliance with the couple's actual agreement are separate variables.
Full access can be unsafe under coercive control, financial abuse, addiction, hidden debt or other conditions the pooling trial was not designed to evaluate.
commonMisreadings: Separate accounts are financial infidelity.
A randomized newlywed study proves every committed couple should merge all money.
Joint accounts prevent hidden financial behavior.

sourceLinks.label: Olson, Rick, Small & Finkel (2023), “Common Cents,” Journal of Consumer Research 50(4):704–721
Garbinsky et al. (2020), “Love, Lies, and Money,” Journal of Consumer Research 47(1):1–24

pressureTests: Is the claim measuring where money sits, or whether conduct was intentionally concealed outside an agreed rule?
Would greater access increase safety and trust in this couple, or increase exposure to coercion or loss?

entries.title: Co-Transition
entries.synopsis: When one partner undertakes a gender transition, the identity and body belong to that person; the relationship nevertheless changes for everyone inside it. A partner may have to revisit attraction, orientation language, intimacy, public presentation, family roles and the future they thought they had.
phrases: public and private intimacy after transition
boundaryConditions: The transitioning partner alone owns their gender identity, body and medical care; relationship impact does not grant a partner veto power over transition.
The other partner retains autonomy over consent, attraction and their own orientation label; acknowledging that process does not require the relationship to continue.
The evidence is qualitative, based on small convenience samples, and often selected couples that stayed together; it cannot estimate survival rates or identify a causal recipe.
This framework is specific to gender transition and should not be generalized to every major life change without evidence.
commonMisreadings: If love is real, attraction, orientation labels and relationship terms should remain unchanged through a partner's gender transition.
Calling the process co-transition gives both partners equal authority over the transitioning person's identity or care.
Couples who communicate well are expected to stay together after transition.

sourceLinks.label: Van Acker et al. (2023), Healthcare 11(11):1535
Ostrander (2025), International Journal of Transgender Health

pressureTests: Which part belongs to individual self-determination, and which part can the couple legitimately decide together?
Is a survivor-selected qualitative finding being converted into a promise of relationship survival?

entries.title: The Care Role Split
entries.synopsis: Chronic illness can place two relationships inside one dyad: partners with a shared life, and caregiver with care receiver. The care role can organize medication, mobility, appointments, money and daily tasks while the couple role still carries reciprocity, privacy, desire, companionship and mutual choice.
phrases: couple relationship and chronic illness care relationship
caregiving partner mourns intimacy after illness
boundaryConditions: The care role and the couple role can overlap without one fully replacing the other; the framework identifies a tension rather than an inevitable outcome.
The qualitative study contains 17 spouses from ten older heterosexual German couples who remained together, so it maps a process but cannot estimate prevalence or survival.

The three-wave dyadic study is observational, convenience-recruited and substantially attrited; within-person covariation does not establish that shared appraisal, communication or coping causes better relationship outcomes.
Shared appraisal means coordinating around an illness that affects both partners; it does not transfer authority over the patient's body, treatment or consent to the caregiver.
commonMisreadings: A loving partner should absorb every caregiving duty while preserving the relationship unchanged.
One partner's chronic illness belongs outside the relationship's shared decisions.
When caregiving begins, devotion naturally preserves equal roles and sexual intimacy.

sourceLinks.label: Niedling & Hämel (2023), Frontiers in Public Health 11:1117786
Shrout, Weigel & Laurenceau (2024), Journal of Family Psychology 38(1):136–148

pressureTests: Is caregiving being treated as proof that the couple relationship remains unchanged, or measured as a second role that can crowd it out?
Does shared illness appraisal mean coordinated coping, or has it been inflated into shared authority over the patient's body and treatment?

entries.title: The Constraint–Dedication Split
entries.synopsis: A relationship can continue because the people in it want it to continue, because leaving has become costly or difficult, or because both are true. Commitment research calls the first ledger dedication: desire for a future together, couple identity and willingness to prioritize the bond.
phrases: desire to stay and cost of leaving
boundaryConditions: Dedication and constraint are separate ledgers that can rise, fall or diverge; persistence alone does not reveal which ledger is active.
The supporting samples concern U.S. different-sex cohabiting relationships, mostly among adults ages 18–35, and do not establish a population-universal transition pattern.
Both studies are observational and self-report; within-person change around a move does not show that cohabitation causes later relationship quality, breakup or divorce.
The dyadic study measured perceived likelihood of dissolution and relationship adjustment over eight months rather than observed breakup or marriage outcomes.
Constraints are neither uniformly protective nor uniformly harmful; leases, shared assets, children and dependency have different meanings under mutual dedication, ambivalence, coercion and abuse.
commonMisreadings: A continuing relationship always proves that both partners feel equally dedicated.
Sharing a lease naturally turns practical constraint into mutual relationship devotion.
A costly breakup means each partner freely wants the relationship to continue.

sourceLinks.label: Rhoades, Stanley & Markman (2012), Journal of Family Issues 33(3):369–390
Rhoades, Stanley & Markman (2012), Journal of Family Psychology 26(3):348–358

pressureTests: Is persistence being treated as evidence of desire even though leaving carries material, social or perceived costs?
Did the transition change dedication, constraints or both, and were those constructs measured separately?
Would the same constraint protect a valued investment here, or make an unwanted or unsafe relationship harder to exit?

entries.title: The Attention Boundary
entries.synopsis: Technoference is technology use that interrupts a shared conversation or activity; partner phubbing is the phone-specific case in which a partner experiences the device as receiving attention that the interaction was supposed to receive. The relationship variable is not device ownership or total screen minutes.
phrases: phone interrupts a conversation with a partner
boundaryConditions: Technoference is an interruption of expected shared attention, not a synonym for device ownership, total device minutes or every visible phone.
The meta-analytic associations are predominantly cross-sectional and heterogeneous, so relationship distress may increase phubbing as well as follow it.
The daily-diary comparison narrows stable person differences but remains contemporaneous self-report in mostly White, different-sex parents of young children.
The controlled evidence concerns brief conversations with strangers and immediate ostracism, politeness, attentiveness and trust-game outcomes rather than sustained romantic satisfaction.
Emergency, work, caregiving, accessibility, navigation, translation and jointly integrated device use can carry different meanings from unexplained disengagement.
An attention boundary must preserve privacy, autonomy and reasonable unavailability; it does not authorize device surveillance, password demands or continuous access to a partner.
commonMisreadings: A partner checking a phone always means the relationship matters less than the device.
Every shared moment requires both partners to keep every device completely out of sight.
Matching device-use totals guarantee that both partners receive equal attention during conversations.

sourceLinks.label: Ni, Ahrari, Zaremohzzabieh, Zarean & Roslan (2025), Frontiers in Psychology 16:1561159
McDaniel & Drouin (2019), Computers in Human Behavior 99
Knausenberger, Giesen-Leuchter & Echterhoff (2022), Frontiers in Psychology 13:883901

pressureTests: Did device use actually displace attention the partners expected to share, or is harm being inferred from minutes or presence alone?
Was the use unexplained disengagement, a communicated necessity, or technology integrated into the couple’s shared interaction?
Do the partners disagree about an attention boundary, and can they renegotiate it without surveillance or continuous-availability demands?

entries.title: The Repair Sequence
entries.synopsis: After harm, four different states are often compressed into “forgive and move on.” The person who caused the harm can acknowledge it, make proportionate amends, and change future conduct. The injured partner can become less retaliatory or avoidant, which forgiveness research treats as a motivational shift. Whether the pair restores trust, access or the relationship is a further decision.
phrases: acknowledge relationship harm and make amends
apologies cause forgiveness through relationship value
boundaryConditions: The four-state sequence is an LE synthesis; no source measured acknowledgement, amends, changed conduct, forgiveness and reconciliation together or established one required order.
The romantic evidence is observational self-report from unusually young, mostly female samples and does not show that forgiveness causes effort, satisfaction or retention.
The randomized apology experiment bundled verbal apology with a one-dollar transfer after a modest online insult between novel strangers.
The apology-versus-restitution experiment used repeated hypothetical burglary imagery in 61 undergraduates and did not observe partner conduct, relationship repair or health outcomes.
Forgiveness describes a motivational shift away from revenge and avoidance; it does not itself restore trust, access, contact or a relationship.
Under coercion, abuse, stalking, repeated harm or credible danger, safety and exit outrank apology, amends, forgiveness and completion of any repair sequence.
commonMisreadings: A sincere apology automatically restores trust and completes repair between romantic partners.
Forgiving a partner requires reopening the relationship and resuming the previous level of access.
Remaining together proves both partners completed accountability, forgiveness, trust, and reconciliation.

sourceLinks.label: Braithwaite, Selby & Fincham (2011), Journal of Family Psychology 25(4):551–559
Forster et al. (2021), Scientific Reports 11:13107
Witvliet et al. (2020), Frontiers in Psychology 11:284

pressureTests: What did the person who caused harm acknowledge, restore and change in future conduct, apart from the apology wording?
Is the injured partner's forgiveness being treated as consent to resume contact, trust or the relationship?
Does the evidence measure apology, restitution, behavior change, forgiveness or reconciliation, and which links remain untested?

entries.title: The Stress Transmission Split
entries.synopsis: External stress can enter a relationship by different routes. Spillover carries one person’s load from work, health, money or another role into that person’s behavior at home. Crossover is the cross-partner path: one person’s load changes the other person’s stress or relationship experience. Shared exposure means both partners face the same event or are strained at once.
phrases: stress crosses from work into relationship conflict
partner workload predicts marital satisfaction decline
external role strain and marital satisfaction
failure to recover from daily stress
spillover crossover and shared stress exposure
boundaryConditions: The three-route split is an LE synthesis; no source measured spillover, crossover, shared exposure, recovery and support matching in one design.
The paired daily-diary study contains 114 long-married urban U.S. parents of adolescents and cannot order stress and conflict within the same day.
Average next-day paths were null in the daily study; persistence appeared only in high-aggression couples and one high family-of-origin-aggression subgroup.
The workload study follows 172 different-sex first-marriage newlyweds recruited from 1993-1994 Los Angeles licenses; six-month lagged associations do not establish causation or mechanism.
The support study contains 101 mostly White, satisfied, low-strain Iowa newlywed couples; its asymmetric and counterintuitive moderation paths require replication and are not gender laws.
Support adequacy compares the recipient's desired frequency with perceived provision; it does not establish support quality, reciprocity, safety or a universal buffering effect.
External stress can explain a shift while responsibility for contempt, coercion, aggression, boundary violations and unrepaired harm remains intact.
commonMisreadings: A stressful workday proves both romantic partners share a permanently incompatible relationship.
One partner's overload always damages both partners equally across every relationship stage.
More support automatically buffers every partner from external stress inside the relationship.

sourceLinks.label: Timmons, Arbel & Margolin (2017), Journal of Family Psychology 31(1):93–104
Neff & Karney (2017), Journal of Family Psychology 31(6):780–790
Brock & Lawrence (2008), Journal of Family Psychology 22(1):11–20

pressureTests: Where did the strain originate, which person carried or absorbed it, and over what recovery window?
Did both partners face one shared stressor, or did load spill across a domain or cross between partners?
Was support matched to the recipient's needs, and which measured path did it actually moderate?

entries.title: The Sleep-Interaction Loop
entries.synopsis: Sleep and relationship functioning can move in either direction, but the arrows are not interchangeable. A night can change one person’s next-day affect or interaction; a daytime interaction can change that person’s or the partner’s sleep; and shared timing can be a third variable rather than a quality score. Name the direction, person, sleep measure and time scale before interpreting the loop.
aliases: nightly sleep and next-day couple conflict
sleep as a dyadic relationship process
phrases: poor sleep predicts negative partner interaction
sleep onset concordance and partner interaction
total sleep deprivation before couple conflict
spousal support predicts partner sleep quality
sleep efficiency actor and partner effects
acute sleep loss reduces positive affect
boundaryConditions: The four-label rule is an LE synthesis; no source jointly estimates direction, actor and partner paths, multiple sleep measures and acute-to-multiyear time scales in a single design.
The seven-day study includes 29 mostly young, happy, different-sex co-sleeping couples; its sex-specific diary and actigraphy paths are preliminary and observational.

The randomized study assigned 30 unusually satisfied young couples to total deprivation or normal sleep, and found affect and cortisol effects while agreement, discussion satisfaction, conflict severity, negative affect and emotion recognition remained null.
Total sleep deprivation in a supervised laboratory is not ordinary short sleep, shift work, infant waking, insomnia or a diagnosed sleep disorder.
The eight-year age-50-plus English result is captured here only as an abstract; coefficient detail, attrition, missing-data handling and robustness specifications were not audited.
Sleep efficiency, subjective sleep quality, insomnia symptoms, onset concordance and offset concordance are separate measures and must not be substituted for one another.
Fatigue can be a temporary sleep-linked state rather than evidence of durable incompatibility; responsibility for aggression, coercion, contempt, repair, medical care and safety remains intact.

Matching bedtimes always improves every couple's intimacy and prevents future relationship conflict.
A sleep-deprived discussion reveals each partner's normal conflict skills inside the relationship.

entries.title: The Substitution Layer
entries.synopsis: Exit from the dating market is not exit to nothing. People who withdraw move toward substitute goods — gaming, pornography, parasocial media, and now synthetic companionship — which deliver a fraction of the reward at a small fraction of the cost, with the rejection risk removed.
boundaryConditions: The leisure-luxury result covers labour supply among young men under an identifying assumption rather than an instrument, contains no dating outcome, and the extension to dating is an inference.
Substitution and complementarity are observationally identical in cross-section, so the causal direction is unavailable in either direction.
How long a withdrawal lasts is itself an unmeasured dating outcome, so duration is this layer's hypothesis rather than its finding.
commonMisreadings: Men stopped dating because video games and pornography are more enjoyable than real relationships.
Cheap substitutes only fill time that a failed dating market had already emptied out.

entries.title: The Stock–Flow Error
entries.synopsis: A stock counts who is in a state right now. A flow counts who enters or leaves it over time. Almost every famous number in this subject is a stock being read as a flow — a photograph of one moment presented as the shape of a life. It is the most productive error in the discourse, and this site is not exempt from it.
phrases: half of marriages end in divorce
boundaryConditions: Period and cohort measures answer different questions, and the direction of a snapshot bias follows composition drift rather than a fixed rule.
Length-biased sampling explains the dating-app case, while the divorce ratio is a malformed statistic built on non-overlapping denominators.
commonMisreadings: Half of all marriages end in divorce, so a wedding today carries roughly even odds.
A quarter of young adults today will stay unmarried for the whole of their lives.
The top twenty percent of men receive eighty percent of the likes on dating apps.

entries.title: The Gray Divergence
entries.synopsis: The parent entry teaches the reading discipline: ask what “the divorce rate” is a rate of. This entry reports what the composition underneath it actually did. Since 1990 the aggregate U.S. divorce rate has fallen — and that fall is a composite of two opposite-moving components: divorce among adults past fifty roughly doubled while divorce among the young married fell by a fifth.

entries.title: Residual Pool Dynamics
entries.synopsis: A two-part population model. Every model above this entry draws candidates from a pool it treats as fixed — an urn whose contents do not change while you are reaching into it. They do change. People pair off and leave, others divorce and return, and the pool’s composition shifts for reasons that have nothing to do with anyone still in it.
phrases: who is still single at forty
boundaryConditions: A composition effect on quality requires exit to be ordered on a shared index, and romantic evaluation becomes largely dyad-specific once people are acquainted.
The unpartnered population mixes never-married with divorced and widowed people, so it behaves as a mixture rather than a sealed residue.
commonMisreadings: Everyone still single after forty was passed over because the better partners were selected first.
The dating pool gets worse with age because desirable people pair off and leave it behind.

entries.title: The Clearing Order
entries.synopsis: People do not leave the market at random, and if they leave in an order then time in the market is not neutral. The discourse assumes it knows the order: the most desirable pair off first, so the pool thins from the top and waiting is expensive. The order is real. It is not that one, and for the first decade it runs backwards.

entries.title: The Supply-and-Demand Rule
entries.synopsis: When a defined dating pool contains more eligible, searching people on one side than the other, the scarcer side can be more selective and the more numerous side must compete harder. The imbalance changes bargaining conditions; it does not change human worth.
commonMisreadings: More single men than women in a city means the average guy is priced out of dating entirely.

entries.title: The Effective Sex Ratio
entries.synopsis: A two-part market measure. When one side of a market is scarcer, it can hold out for more and the abundant side concedes more — and nobody in the market chose any of it. Two identical people in two markets face different prices. This site has asserted that for years in a single sentence, sourced to a single book, tagged Mixed. The claim is real and better evidenced than we have been giving it credit for.
boundaryConditions: Sex-ratio effects are established by instrumented shocks; a correlation between a place’s ratio and its outcomes is unreliable and has been shown to produce significant results on randomly chosen variables.
The measured outcomes are marriage rates, spouse class, labour supply and fertility, so claims about dating etiquette or what either sex can demand have no support in this literature.
commonMisreadings: A city with more single men gives every woman living there substantially better romantic bargaining power.

entries.title: The Counting Correction
entries.synopsis: “There are more single men than single women” sounds like a headcount, and headcounts sound like facts. Underneath it sit two choices — which pool you count, and whether you count people who are actually in the market — and each one is large enough on its own to reverse the answer. Anyone quoting the single sex ratio without naming both is quoting a decision, not a measurement.
boundaryConditions: The adjustment rests on self-reported search intent, measured on a narrower definition of single than the census uses and pooled across a fifty-year age span.
Crude sex ratios have once been shown to outpredict refined availability ratios, so refining a pool carries its own risk of predicting worse.
commonMisreadings: Counting every unmarried adult gives the real ratio of men to women in a market.
Older single women face a market crowded with women and starved of available men.

entries.title: The Ideological Filter
entries.synopsis: Part 2 corrected the count for who is actually searching. This part corrects it for what the searchers will accept, because a screen applied before anything else is evaluated works exactly like a smaller pool. Political identity is the newest screen large enough to move the arithmetic: young men and women have drifted apart politically, part of the market now filters on politics first, and the filter is applied at…
phrases: shared political views in a partner
political divide between young men and women
boundaryConditions: Gallup measures self-reported ideological identification, not party registration and not dating behaviour.
The filter rates come from a single IFS/YouGov survey of US 18-29 year olds read through a think-tank write-up.

entries.title: The Local Market
entries.synopsis: Nobody participates in “the dating market.” People participate in a metro, a campus, a workplace, a congregation — and those differ from each other far more than the national average differs from year to year. National statistics describe nobody’s actual market. This entry makes three claims that do not share a tier, and the one people most want to act on is the one that fails.
boundaryConditions: Metro-level ratios average over age, ethnicity and education submarkets whose own ratios differ widely from the city figure.
The migration result is a correlated-random-effects correction rather than an instrument, and it describes an average person rather than every person.
commonMisreadings: Moving to a city with a better sex ratio measurably improves a person’s chances of marrying.
National dating statistics describe the market that an individual actually competes in.

entries.title: The Border Bundle
entries.synopsis: The parent entry prices the container you compete in. This one prices what happens when a pairing joins two containers: a cross-border relationship can bundle itself with mobility, legal status, language, employment, family separation, and access to another social network — resources that expand the migrating partner’s options and create leverage inside the relationship at the same time.
boundaryConditions: Dating abroad, nationality difference, and intercultural attraction alone do not establish the bundle; at least one mobility, legal-status, language, employment, network, or relocation channel must enter the pairing's bargaining conditions.
The 40%/20% legal-status estimates are bounded to the Italian EU-enlargement natural experiment and are not universal effect sizes.
The South Korean well-being result is observational and context-bound, and mixed economic, citizenship, family, and affection-driven motives neither prove fraud nor erase attachment.
commonMisreadings: A foreign partner always gains equal leverage once the relationship crosses a national border.
International matchmaking proves each partner values romance above migration, money, and citizenship.
A larger global pool gives every couple better options than either local market.

entries.title: The Saturation Rule
entries.synopsis: The intuition is that advice which works is advice that has not spread yet — a tactic’s edge dies as everyone adopts it. The decay is real and it is large. The reason is not the one everybody gives. Edges do not die because the knowledge got out.
boundaryConditions: The measured decay comes from asset and matching markets; no study has ever tested whether a dating tactic loses effectiveness as it spreads.
Apparent decay must first beat two explanations that involve no diffusion at all: an overstated original estimate, and a programme being tried on its easiest targets first.
commonMisreadings: A dating tactic stops working as soon as enough people have heard about it.
Improving yourself keeps its full value even when everyone else improves by the same amount.

entries.title: The Survivorship Channel
entries.synopsis: Dating advice is produced almost entirely by people selected for having succeeded, or for being able to sell — and the part of the genre that actually sells has essentially never been tested. Not tested and failed. Tested at all. The failures do exist, and the sharper finding of this entry is where they go: they survive inside the literature and get stripped out on the way to you.
boundaryConditions: The charge against popular dating advice is that it is unmeasured rather than disproved, and several widely mocked recommendations are supported by the best randomised evidence available.
Some failures are published rather than hidden, and the loss happens between the study and the advice rather than inside the literature.
commonMisreadings: A dating tactic with a plausible mechanism and confident advocates has been shown to work.

entries.title: The Virality Filter
entries.synopsis: Every claim you hold about dating arrived through a filter, and the filter was not selecting for accuracy. It selected for novelty, for out-group targeting, for negative framing, and above all for confidence. The comfortable version of this entry blames an algorithm. The evidence says the filter is people — which includes you, and includes us.
boundaryConditions: The measured spread advantage for falsehood applies within fact-checked contested rumours, and amounts to a likelihood ratio near 1.7, which flips almost no prior beliefs.
The causal agent identified by the evidence is human sharing preference rather than algorithmic ranking, and one large randomised test found that removing the ranking made information diets worse.
commonMisreadings: A dating claim that goes viral online is for that reason likely to be inaccurate.

entries.title: The Surplus
entries.synopsis: A pairing exists because it produces something neither person could produce alone. How big that something is and how it gets divided are two different questions — and nearly every argument about relationships answers the second while borrowing the authority of the first. “What do men get out of marriage” is a split question wearing a size question’s clothes.

two can live cheaper than one
she brings nothing to the table
boundaryConditions: The size of a pairing’s surplus is separately identified from its division, and only the size half replicates across studies.

The largest measured component is insurance through family labour supply, which is asymmetric by earnings weight rather than equal across partners.
commonMisreadings: Marriage is a straightforwardly bad deal for men and a good one for women.
Specialisation by comparative advantage is the established reason marriage produces gains.
A lasting marriage is worth about a hundred thousand dollars a year to a person.

entries.title: The Outside Option

entries.title: The Commitment Problem
entries.synopsis: Commitment is almost always discussed as a feeling — how much someone means it. Is the commitment located in an asset or an option, or only in how someone feels?

entries.title: The Wall
entries.synopsis: The most-cited claim about women and age: that a woman’s market value falls off a cliff around 30. We take the canonical version at face value, then check it — same two-part format as the Charm Ceiling and the Status Trade above. The short version: there is a real curve here, but it is a slope, not a cliff — and it measures the one thing that decides least.
boundaryConditions: LE treats the pattern as a gradual, outcome-specific slope shaped by fertility plans, stranger attention, cohort, and market—not a universal cliff.
commonMisreadings: Changes in average attention or fertility are not proof of zero pairing prospects, lost human worth, or an exact birthday cutoff.
pressureTests: Which outcome is changing—fertility, app attention, partner age, marriage probability, or satisfaction—and how continuous is the change?

entries.title: Body Count & Pair-Bonding
entries.synopsis: The Red Pill claim that a high “body count” — a woman’s number of prior sexual partners — wears out her ability to bond, predicting cheating and divorce. Same two-part format as the dualities above. The short version: the correlation is real but confounded, the dose-response is the wrong shape, and the biology underneath it is invented.
phrases: how many people she's slept with
boundaryConditions: A group-level association cannot establish an individual's character, cause, future behavior, or relationship outcome.
commonMisreadings: A close-call prior or correlational risk marker should not be presented as certainty or a gender-wide moral verdict.
pressureTests: Does the evidence distinguish causation from selection effects, reporting bias, religiosity, age, and relationship history?

entries.title: The Bone Pill
entries.synopsis: The Black Pill / looksmaxxing claim — popularised by face-analysis channels like QOVES and the PSL forums — that attraction is mostly the face, the face is mostly bone (canthal tilt, jaw, maxilla, cheekbones), and your bone-score is therefore a fixed verdict on your romantic life. Same two-part format as the dualities above.
boundaryConditions: Agreement at first glance is high and it dissolves with acquaintance, so the two measurements disagree by design.
commonMisreadings: Bone structure settles attraction permanently, so a man's skeleton decides whether women will date him.

entries.title: The Courtship Buffer
entries.synopsis: Alcohol sits underneath a great deal of early courtship, and the discourse treats its removal as a reveal: meet without it and you finally see what a person is really like. The measured effects are real, small, and land on different rungs of the ladder above. Naming the rung, and naming the state actually observed, is the whole discipline here.
phrases: offering a drink at a bar
boundaryConditions: The group experiment measured how three unacquainted people behaved together, which is not pair-specific attraction, mutual interest, consent or relationship formation.
The perception synthesis covers ratings of how attractive others look, its overall estimate is small, and its same-sex estimate did not reach significance.
The diary result is observational and cannot identify who made the offer, with whom sex occurred, or the timing, so it points at a social cue rather than a dose.
A state-dependent social experience can be genuine in that state, and removing the state does not expose a fixed authentic self.
Sobriety can be a substantive personal value rather than an interaction variable, and that screen is a separate question from the acute mechanism.
Venue supply and the disappearance of third places stay outside this entry.
The experiments cover young adult social drinkers at controlled doses and say nothing about recovery populations or alcohol-use disorder.
commonMisreadings: Alcohol reveals courtship chemistry by showing how easily two people bond and approach each other.
A sober encounter exposes a partner's authentic personality and lasting character.
Liquid courage makes courtship conversation easier and a person's intentions seem clearer.

sourceLinks.label: Sayette et al. (2012), “Alcohol and Group Formation,” Psychological Science 23(8):869–878
Bowdring & Sayette (2018), Addiction 113(9):1585–1597
Hamilton, Armeli & Tennen (2022), Journal of American College Health

pressureTests: Which rung is this evidence on: a rating, a group behaviour, an attempted approach, or an outcome?

entries.title: The Ambiguity Tax
entries.synopsis: The gate above holds that interaction, and only interaction, selects people in. Running that interaction has a price, and the price is interpretive: hints have to be caught, tone has to be weighed, a soft answer has to be graded, and an outcome has to be classified as a refusal or as nothing much. This site already treats courtship vagueness as a tactic and as a shield.
boundaryConditions: The diffusion-chain result is a laboratory task among strangers, so it supports a pairing-level account of communication difficulty and predicts nothing about courtship outcomes.
The camouflaging and rejection-sensitivity legs are qualitative accounts, one of them from five people in two focus groups, so they carry no prevalence figure and no magnitude estimate.
A high bill is a property of a channel and a pairing rather than a score attached to one participant, and the same person can find one venue unreadable and another easy.
Making a courtship protocol fully explicit relocates the cost onto whoever must refuse in plain words; it does not remove it.
Neurodivergent courtship is the case that makes the distribution visible, not the only place the cost falls.
commonMisreadings: Someone who misses a flirting hint is simply worse at drawing a partner in.
Direct plain communication between two people removes the difficulty from early courtship signalling.
A person who hides their natural reactions while flirting will build a stronger connection.

sourceLinks.label: Crompton, Ropar, Evans-Williams, Flynn & Fletcher-Watson (2020), Autism 24(7):1704–1712
Hull, Petrides, Allison, Smith, Baron-Cohen, Lai & Mandy (2017), Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 47(8):2519–2534
Rowney-Smith, Sutton, Quadt & Eccles (2026), PLoS One 21(1):e0314669

pressureTests: Is this difficulty being priced to one participant, or to the channel and the pairing that produced it?

entries.title: The Typology Shortcut
entries.synopsis: A folk type — a star sign, a four-letter code, a love language — begins as vocabulary and becomes an instrument the moment it is used to rank or delete somebody. The gate above reserves positive compatibility for real interaction. This entry asks the prior question: was the mismatch a type implies ever actually known, or only inferred from the category?
boundaryConditions: A folk type can work as an icebreaker, a vocabulary, an identity or a ritual without functioning as a compatibility score.
A stated preference can carry information even when the category system containing it lacks predictive validity, and responding to an expressed need differs from matching labels.
A label can surface a genuine value mismatch about how much astrology or personality systems matter, and that mismatch belongs to the expressed value rather than to the chart.
The love-language matching result is a conference abstract whose methods are unpublished, and its sample is established partners in later life rather than forming pairs.
The Myers-Briggs review dates from 1993, evaluates the instrument in general rather than any application to courtship, and does not speak to later revisions.
A profile filter changes who receives consideration and does not establish that the excluded category would have produced a worse interaction.
Pop-clinical labels such as attachment, trauma, narcissism and therapy-speak stay with the Diagnostic Turn.
commonMisreadings: Matching folk types predicts easier communication and lasting harmony for prospective partners.
An incompatible zodiac sign reveals how a partner will behave after commitment.
A common love language label forecasts pair compatibility better than steady responsiveness does.

sourceLinks.label: Chopik et al. (2025), Innovation in Aging 9(Suppl 1):1395
Mostova, Stolarski & Matthews (2022), PLOS ONE 17(6):e0269429
Pittenger (1993), “The Utility of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator,” Review of Educational Research 63(4):467–488

pressureTests: What person-level claim is this type supposed to predict, and has anything tested that prediction at this stage?

entries.title: The Authority Firewall
entries.synopsis: Where two people met and whether the institution will tolerate the pairing are separate questions, and the second one has an owner. Once a supervisor, principal investigator, instructor, evaluator or coach enters the pairing, agreement between the two of them coexists with one of them holding the other’s assignments, pay, references, funding or promotion.
boundaryConditions: Peer pairings carrying no evaluative authority sit outside the core rule unless some separate conflict exists.
Consent, disclosure, recusal and prohibition are four distinct institutional responses, and adopting one does not imply the others.
That an institution wrote a rule is evidence it is managing a conflict of interest, not evidence that any covered pairing caused harm.
Employee attitudes about hierarchy record opinion, not harassment, favouritism, productivity or how a pairing turned out.
Policy scope varies by institution, jurisdiction, role and chain of command; NIH and UNC Charlotte are worked examples rather than a general law.
Some policies extend beyond current authority to earlier relationships and to authority a person is expected to acquire later; Stanford supplies one such example.
Pool composition, repeated exposure and screening order stay with the parent entry; this one begins at authority after contact.
commonMisreadings: Any romance between coworkers creates coercion and favoritism throughout the workplace.
Hierarchy becomes harmless whenever workplace romance receives voluntary approval from both people involved.
Institutional disclosure fully neutralizes supervisory power across every workplace relationship.

sourceLinks.label: La France (2022), “Don’t Get Your Meat Where You Get Your Bread”: Beliefs and Advice about Workplace Romance, Behavioral Sciences 12(8):278
NIH Relationship Policy
UNC Charlotte University Policy 101.3
Stanford Administrative Guide

pressureTests: Does one of these two people hold the other’s evaluation, pay, references or advancement?

entries.title: The Retention Gap
entries.synopsis: This site models Seen, Noticed, Desired and Chosen in exhaustive detail — SMV, the Hierarchy, the five levers, the whole Conversion Ladder. Kept gets a rule for good news, a lens for spotting shams, and then almost nothing. The gap is not unique to this site: a 2016 paper on mate preferences after pairing states the same absence about its own field, unprompted, in its introduction.
phrases: mate preference psychology after mate selection
boundaryConditions: The gap is comparative thinness against this site's own formation-side coverage, not a claim that no maintenance doctrine exists here.
commonMisreadings: The site says nothing about relationships once they have formed.

sourceLinks.label: Conroy-Beam, Goetz & Buss (2016), Evolution and Human Behavior 37(6):440–448

pressureTests: Which Kept-rung claim on this site rests on a primary source rather than on inference from formation-side doctrine?

entries.title: The Attribution Fork
entries.synopsis: The entry above establishes that a desire gap belongs to the pair. This one is about the move that comes next. Before anyone acts on a gap, somebody decides where it lives — in a body, in a person, in the relationship, or in the situation. Those four locations are rarely exclusive.
boundaryConditions: The four locations are not exclusive: a desire gap can carry somatic, personal, relational and situational components at once, and the fork is about which one gets acted on rather than which one is true.
A somatic cause remains a live possibility throughout: medication effects, endocrine conditions and post-partum recovery are documented contributors with real treatments.
The belief-outcome evidence is self-report and largely cross-sectional with one experimental leg, so an attribution style is associated with outcomes rather than shown to produce them.
The critical-scholarship leg argues about a diagnostic category and states one side of a live disagreement, carrying no effect size of its own.
The DSM-5 criteria described here were corroborated at two independent restatements rather than read in the manual, so the wording is a paraphrase.
commonMisreadings: Low desire in one partner becomes a medical condition as soon as the couple feels distress.
Sexual compatibility is something a couple discovers early rather than something two partners keep building.
A count of how often two partners have sex identifies why their desire diverged.

sourceLinks.label: Maxwell, Muise, MacDonald, Day, Rosen & Impett (2017), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 112(2):238–279
Thomas & Gurevich (2021), Feminism & Psychology 31(1):81–98
Donnelly (1993), “Sexually inactive marriages,” The Journal of Sex Research 30(2):171–179

pressureTests: Which of the four locations is this explanation choosing, and was the other partner present when it was chosen?

entries.title: The Distance Discount
entries.synopsis: Separation gets read as a defect in a bond rather than a feature of its arrangement, and the discount is applied before anyone looks at the bond. The measured picture declines to cooperate: people separated by geography rate their bonds at least as warmly as those living at one address. What the separation changes is the machinery, not the grade — and that machinery has a bill that comes due if the gap ever closes.
boundaryConditions: Both supporting studies are observational and centre young dating couples in North America, so separation is associated with these patterns rather than shown to produce them.
Nothing here covers separation imposed by deployment, incarceration, migration or caregiving, where the constraint and the stakes are different.
High marks during separation and a high reunion failure rate describe different phases of one arrangement and are not in tension.
Idealisation is named as a mechanism rather than a verdict, and the closeness reported during separation is not thereby counterfeit.
The same-direction replication is cited without any figure, because its abstract could not be read at source.
commonMisreadings: Two partners living far apart have a weaker bond than two who live at one address.
A separated couple who finally live in one place will find that things get easier.
A couple who live in different cities are simply waiting for their real relationship to start.

sourceLinks.label: Jiang & Hancock (2013), “Absence Makes the Communication Grow Fonder,” Journal of Communication 63(3):556–577
Stafford, Merolla & Castle (2006), “When long-distance dating partners become geographically close,” Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 23(6):901–919

pressureTests: Is this a judgement about the arrangement, or about the bond that happens to be inside it?

entries.title: Ended
entries.synopsis: The Conversion Ladder ran Seen, Noticed, Desired, Chosen, Kept — and stopped. But every pairing reaches a sixth state, by separation or by death, and the exit has its own drivers, its own asymmetries and a re-entry price that nothing on the formation side ever charges for. Ended is now drawn on the ladder as a dashed terminal cell rather than a sixth box, because it is a state that arrives, not a rung you climb.
boundaryConditions: Ended is a state with a base rate of one hundred percent over a long horizon, so reaching it grades where a bond stopped rather than whether it was worthwhile.
The institution-specific contrast strains a trait explanation without excluding one: selection into marriage is not random and the source leaves the mechanism open.
The re-entry discount has no instrumented source and is the weakest claim in this group.
commonMisreadings: A romance that ended was a failed relationship, so the years spent were wasted.
Women leave relationships more readily than men, in marriage and in dating alike.
pressureTests: Is the exit pattern being explained by a trait, when the data localises it to marriage?

entries.title: Synthetic Reciprocity
entries.synopsis: A companion chatbot can be attentive, validating and always available while the party on the other side has no needs, no welfare and no independent claim on the user. That combination is not a smaller version of a human bond; it is a bond with one side of the ledger removed.
boundaryConditions: Felt connection is an outcome measured in a person and establishes nothing about machine feeling, care, consciousness or moral standing.
Connection recorded immediately after a single session is not durable well-being, a strong bond, or improved social skill.
Supplement, rehearsal and displacement are three separate states and must be measured apart rather than inferred from how much someone uses a product.
Companion products are distinct from task assistants, scripted clinical tools, static parasocial media and human-mediated telehealth.
Brief ratings of noninteractive synthetic characters, and one-off scripted-message experiments, fall outside this standard because neither supplies repeated contingent interaction.
Adolescent use changes the safety, agency and skill-transfer stakes, and current reviews describe competing hypotheses rather than settled effects.
Longitudinal work must separate who selects into heavy use from what use later does, and keep emotional isolation distinct from broader social connection.
Whether substitutes begin a withdrawal, prolong one, or occupy time it had already freed stays an open question held by the parent entry.
commonMisreadings: Simulated responsiveness guarantees reciprocal sacrifice and accountability within every chatbot relationship.
Synthetic reciprocity inevitably displaces offline relationships whenever chatbot companionship feels emotionally responsive.
Artificial empathy proves bilateral agency and welfare inside every chatbot relationship.

sourceLinks.label: Folk, Heine & Dunn (2025), “Individual differences in anthropomorphism help explain social connection to AI companions,” Scientific Reports
Ta et al. (2020), Journal of Medical Internet Research
Smith, Bradbury & Karney (2025), Perspectives on Psychological Science
Fang et al. (2025)

pressureTests: Does the function under discussion need a second party with needs of their own, or only attention?

entries.title: The climb — building SMV
entries.synopsis: Male leverage is often accumulative. Looks can improve through fitness and presentation; money and status usually compound through time; charm improves through practice; exposure increases by entering more social arenas. The climb is uneven, but it is one of the few areas where disciplined self-improvement can materially change outcomes.
boundaryConditions: The climb is described as uneven and partial; naming it one of the few movable areas is not a promise that any given man moves.
commonMisreadings: Every lever climbs at the same rate, so any man who trains will attract women.

entries.title: The inversion threshold
entries.synopsis: Once a man crosses a certain SMV threshold, the dynamic starts to invert. He is no longer only making offers; he is receiving them. Women compete for access, he filters more aggressively, and the same dating market starts behaving like a different machine.
boundaryConditions: The inversion is a change in who makes offers, not a change in whether the market can move against him again.
commonMisreadings: Crossing the SMV threshold means women want a man permanently, so he stops filtering altogether.

entries.title: The male window
entries.synopsis: The male timeline can be back-loaded. A man may have weak leverage early and stronger leverage later if he builds competence, money, status, body, confidence, and social proof. The risk is using early rejection as proof of permanent value instead of treating it as a signal to build.
boundaryConditions: Back-loaded describes a typical shape, not a guarantee; the card's actual claim is about how early rejection should be read.
commonMisreadings: A man rejected early has weak leverage permanently, so building competence and status changes little.

entries.title: Commentary
entries.synopsis: The healthy male response is not bitterness. It is construction. If men are the offer by default, then the rational move is to make the offer stronger: better body, better skills, better emotional control, better standards, better exposure, and better calibration.
boundaryConditions: Construction is offered as the rational response to being the default offer, which is a claim about strategy rather than about fairness.
commonMisreadings: Bitterness is the rational male response once a man sees that women want the strongest offer.

entries.title: The "just tell me what you want" trap
entries.subcategory: Male · Directness, delivery & the indirect game
entries.synopsis: There's a version of the punished-directness pattern that's even more frustrating. Someone says "just tell me what you want," so you do — "I want to have sex" — and you get a flat "no." Think about what that actually communicates: that "just tell me what you want" was never sincere.
aliases: "just tell me what you want" trap
boundaryConditions: A flat refusal after an invitation to be direct is read here as the invitation being insincere, not as an obligation to say yes.
commonMisreadings: A woman asking a man to say what he wants will welcome any answer he gives.

entries.title: It's not what you want, it's how you frame it
entries.subcategory: Male · Directness, delivery & the indirect game
entries.synopsis: The fix for the blunt line isn't to stop wanting sex — it's to wrap it. "I want to make you feel good" lands completely differently than "I want to have sex." Same intention, but it points at her experience instead of just your own appetite. It's still direct about where things are headed; it just isn't aggressive about it. Most women react far better to that. The difference isn't honesty vs.
boundaryConditions: The card changes the framing and keeps the intent; it is a claim about delivery, not permission to conceal what is wanted.
commonMisreadings: Wrapping the intention is dishonest, so a man who wants sex should state it bluntly.

entries.title: Smooth isn't the same as coy
entries.subcategory: Male · Directness, delivery & the indirect game
entries.synopsis: You could argue "I want to make you feel good" is vague — technically it could mean buying her dinner. But in context that's a cop-out. When she's already on your lap, making out, and you whisper it in her ear, nobody's confused about what it means. That's not being coy or hiding the ball — that's having game. Reading the moment and matching your delivery to it is a skill, not a dodge.
boundaryConditions: The defence depends on context making the meaning obvious; the same line in an ambiguous setting would be the cop-out the card names.
commonMisreadings: A man who whispers that he wants to make her feel good is hiding the ball.

entries.title: The transactional-attention problem is real
entries.subcategory: Male · Directness, delivery & the indirect game
entries.synopsis: Flip the lens for a second — a lot of what women complain about on the apps is legitimate. For many of them, the majority of male attention feels purely transactional: a guy makes small talk only as a toll to pay on the way to sex, loses interest or ghosts the moment he realizes she's not down to hook up fast, and lays on fake niceness and over-the-top compliments just to get in her pants.
boundaryConditions: This card grants the other side's complaint; granting it does not withdraw the punished-directness claim it sits beside.
commonMisreadings: Women complaining that male attention feels transactional on dating apps are inventing the pattern.

entries.title: Women train men to hide their intentions
entries.subcategory: Male · Directness, delivery & the indirect game
entries.synopsis: Put it all together and you get the game: a lot of women say they want direct guys, then punish directness the moment it's about sex. So men learn — be indirect, slow the escalation down, disguise the intent. And the uncomfortable part is that it works, because most women respond to it. They want you to want them; they just don't want to feel like that's the only thing on offer.
boundaryConditions: Training is meant in the behavioural sense of what gets rewarded, which is a claim about aggregate response rather than intent.
commonMisreadings: Women reward direct men, so hiding intentions costs a guy attraction on every date.

entries.title: The "wine at my place" move
entries.subcategory: Male · Directness, delivery & the indirect game
entries.synopsis: Every dating coach says the same thing: never ask directly, just ask if she wants to come over for wine. And it works — most women would much rather be invited over for a drink than asked "do you want to have sex," even when both of you know exactly what the wine means. The whole point is plausible deniability.
boundaryConditions: Plausible deniability is described as the mechanism; describing why the move works is not an endorsement of using it to obscure consent.
commonMisreadings: Inviting a woman over for wine works because both sides want the deniability removed.

entries.title: Punishing honesty filters the pool
entries.subcategory: Male · Selection, hypocrisy & how guys respond
entries.synopsis: There's a self-inflicted cost to all this. By rewarding the guys who are best at playing the game — the smooth talkers who say things without being direct, the ones who escalate slowly — and friend-zoning the blunt, honest ones, women slowly filter their own dating pool. Over time the players get rewarded and the straightforward guys get screened out.
boundaryConditions: The filtering is an aggregate effect across many individual choices, so it implies nothing about any one woman's dating pool.
commonMisreadings: Women who reject blunt men keep their dating pool exactly as wide as before.

entries.title: "No good men left" dodges the real question
entries.subcategory: Male · Selection, hypocrisy & how guys respond
entries.synopsis: There's a popular lament: "there are no good men left," "why doesn't anyone approach me anymore?" It carefully avoids the one question that actually matters: why am I undesirable to the kind of men I want? It's far easier to blame men for not approaching than to examine your own standards, attitude, or how you've been behaving.
boundaryConditions: The card redirects the question inward; doing so does not establish that the market has stayed the same underneath.
commonMisreadings: Asking where the good men went settles why a woman attracts fewer of the men she wants.

entries.title: The disconnect breeds resentment
entries.subcategory: Male · Selection, hypocrisy & how guys respond
entries.synopsis: Guys are catching on, and it's curdling into resentment. When someone says one thing but their actions show the opposite, it reads as lying — and when honesty gets punished while game and manipulation get rewarded, it makes the whole thing look cowardly, like they can't even admit what they actually want. That disconnect is real, and it's turning a lot of guys bitter.
boundaryConditions: Explaining where the resentment comes from is not a defence of it; the neighbouring cards argue against letting it curdle.
commonMisreadings: Men resent the gap wrongly, since women want honest guys and smooth talkers equally.

entries.title: It's conditioning, not conspiracy
entries.subcategory: Male · Selection, hypocrisy & how guys respond
entries.synopsis: This isn't a coordinated lie — there's no group of women working in cahoots. It's that most are raised on the same social programming: taught from a young age that they're supposed to want the nice, honest guy. So even when actual attraction doesn't match the script, they keep repeating it, because admitting the truth makes them look bad.
boundaryConditions: Conditioning is the weaker and more defensible claim: shared programming produces a shared pattern without anyone coordinating it.
commonMisreadings: Women want the script they were taught, and they coordinate the mismatch deliberately.

entries.title: Why "game" became a whole industry
entries.subcategory: Male · Selection, hypocrisy & how guys respond
entries.synopsis: This is the whole reason game blew up as a topic. A lot of guys finally clocked that being a good, honest, direct person isn't enough anymore — that raw honesty and good character alone usually get you ignored or friend-zoned. Women say they want honesty, but behavior consistently rewards the guys who flirt, tease, escalate smoothly, and play the social game.
boundaryConditions: This explains why the industry grew, which is a different question from whether what it teaches is true or worth learning.
commonMisreadings: Game became an industry because honest men were already attracting the women they wanted.

entries.title: Two types of guys left
entries.subcategory: Male · Selection, hypocrisy & how guys respond
entries.synopsis: It's split the field into two groups. The first learn game and play it — even if they think it's dirty or manipulative — because they can see it works; that's how you get rewarded. The second refuse on principle: they think it's dishonest, so they stay honest and direct, and usually end up alone or used.
boundaryConditions: Two types is a deliberate simplification of a spectrum; most men sit somewhere between playing fully and refusing entirely.
commonMisreadings: Every man learns game eventually, so the honest and direct ones date just as well.

entries.title: The raw deal cycle
entries.synopsis: For an honest guy the pattern can turn into a brutal loop. Good guys get rejected for being too honest → women chase players and get emotionally damaged → they eventually settle for the good guy but don't actually desire him → they keep him as a safe backup plan while still craving the excitement of the bad boy → the good guy ends up feeling disrespected and miserable.
boundaryConditions: The loop is a pattern some men live through, not a law; plenty of honest men never enter it and some settled pairings work.
commonMisreadings: A woman who settles for the honest guy comes to desire him once she commits.

entries.title: Modern dating feels like a job hunt
entries.synopsis: Here's a framing that clicks for a lot of guys: modern dating is like a job hunt. You want the reward — a relationship — but the actual process of getting there feels like endless applications and interviews: optimizing your profile, performing on dates, being constantly evaluated, getting ghosted or passed over. You want the job; you just hate everything about applying for it.
boundaryConditions: The analogy is offered for how the process feels, and it breaks down precisely where volume stops helping.
commonMisreadings: Modern dating rewards effort like a job hunt, so more applications reliably win a partner.

entries.title: The low-investment middle path
entries.synopsis: There's a third option between grinding the apps until you're miserable and quitting entirely: play very lightly. Stay in the game, but at low effort and low investment — toss out a casual line here and there, go on the occasional date, and don't get emotionally attached to any single outcome.
boundaryConditions: Low investment lowers the emotional cost and the odds together; it is a way to stay in without grinding, not a strategy for winning.
commonMisreadings: Playing lightly means quitting dating, since low investment and total withdrawal are identical.

entries.title: The cop-out slogans
entries.synopsis: Bring any of this up and you'll get the standard deflection: "just be yourself, you'll find the right person when you least expect it." It's the feel-good cop-out. A lot of people will dismiss the whole pattern as red-pill nonsense — not because it's false, but because admitting their choices are driven by emotion and attraction rather than logic and values makes them look bad. So they repeat the slogans instead.
boundaryConditions: Calling the slogans a deflection is a claim about why they get repeated, not proof that every pattern they dismiss is real.
commonMisreadings: Being yourself and waiting for the right person is the advice that actually finds partners.

entries.title: Decoding "just be nice" and "just be yourself"
