entries.synopsis: A lot of responsible people got fed a half-truth: "focus on school, get good grades, be responsible, don't waste time partying." It's not wrong — it's just half the story. What nobody told you is that your social and dating development during those years mattered just as much, and that the window for building it cheaply closes.
boundaryConditions: The advice is called half-true rather than false; the omission is what the card is about.
commonMisreadings: Focusing entirely on school and grades leaves a person's dating development fully intact.

entries.title: Naming the enemy helps — even when it can't fix anything
entries.subcategory: Both Sides · Regret, the missed window & seeing clearly
entries.synopsis: If you're the analytical type, you'll pry under every rock to trace exactly where things went wrong — childhood programming, missed signals, bad societal advice, the college years you didn't use, the personality mismatch with the modern dating environment. A fair question is whether all that dissection actually helps, or just makes the weight heavier by showing you precisely how many things lined up against you.
boundaryConditions: The card raises the question of whether the dissection helps and leaves it genuinely open.
commonMisreadings: Tracing the exact causes always lightens the weight for a man analysing his dating history.

entries.title: Self-awareness isn't the same as change
entries.subcategory: Both Sides · Regret, the missed window & seeing clearly
entries.synopsis: There's a strange, rare posture worth naming: seeing your situation with total clarity — the mistakes you made, the environment you're in, exactly how you got here — and still choosing to mostly stay the same. In one sense that's genuinely uncommon. Most people do one of two things: cope hard, or stay flatly delusional about why they're single.
boundaryConditions: Clarity without change is described as rare rather than admirable; the card names the posture without recommending it.
commonMisreadings: Seeing his situation with total clarity means a man will change how he approaches dating.

entries.title: Stop waiting for the other side to change
entries.subcategory: Both Sides · Regret, the missed window & seeing clearly
entries.synopsis: Notice how almost every proposed "solution" asks the other team to change. Women say men need to do better and stop objectifying them; redpill men say women need to lower their standards and stop chasing the top 10%. Both put the responsibility entirely on the other side — which is exactly why nothing moves.
boundaryConditions: The symmetry argument says why nothing moves; it does not establish that both sides carry equal responsibility for the situation.
commonMisreadings: Asking the other side to change is what finally moves dating, so women and men should wait.

entries.title: Why people are actually on the apps
entries.synopsis: Before splitting anything by gender, look at the whole population: a long-term partner is the top major reason, and casual sex sits near the bottom. These don't sum to 100% because they aren't either/or — the same person can want a relationship and be open to casual. That overlap is exactly why the "82% want love / 18% want sex" framing (see the last group) is a category error.
phrases: Share of recent dating-app users calling each a major reason — you can pick more than one:
boundaryConditions: Method Nationally representative online probability panel (Pew ATP, address-recruited), weighted to U.S. adults. Base: used a dating site/app in the past year. MOE ±5.8 pts.
The reasons do not sum to 100% because they were not asked as alternatives; one respondent can select several.
commonMisreadings: Since 82% of women want a relationship and 18% want casual sex, the two exclude each other.

entries.title: Casual sex is the only reason with a gender gap
entries.synopsis: Casual sex is the one reason where men and women diverge — men out-cite it by about two and a half to one. On the other major reasons (long-term partner, casual dating, friends) Pew found no significant gender gap. So the honest story isn't "men want sex, women want love" — both rank a relationship first; men simply layer more casual openness on top. It's an overlay, not a different species.
phrases: Among current or recent dating-platform users, who calls casual sex a major reason?
boundaryConditions: Method Same Pew ATP probability panel, weighted. Base: past-year dating-app users. The gender gap is statistically significant only for casual sex — the other reasons show no significant gap.
Both sexes rank a long-term partner first; the gap is an additional male openness to casual, not a different first choice.
commonMisreadings: Men want casual sex and women want love, which is why dating apps pair them badly.

entries.title: Women want taller men more than men want shorter women
entries.synopsis: Both sexes want the man taller — but women's pull is the stronger one, and it shows up in real couples: the man is taller in ~92% of couples — a few points above the ~90% that random pairing of the height distributions alone would produce (Stulp), while the sharper sign is how rare the reverse is: female-taller couples turn up roughly 14× less often than chance (Gillis & Avis found 1 in 720, vs ~1 in 50 expected).
phrases: The ideal height gap each sex prefers between themselves and a partner:
boundaryConditions: Method Stated-preference + satisfaction-with-partner survey of university students (the ~21 cm / ~8 cm are curve-fit optima); not a measured-couples dataset. The male-taller norm comes from separate records-based couple samples.
Random pairing of the two height distributions already produces roughly 90% man-taller couples, so only the few points above that are preference.
commonMisreadings: Men want shorter women as strongly as women want taller men, so the height gap is symmetric.

entries.title: Women's odds of orgasm: casual vs. committed
entries.synopsis: In first-time hookups about one in nine women orgasm, versus two-thirds in committed sex. This helps explain why lower casual openness can be rational rather than prudish: when researchers held expected pleasure and anticipated stigma constant, the gender gap in accepting casual-sex offers largely vanished.
phrases: Among heterosexual undergraduate women, how much does context change the payoff — a first-time hookup with that partner vs. an established relationship? (College sample — solid, but not nationally representative, so Tier 2.)
boundaryConditions: Method Online College Social Life Survey — convenience sample of students across 21 colleges (not nationally representative → Tier 2). The 11% / 67% are women's descriptive orgasm rates from separate hookup and relationship analyses (overlapping analytic event counts), not one model that “controls for” context.
The orgasm gap by context is an average over encounters and says nothing about any individual couple's experience.
commonMisreadings: Women orgasm as often in first-time hookups as in committed sex, so casual dating costs little.

entries.title: Across sexual intimacy, the gender gap persists
entries.synopsis: The broader gender gap persists beyond the hookup context: ~95% of heterosexual men usually orgasm versus ~65% of heterosexual women when sexually intimate. So the Armstrong chart can show that relationships improve women's odds without implying commitment fully solves the gap. Casual isn't the only place the deal is lopsided; it's just the most lopsided.
phrases: In a large U.S. sample, who usually or always orgasms when sexually intimate?
boundaryConditions: Method Large opt-in online survey (via NBC News) — non-probability but very large; het. men 26,032 / het. women 24,102; logistic regression. The ~95/65 gap holds across other studies, which is what carries the Tier-1 tag.
Commitment narrows the gap without closing it; the ~95% versus ~65% figures are measured across sexual intimacy generally, not within hookups.
commonMisreadings: Marriage closes the orgasm gap between husbands and wives completely once a couple is established.

entries.title: The same market floods one side and starves the other
entries.synopsis: This is the demand asymmetry made personal, and it cuts both ways. Women are far more likely to feel buried in attention; men are far more likely to feel invisible for the lack of it. Same market, opposite complaints — which is also why "she feels like a body, he feels like a wallet" has a quieter cousin: she feels swarmed, he feels ignored. The market's response is one chart down: pay-to-play →
aliases: same market floods one side and starves the other
phrases: Recent dating-app users who said their experience left them feeling…
overwhelmed by the number of messages
insecure because of the lack of messages
boundaryConditions: Method Same Pew ATP probability panel, weighted. Base: past-year dating-app users (the smaller 951 base, not the 3,128 ever-used base below). MOE ±5.8 pts.
The chart measures platform attention concentration, not the share of people who date, pair, commit, or remain together.
commonMisreadings: Online attention inequality should not be universalized to all dating venues or converted into a causal claim about partner outcomes.
pressureTests: What happens to the concentration after moving from likes and messages to mutual dates and relationships?

entries.title: Where the safety risk concentrates
entries.synopsis: Read this as a baseline-vs-subgroup comparison, not a clean gender split: the all-user bars already include these women, and Pew doesn't publish a tidy men-vs-women breakdown here — but women under 50 run well above the overall rate, and Pew reports men experience all three at lower rates.
phrases: Online daters who say this has happened to them — overall baseline vs. women under 50:
boundaryConditions: Method Same Pew ATP probability panel, weighted. Base: ever used online dating (the larger 3,128 base). Women-under-50 figures from Pew's age/gender breakdown.
This is a baseline-versus-subgroup comparison, not a gender split: the all-user bars already contain the women shown beside them.
commonMisreadings: Pew's dating-app harassment figures show women under fifty and men at the same rate.

entries.title: Pay-to-play: who buys reach, and what it buys
entries.synopsis: The market's answer to the attention asymmetry one chart up: men are the buying side — 41% of male users have paid versus 29% of women — and the gradient runs exactly where you'd predict: with income (45% upper / 36% middle / 28% lower) and with age (41% of users 30+ vs 22% under 30). Paid users also report better experiences, 58% vs 50%.
phrases: Online-dating users who have ever paid to use a dating site or app — including for extra features — and how reported experience splits by paying:
paid to use a dating site or app
boundaryConditions: Method Same Pew ATP probability panel, weighted. Base: ever used online dating (the 3,128 base). “Paid” includes one-off purchases and extra features, not just subscriptions; the income and age gradients quoted in the note come from Pew's published breakdowns of the same item. Bar widths are the percentages themselves.
The paid-versus-never-paid experience gap is a selection effect until proven otherwise: payers skew richer, older, and more intent, and the survey cannot separate the boost from the buyer.
commonMisreadings: That paid users report better experiences is not evidence that paying causes better outcomes.
pressureTests: Does the experience gap survive holding income, age, and stated dating intent constant?

entries.title: Couples match on looks — they don't relentlessly trade up
entries.subcategory: Who pairs, what lasts, who leaves
entries.synopsis: Across 27 samples of real couples, partners' rated looks correlate at about r =.39 — real matching, far from random, and equally far from lockstep. This is the statistical spine under the SMV-Matching framework: on looks alone the market sorts assortatively — the average couple matches rather than one side relentlessly trading up (the "trading up" people notice enters through status instead).
phrases: Correlation between partners' rated physical attractiveness across already-paired couples (0 = random pairing, 1 = perfect lockstep):
boundaryConditions: Method Dyadic meta-analysis re-analyzing Feingold's (1988) paired-couples corpus — attractiveness rated by independent judges, correlated within actual couples. Consistent with sorting found in speed-dating and online-dating data.
Average assortative matching permits meaningful dispersion, evaluator disagreement, and compensation across other traits.
commonMisreadings: A population matching curve is not an individual ceiling.
pressureTests: How wide is the observed distribution around parity, and which stable exceptions does the average conceal?

entries.title: More young adults are going without sex entirely
entries.subcategory: Who pairs, what lasts, who leaves
entries.synopsis: No-sex-in-a-year among young adults roughly 2.4×ed in a decade — and the rise skews male. Ueda et al. (2020, JAMA Network Open) put men aged 18–24 reporting no sex in the past year at 18.9% → 30.9% between 2000–02 and 2016–18 — a far steeper climb than women the same age.
phrases: Share of 18-to-34-year-olds reporting no sex in the past year:
boundaryConditions: Method GSS — NORC nationally representative in-person area-probability sample of U.S. household adults. The sexlessness rates sit on the 18–34 subsample (~400–480 per wave; sex-specific young-men cells smaller, ~150–300), so single-year points carry meaningful margins of error.
The measure is no partnered sex in the past year among 18-to-24-year-olds; it does not track frequency among the sexually active.
commonMisreadings: The sex recession hit young men and young women equally, so both date less now.

entries.title: Women want most divorces — but not most breakups
entries.subcategory: Who pairs, what lasts, who leaves
entries.synopsis: Women wanted roughly 69% of the marriages that ended — though that figure rests on just 92 marital breakups in the panel (95% CI 61–78%). The surprise: non-marital breakups ran about 56% women-wanted among cohabiters (~53% among never-cohabiting couples) — neither significantly different from 50/50.
phrases: Among heterosexual marriages that ended, who wanted the divorce?
boundaryConditions: Method How Couples Meet and Stay Together — nationally representative probability panel (RDD-recruited, surveyed online via KnowledgeNetworks/GfK); discrete-time event-history models controlling for relationship duration, quality, income gap, education, and children.
The 69% marital figure rests on 92 breakups with a 61–78% confidence interval, so it is directional rather than precise.
commonMisreadings: Women want most divorces, so women also end most cohabiting and non-marital relationships.

entries.title: Divorce risk by number of premarital partners
entries.subcategory: Who pairs, what lasts, who leaves
entries.synopsis: Two things break the "every partner chips away at bonding" story. First, the biggest jump is from 0 to 1 — having any premarital sex, not the marginal extra partner — which points at who stays at zero (highly religious, traditional, already low-divorce) rather than a dose effect.
phrases: 5-year divorce rate for women, by premarital sex partners (women marrying in the 2000s):
boundaryConditions: Method National Survey of Family Growth — NCHS/CDC nationally representative in-person probability sample. Bars are raw 5-year life-table divorce rates; multivariate controls (race, family-of-origin, age at marriage, church attendance) were checked separately and don't explain the pattern away.
The largest step is from zero to one partner, which points at who stays at zero rather than at a dose-response effect.
commonMisreadings: Each extra premarital partner a woman has raises her divorce risk, so counts predict marriage stability.

entries.title: Inside a relationship, the relationship beats the résumé
entries.subcategory: Who pairs, what lasts, who leaves
entries.synopsis: Actor and partner personality are not the same channel. A separate nine-year cohort study of 972 people in 486 different-sex German couples found longitudinal associations between a person’s own lower neuroticism and higher conscientiousness and that person’s relationship satisfaction, but no detectable partner-personality effects.
phrases: Meta-analytic share of baseline relationship-satisfaction variance accounted for by four separate self-report model families. Bars show point estimates; dark whiskers show 95% confidence intervals on a 0–60% scale. The models do not add together:
boundaryConditions: Method Raw-data collaboration across 29 laboratories; dyadic longitudinal datasets, random-forest prediction within each dataset, then random-effects meta-analysis. Each dataset used a preregistered analysis plan. Displayed intervals are k=43 random-effects estimates, Fisher-z transformed and back-transformed as described in the paper.
The result concerns variation among established relationships and does not answer who receives attention or enters a relationship.
commonMisreadings: Predictive association is not proof that changing one relationship report will cause the full outcome.

sourceLinks.label: Primary study →
Canonical article →
Public meta-analysis CSV →

pressureTests: Is an established-couple finding being used outside its sampled population or dating stage?

entries.title: A good moment shared is not just two good moods
entries.subcategory: Who pairs, what lasts, who leaves
entries.synopsis: Across three intensive-measurement studies of older couples, moments when both partners were above their own usual positive-emotion level were associated with lower concurrent cortisol even after accounting for either person’s positive affect and a long list of person, medication, behavior and diurnal controls.
phrases: Share of occasions together when both partners reported more positive emotion than was usual for them:
boundaryConditions: Method Harmonized intensive longitudinal data from three studies in Germany and Canada; repeated momentary positive affect and salivary cortisol while partners were together. Models adjusted for individual affect, stable couple differences, time of day, medication and cortisol-relevant behaviors.
The evidence is observational and limited to older cohabiting couples in Germany and Canada; it does not establish that producing shared positivity lowers cortisol.
Cortisol is a proximal biomarker, not a direct measure of relationship quality, physical health or longevity.
The next-assessment result improves temporal ordering but does not eliminate time-varying confounding.
commonMisreadings: Happy couples have lower cortisol because sharing positive emotion improves their health.
One partner feeling positive is physiologically equivalent to both partners sharing the same positive moment.

sourceLinks.label: Primary study →

pressureTests: Is the claim about a measured momentary biomarker association, or has it been promoted into a causal health or relationship benefit?

entries.title: Men send the overwhelming majority of first messages
entries.synopsis: Initiation is male-default, and not narrowly: across four U.S. cities, ~81% of first messages came from men, and women's average reply rate ran under 20%. It's the demand asymmetry from the attention chart seen from the other side — men do the reaching, women do the selecting. The pattern repeats off the apps: marriage proposals run ~95%+ male, and the man still pays the first date about three-quarters of the time.
phrases: Share of opening messages sent by each sex, from full records on a major dating platform:
boundaryConditions: Method Full one-month messaging records (not a poll) on a large free U.S. dating site — complete data, but a single platform; heterosexual users, four cities, Jan 2014. 81% of initial contacts male; women's reply rate <20%.
The ~81% figure covers four U.S. cities on one platform; the direction repeats elsewhere but the exact share is not national.
commonMisreadings: Women send first messages on dating apps about as often as men do.

entries.title: A record share reach 40 having never married
entries.synopsis: The permanent-single class is real Tier-1 data, not a meme: never-married-at-40 more than quadrupled in four decades, and Pew projects ~1 in 4 of today's young adults will never marry. The gender twist matters. Under 30, men are the more-single sex — Pew puts it at 63% vs 34%, though the GSS gap is far narrower (~56/54), so trust the direction, not the exact spread.
phrases: Share of U.S. 40-year-olds who have never been married:
boundaryConditions: Method U.S. Census + American Community Survey microdata (IPUMS) — the ACS is a very large mandatory probability household survey (~3.5 million addresses sampled per year), not a small opinion poll. This is the population-scale end of the spectrum vs. the ~1,000-person surveys elsewhere on this page.
Pew's 63/34 under-30 gap and the GSS's ~56/54 disagree sharply on size, so trust the direction and not the spread.
commonMisreadings: Women under thirty are the more single sex, and marriage rates have held steady for decades.

entries.title: Why singles who aren't looking stay out
entries.synopsis: Most checked-out singles say they simply have other priorities or like it that way — but read these as self-reported: the flattering answers run high, the stigmatized one runs low, so the involuntary share is almost certainly understated. The one reason that splits sharply by sex is exactly that stigmatized one — "no one would be interested in me": men 26% vs women 12%, the involuntary-singlehood tell.
phrases: Single adults who aren't looking to date — share calling each a major reason (more than one allowed):
boundaryConditions: Method Pew ATP probability panel (full sample N = 4,860), fielded Oct 2019, weighted. These reasons are asked only of the 787 single non-daters; the ±2.1-pt MOE is for the full sample, so this subgroup's band is wider.
These are self-reports, so the flattering answers run high and the involuntary share is almost certainly understated.
commonMisreadings: Singles who stay out of dating chose it freely, and men report the same reasons as women.

entries.title: "Player" vs. "slut" — the sexual double standard
entries.synopsis: This one we deliberately don't chart with hard numbers, because the evidence is genuinely mixed. Belief in the double standard is widespread, but controlled studies often find it weaker than expected — sometimes men and women both get judged for high partner counts.
phrases: Is a man really praised for the same sexual history a woman is shamed for?
boundaryConditions: Method Vignette experiment (target's gender × partner count manipulated); 8,080 online + 144 undergrads. Genuinely mixed across methods — vignette designs detect a small effect, attitude scales find none (Endendijk et al. 2020 meta-analysis).
Belief in the double standard is well documented; the size of the actual penalty is what the controlled evidence disputes.
commonMisreadings: Women who date many men are judged far more harshly than men, in every controlled study.

entries.title: Median age at first marriage, U.S.
entries.synopsis: The 1950s marriage age is the anomaly on this chart. Men bottomed at 22.5 in 1956 and women at 20.1 — the lowest in the entire 1890-to-present series — before climbing nearly eight years to 30.2 and 28.6 by 2024. The mid-century floor wasn't the deep historical baseline; it was a brief postwar compression that the rest of the century slowly unwound.
phrases: When Americans first marry — the postwar low (1956), the turn of the century, and today's record high:
boundaryConditions: Method U.S. Census Bureau Current Population Survey, historical table MS-2 (“Estimated Median Age at First Marriage, by Sex: 1890 to Present”). Survey-based medians — not means, and not vital records.
The series runs from 1890, and the mid-century floor is its lowest point — a postwar compression rather than a long historical norm.
commonMisreadings: The 1950s marriage ages of twenty-two and twenty were the baseline couples had always married at.

entries.title: The provider norm is halving
entries.synopsis: The economic architecture under the Status Trade, measured across fifty years. The husband-provides marriage fell from 85% to 55% — still the majority, but its dominance has halved, and ~45% of marriages are now equal- or female-earning.
phrases: U.S. opposite-sex marriages by who earns more — fifty years apart:
boundaryConditions: Method Pew analysis of Census Bureau data on opposite-sex marriages (earnings shares); the accompanying attitudes survey (n = 5,152, Jan 2023) is separate from the trend series.
It fell from 85% to 55%, which is a halved dominance and still a majority of marriages.
commonMisreadings: The husband-provides marriage has collapsed, so most wives now out-earn their husbands.

entries.title: Online displaced everyone else
entries.synopsis: By 2017 the single most common way heterosexual couples met was online — 39%, ahead of every traditional venue. That share was near zero before 1995 and 22% as recently as 2009; meeting through friends, which had held around a third through the mid-'90s, fell to 20% and was overtaken around 2013.
phrases: How heterosexual U.S. couples met, by venue, in 2017 — ranked:
boundaryConditions: Method How Couples Meet and Stay Together — nationally representative probability surveys (2009 and 2017 waves; 2009 wave n = 2,473). Trends are Lowess-smoothed except online (5-yr moving average). Venue categories are not mutually exclusive.
The 39% online share is for heterosexual couples as of 2017 and is a share of new pairings, not of existing relationships.
commonMisreadings: Couples still meet mostly through friends, with online dating a minority route into marriage.

entries.title: Time spent in person with friends
entries.synopsis: In-person time with friends fell from roughly 60 minutes a day in 2003 to about 20 by 2020, and among 15-to-24-year-olds the drop was steeper still — around 70% over the same span. Most of that decline had already happened before 2020, so the pandemic accelerated a slide that was long underway; the contaminated 2020 endpoint marks the floor of the trend rather than its cause.
phrases: Average minutes per day Americans spend face-to-face with friends:
boundaryConditions: Method American Time Use Survey (BLS, nationally representative time diaries), as compiled in the 2023 U.S. Surgeon General's advisory. The 2020 endpoint includes pandemic effects — but the pre-2020 trend line already showed most of the decline, so read the trend, not the endpoint.
Most of the decline had already happened before 2020, and the contaminated 2020 endpoint marks the floor of the trend rather than its cause.
commonMisreadings: The pandemic caused the collapse in the in-person time where couples used to meet partners.

entries.title: The old third places, now single-digit
entries.synopsis: Seen from the third-places angle, the settings that once did the introducing are now rounding errors: by 2017 family accounted for 7% of how couples met, church 4%, and the neighborhood just 3%. These are the same figures as the ranking above, pulled out because they are precisely the venues a third place used to be — when the room empties, so does its role as somewhere people pair off.
phrases: Share of couples who met there, 2017 — the venues a “third place” used to be:
boundaryConditions: Method Same How Couples Meet and Stay Together 2017 wave as the how-couples-meet chart above; these single-digit shares are the third-place venues drawn from that same breakdown, not new figures.
These are the same 2017 figures as the meeting-venue ranking, pulled out by venue type rather than measured separately.
commonMisreadings: Family, church and the neighborhood still introduce a large share of couples who marry.

entries.title: The global fertility arc
entries.synopsis: Global fertility has been falling along one long curve: about five births per woman in the 1960s, 3.3 by 1990, and 2.2 in 2024, with the UN projecting the 2.1 replacement level around 2050. The regional spread the Deep Dive lays out — Sub-Saharan Africa at 4.3, Europe and North America near 1.6, East Asia and the Pacific down at 1.3 in 2023 — is best read as one snapshot of that descent, each region sitting at a…
phrases: Total fertility rate (births per woman) — the global descent over time, and where the regions sit on it:
boundaryConditions: Method UN World Population Prospects / UN DESA “World Fertility 2024”; regional 2023 figures via World Bank aggregates (the “Europe & Central Asia” and “North America” aggregates both sit near 1.6).
The regional figures are one snapshot of a shared descent, so a high-fertility region is early on the same curve rather than off it.
commonMisreadings: Falling fertility is a Western problem, since couples elsewhere still marry early and have five children.

entries.title: Korea: the attitude floor under one of the world's lowest fertility rates
entries.synopsis: South Korea, home to the world's lowest recorded fertility rate in 2023, shows the attitudes shifting underneath the number. The share calling marriage “a necessity” slipped from 56.8% in 2014 to 52.5% in 2024 — and split sharply by sex, 58.3% of men versus 46.8% of women — while acceptance of cohabitation without marriage jumped from 46.6% to 67.4%.
phrases: Statistics Korea social survey (ages 13+) — how attitudes to marriage and cohabitation shifted, 2014 to 2024:
boundaryConditions: Method Statistics Korea social survey — large government household survey, ages 13+, biennial. TFR and marriage counts from Statistics Korea vital statistics.
Attitude shares are self-reported intentions; they sit alongside the fertility rate rather than explaining it.
commonMisreadings: Korean men and women value marriage identically, which is why their fertility fell lowest.

entries.title: Child marriage: highest where the ladder tops out
entries.synopsis: At the high-fertility end of the Deep Dive's ladder sits its harshest floor: child marriage. Among women now aged 20–24, 31% in Sub-Saharan Africa were married before 18 — the highest of any region, though down from about 38% a decade earlier — and West and Central Africa still run near one in three, home to six of the world's ten highest-prevalence countries.
phrases: Women aged 20–24 who were married before 18 — a decade ago vs. the latest, by region:
boundaryConditions: Method UNICEF global databases — the standard indicator is the share of women aged 20–24 first married or in union before 18, from Demographic and Health Surveys and MICS.
The 31% figure describes women now aged 20–24 looking back, so it lags current practice by up to a decade.
commonMisreadings: Child marriage has ended across sub-Saharan Africa, where women now marry as consenting adults.

entries.title: Fertility by age: a slope with two turns, not a cliff at 30
entries.synopsis: The one part of “the wall” that comes from the body, measured where the logging is best. ACOG marks the real turns at 32 (gradual) and 37 (faster) — not 30 — and IVF outcomes trace the same slope. Egg donation is the tell: when the eggs are young, success barely tracks the recipient's age, which points at egg quality rather than the womb or her general health.
phrases: IVF cycles using a woman's own eggs that end in a live birth, by age at the start of the cycle:
boundaryConditions: Method Live births as a share of own-egg IVF cycles started, by age band, as compiled in ACOG Committee Opinion 589. “Advanced maternal age” (35) is a monitoring threshold, not either turn in the curve.
ACOG marks the turns at 32 and 37 and describes a slope; this chart carries the biological curve only, not desirability or market position.
commonMisreadings: A woman's fertility falls off a cliff at thirty, which is when men stop wanting her.

entries.title: The U.S. leads the world in one-parent households
entries.synopsis: Across 130 countries and territories, no nation houses a larger share of its children with a lone adult: 23% of American kids, more than triple the global 7% — and the highest rate in the study. Two definitions do real work here. This counts solo -parent households: one parent, no other adult under the roof. And part of the U.S.
aliases: U.S. leads the world in one-parent households
phrases: Children under 18 living with one parent and no other adult — the U.S. against the world:
boundaryConditions: Method Pew analysis of census and survey microdata; “single parent” = a sole adult living with at least one biological, step, or foster child under 18. Bar lengths scaled ×3 for readability; labels carry the real shares.
This counts solo-parent households — one parent and no other adult — so a household sharing with a grandparent falls outside it.
commonMisreadings: American marriage produces solo-parent households at roughly the rate seen worldwide, around seven percent.

entries.title: The route into single parenthood flipped
entries.synopsis: Two series, one flip. Births outside marriage went from one in twenty to about four in ten — and have sat near 40% since 2009: a resettled baseline, not a spike. Underneath, the never-married share of single mothers grew elevenfold, pulling nearly level with the divorced, separated, and widowed combined — the widow who defined the category in 1950 has nearly vanished from it.
phrases: Births outside marriage as a share of all U.S. births — and who single mothers are:
boundaryConditions: Method NCHS national vital statistics — complete birth registration, not a poll; single-mother composition from Pew's Census/CPS analysis (1960 vs 2011).
The never-married share grew elevenfold and pulled nearly level with the rest combined; the two series describe route, not outcome.
commonMisreadings: Single mothers are mostly divorced or widowed women, as they were when marriage was near-universal.

entries.title: What the one-adult house pays — and who carries it
entries.synopsis: The money line is brutal and undisputed: single-mother families run near six times the married-couple poverty rate — a second adult in the house is the largest anti-poverty program in American life. And the load lands asymmetrically: four custodial parents in five are women, a split that has moved only a few points in three decades of Census measurement.
phrases: Families with children below the official poverty line (2023), and who the custodial parent is:
boundaryConditions: Method Official poverty measure, families with related children under 18 (poverty bars scaled ×2 for readability; labels carry the real rates). Custody split from the CPS Child Support Supplement (2018 report).
The poverty ratio is a comparison of household types, not a causal estimate of what removing one adult does to a given family.
commonMisreadings: Single mothers and couples who marry raise children under similar poverty rates once income counts.

entries.title: Commitment is more than satisfaction
entries.synopsis: Across the Investment Model literature, satisfaction is the strongest single correlate of commitment — but the exit door and the life already built matter almost as much. In relationship samples, satisfaction, alternatives, and investments together accounted for about 63% of the variance in commitment; commitment in turn correlated with stay/leave behavior at r =.47.
phrases: Meta-analytic correlations with relationship commitment (bar length shows the magnitude of r):
boundaryConditions: Method Meta-analysis of Investment Model tests. Bars are relationship-specific pooled correlations; the 63% figure pools relationship samples reporting multivariable R². Correlation is not intervention evidence.
commonMisreadings: How satisfied someone feels is what decides whether they stay in a relationship.

sourceLinks.label: Article →

entries.title: The demand-withdraw loop travels with worse outcomes
entries.synopsis: One partner pushes harder to discuss or change; the other evades, shuts down, or leaves; each response intensifies the other. Across 74 studies, that loop had a moderate association with worse outcomes. The useful unit is the cycle, not a villain: the meta-analysis combined who demanded and who withdrew, and the pooled result does not establish which behavior started the conflict or whether outside stress caused both…
aliases: demand-withdraw loop travels with worse outcomes
phrases: Pooled association between demand-withdraw communication and adverse individual, relationship, and communication outcomes:
boundaryConditions: Method Meta-analysis of observed and self-reported demand, withdrawal, and demand-withdraw patterns. The published r =.36 is the average effect magnitude across coded outcomes; most links are reciprocal and observational, not causal.
commonMisreadings: The partner who withdraws during conflict is the one driving the relationship downward.
Once a spouse quits complaining about the relationship, the marriage has finally found peace.

sourceLinks.label: Article →

entries.title: Marriage and cohabitation do not feel identical from inside
entries.synopsis: Married adults report a deeper center of gravity around the relationship. The gap survives statistical adjustment for age, gender, education, religion, race, and relationship duration, but that still does not prove the certificate caused it: people with stronger commitment may be more likely to marry.
phrases: Partnered U.S. adults describing the relationship as going “very well,” and naming their spouse or partner as the adult they feel closest to:
boundaryConditions: Method Weighted Pew American Trends Panel probability survey of 9,834 U.S. adults (2019); these bars use the partnered subsamples. Self-reported relationship appraisal, cross-sectional.
commonMisreadings: Getting married itself deepens commitment, which is why married people report more of it.

sourceLinks.label: Report →

entries.title: The first baby brings a shared satisfaction dip
entries.synopsis: The average drop is about three-tenths of a standard deviation and remarkably similar for mothers and fathers. That makes the transition a predictable load, not evidence that one sex suddenly values the relationship less. The strongest caution is the comparison group: only nine independent samples followed nonparents over a comparable span, and satisfaction can decline with relationship time even without a baby.
aliases: first baby brings a shared satisfaction dip
phrases: Standardized change in marital satisfaction from pregnancy through the first 12 months after birth:
boundaryConditions: Method Meta-analysis of prepartum-to-postpartum satisfaction change. Women: 50 samples / 139,791; men: 45 samples / 4,625. Heterogeneity was high, so the pooled effect is a center, not a universal trajectory.
commonMisreadings: After a first baby arrives, mothers disengage from the relationship far more than fathers.

sourceLinks.label: Open article →

entries.title: A first cohabitation is neither a sure audition nor a dead end
entries.synopsis: Three years in, marriage is the single largest destination, but a majority have not married that partner: roughly a third remain together without marrying and just over a quarter have split. Education changes the route sharply — 53% of first cohabitations among women with a bachelor’s degree transitioned to marriage, versus 30% among women without a high-school diploma.
phrases: Where women’s first premarital cohabitations stood three years after moving in together:
boundaryConditions: Method Nationally representative 2006–2010 NSFG, women ages 15–44; retrospective union histories analyzed with a multiple-decrement life table. Percentages sum to 99% from rounding. Dated cohort, so use as a durable baseline rather than a current forecast.
commonMisreadings: Moving in together is the step just before marriage for most couples who do it.

sourceLinks.label: Report PDF →

entries.title: Equal earnings still do not buy equal time
entries.synopsis: Even when paychecks are nearly even, wives average about 4.5 more hours of unpaid care and housework each week, while husbands average 3.6 more leisure hours and 3.1 more paid-work hours. Among parents in these marriages the care gap widens: mothers log 12.2 hours versus fathers’ 9.0.
phrases: Average weekly hours in opposite-sex “egalitarian” marriages, where each spouse earns 40%–60% of joint earnings:
boundaryConditions: Method Pew analysis of pooled 2016–2021 American Time Use Survey diaries. Weekly care, housework, and leisure equal reported daily time ×7; paid work is usual weekly hours. Bar lengths use a 50-hour scale; labels carry the actual hours.
commonMisreadings: Once a wife earns as much as her husband, household labour divides about evenly.

sourceLinks.label: Report →

entries.title: Intermarriage moved from exception to one in six
entries.synopsis: The share rose more than fivefold after Loving v. Virginia, and 11 million married Americans were in an intermarriage by 2015. Composition matters: growth in Asian and Hispanic populations expanded the number of cross-group pairings available, while acceptance also changed sharply.
phrases: U.S. newlyweds married to someone of a different race or ethnicity:
boundaryConditions: Method Pew analysis of decennial Census and American Community Survey microdata. “Newlywed” means married in the prior 12 months in 2008–2015; the 1967–1980 series is limited to first marriages, while later years include remarriages. Bar lengths use a 20% scale.
commonMisreadings: The rise in intermarriage measures how far American racial attitudes improved after Loving.

sourceLinks.label: Report →

entries.title: After a marriage ends, men are more likely to marry again
entries.synopsis: The behavior gap and the stated-desire gap point the same way. More than half of previously married women said they did not want to remarry (54%), compared with 30% of men. But age carries much of the aggregate: among eligible adults ages 25–54, women and men were about equally likely to have remarried; the large difference remained among adults 55 and older.
phrases: Among adults eligible to remarry because a first marriage ended in divorce or widowhood:
boundaryConditions: Method Remarriage prevalence from Pew analysis of Census/ACS microdata; stated desire from a separate nationally representative Pew survey in 2014. Eligibility combines divorce and widowhood, which have different age profiles.
commonMisreadings: Women are far less interested in remarrying than men at every stage of adult life.

sourceLinks.label: Report →

entries.title: Any partner violence is near-even; lifetime severity is not
entries.synopsis: A binary “ever hit” frame hides the severity gradient. Men and women report nearly identical lifetime exposure to the broad physical-violence category, while women report substantially more severe acts such as being choked, beaten, burned, having a knife or gun used against them, or being slammed into something.
phrases: U.S. adults reporting physical violence by an intimate partner at any point in their lifetime:
boundaryConditions: Method CDC NISVS 2016/2017 nationally weighted random-digit-dial survey, behaviorally specific questions, adults 18+. Weighted response rate was 7.6% (cooperation 58.6%), an important nonresponse caveat despite weighting.
commonMisreadings: Partner violence lands on men and women about equally, so gendered framing overstates it.

sourceLinks.label: Report PDF →

entries.title: Nearly half of nonparents under 50 now say children are unlikely
entries.synopsis: This is an intention shift before it is a completed-fertility statistic: younger respondents can change their minds, and “unlikely” is not “never.” Still, the same question moved ten points in five years. In a 2024 follow-up limited to under-50 nonparents who already said children were unlikely, 57% named simply not wanting children as a major reason; 44% cited other priorities, 38% the state of the world, and 36%…
phrases: U.S. adults ages 18–49 without children saying they are “not too” or “not at all” likely to have children someday:
boundaryConditions: Method Pew American Trends Panel probability surveys with matched wording; 2023 full wave N=11,945, including 1,916 nonparents ages 18–49. The 2024 reasons survey used a separate screened base of 770 under-50 nonparents already unlikely to have children.
commonMisreadings: Roughly half of American adults under fifty will finish their lives childless.

sourceLinks.label: Report →

entries.title: The part you most want predicted is the part nobody could predict
entries.synopsis: Traits and preferences do predict something: who is broadly desirable, and who is broadly hard to please. What they do not predict is the thing every matching service sells — that two particular people will click. And this is not a case of a small target: unique, person-specific desire was the largest component of the outcome (about 35% of the variance in desire), which means the model had the most room to work…
aliases: part you most want predicted is the part nobody could predict
phrases: Share of romantic-desire variance a machine-learning model recovered from more than 100 self-report measures collected before the daters met — and, in the last row, from what they reported right after a four-minute date:
boundaryConditions: Method Two independent undergraduate samples (163 daters in 2005, 187 in 2007), each attending roughly twelve four-minute dates. Desire was split into actor, partner and relationship components with a social-relations model, then predicted by random forests trained on one sample and tested on the other (181 predictors in one, 112 in the other).
commonMisreadings: A dating algorithm with enough data will predict which two people click before they meet.

sourceLinks.label: Article →

entries.title: The pool is not the population
entries.synopsis: Headcount says there is a surplus of never-married young men — 126 for every 100 women. Apply one filter that most women say they care about, a job, and the surplus becomes a shortfall: 91. Then the ratio flips again by education, and it flips hard.
phrases: Never-married men per 100 never-married women, ages 25–34 — all of them, and the employed subset:
boundaryConditions: Method Pew analysis of the 1960–2000 decennial censuses and the 2010–2012 American Community Survey via IPUMS; figures shown are 2012. Bars use a 200-per-100 scale, so widths are half the printed values.
commonMisreadings: The dating pool follows the headcount, so a surplus of young men means women hold the advantage.

sourceLinks.label: Report →

entries.title: Being friends first changes who you can pair with
entries.synopsis: Looks-matching is real, but its strength is not fixed — it depends on how the couple met. Strangers agree strongly about who is attractive, and where there is consensus there is a market, so couples who paired off quickly were tightly sorted by appearance.
phrases: Correlation between partners’ rated physical attractiveness, by whether they were platonic friends before dating (bar length shows the magnitude of r):
boundaryConditions: Method Coder-rated physical attractiveness for both partners; acquaintance length computed as months known minus months romantically involved (mean 3.8, median 2.0), with 20 couples beyond Tukey’s outer fences excluded.
commonMisreadings: Couples always match on looks, so dating someone better looking than you is impossible.

sourceLinks.label: Article →

entries.title: Getting back together is common, and it leaves a mark
entries.synopsis: Reconciliation is not a rare event — more than a third of cohabiting couples and nearly a quarter of married ones had already ended the relationship at least once and restarted it. But cyclers looked different afterward, in the same direction on both sides of the couple and at both stages: more uncertainty about the relationship’s future, and lower satisfaction (cohabiting women averaged 14.98 versus 16.72 on the…
phrases: Share who report having broken up and reconciled with the partner they are currently with:
boundaryConditions: Method National sample of couples, both partners surveyed; retrospective reports of a breakup and renewal within the current relationship; dyadic regressions accounting for the non-independence of partners’ answers. Among married cyclers, 87% of the breakups happened while dating rather than while living together.
commonMisreadings: Getting back together after a breakup restores the romance completely, leaving the couple exactly as before.

sourceLinks.label: Article →

entries.title: When you moved in beat whether you moved in
entries.synopsis: The people who moved in together before making any commitment to marry later reported lower marital satisfaction, less dedication, less confidence in the marriage, more negative communication, and more proneness to divorce. The people who moved in after getting engaged looked no different from the people who never cohabited at all — which is why the finding is about sequence, not about living together.
phrases: Route into marriage, among adults married within the previous ten years:
boundaryConditions: Method Random-digit telephone survey of men and women married within the past ten years; self-reported route and self-reported marital quality, measured at one point in time. Selection is the standing caveat — the survey did not assign anyone to a sequence, and people who wait for a commitment may differ from those who do not in ways no control variable…
commonMisreadings: Moving in early ruins a couple's odds, whatever they had intended about the wedding.

sourceLinks.label: Article →

entries.title: What the wedding predicts about the marriage
entries.synopsis: Every association here runs against the advertising. Spending less than $1,000 on the wedding went with a lower divorce hazard; spending $20,000 or more went with a higher one. Filling the room, on the other hand, went the industry’s way — 101 to 200 guests carried the lowest hazard on the board, and taking a honeymoon of any cost went with a lower one.
phrases: Hazard of divorce relative to the comparison group, from one multivariate survival model. Below 1.00 means a lower hazard; the bars run on a 0–1.60 scale:
boundaryConditions: Method Cox proportional-hazards model, population-weighted against the 2012 ACS, controlling for age, age at marriage, sex, race, education, employment, household income, region, religious attendance, spousal differences in age/race/education, and children.
commonMisreadings: Spending more on the wedding signals commitment, so an expensive celebration predicts a lasting marriage.

sourceLinks.label: Article →

entries.title: The skills are teachable, and the effect is real but modest
entries.synopsis: This is the rare place in this literature with randomized trials behind it, and the answer is neither “communication fixes everything” nor “nothing works.” Taught couples ended up roughly a third to a half of a standard deviation ahead of untaught ones — a real, moderate shift, larger for observable skills than for how happy people felt. Dosage mattered: moderate-length programs beat short ones.
aliases: skills are teachable, and the effect is real but modest
phrases: Average effect of marriage and relationship education programs across experimental studies, in standard deviations (Cohen’s d):
boundaryConditions: Method Meta-analysis of 86 codable reports; bars show the midpoint of each published experimental range and are drawn on a 0–1.00 d scale, so they are standardized mean differences, not percentages. Quasi-experimental studies produced smaller effects, attributable to pretest group differences.
commonMisreadings: A communication course fixes a struggling marriage, because taught couples keep the gains permanently.

sourceLinks.label: Abstract →
Open article →

entries.title: How well couples talk about sex outranks how often
entries.synopsis: Pooled across the whole literature, sexual communication correlated with sexual satisfaction at r =.43 and with relationship satisfaction at r =.37 — among the larger associations anything in this field posts. The internal ranking is the usable part: quality beat both frequency and raw disclosure on both outcomes. Bringing it up more often is not the lever; being able to have the conversation well is.
phrases: Pooled correlations between three dimensions of couples’ sexual communication and satisfaction (bar length shows the magnitude of r):
boundaryConditions: Method Multilevel meta-analysis of individuals currently in a relationship, with moderators for age, relationship length, marital status, individualism and national gender inequality. Bars map r directly to width. Self-report on both sides of every correlation, and no study here randomly assigned couples to talk.
commonMisreadings: How often a couple has sex decides romantic satisfaction, so talking about desire changes little.

sourceLinks.label: Abstract →

entries.title: More is not better past about once a week
entries.synopsis: A straight line fits the data at first glance, and that is the version that circulates. Add a squared term and the curve wins: well-being rises with frequency up to roughly once a week and stops rising after that. Two findings sharpen it.
phrases: Across three samples totalling 30,645 people, the link between how often partnered people have sex and how well they report doing is curved, not straight — it climbs, then flattens:
boundaryConditions: Method Study 1: 25,510 respondents across 14 waves of the nationally representative General Social Survey, 1989–2012. Study 2: 335 partnered adults, using the Satisfaction With Life Scale and the income benchmark quoted above. Study 3: the National Survey of Families and Households, 2,400 married couples across three waves spanning 14 years.
commonMisreadings: More sex always means a happier romance, so couples should push frequency as high as possible.

sourceLinks.label: Article →

entries.title: Numbers carried by Mythbuster rulings
entries.synopsis: Tier 1 Similarity–attraction: actual similarity predicts attraction at r =.47, perceived similarity at.39, across 313 studies (Montoya et al. 2008). Ruling M-TBD-9 →
phrases: Statistics already established by graded rulings on The Mythbuster — docket entries contribute nothing here until they clear the gate. Follow a ruling link for the full trial: claims, verdict, and sources.
boundaryConditions: This entry carries numbers already ruled on elsewhere, so the ruling and its tier live with the Mythbuster docket rather than here.
commonMisreadings: Perceived similarity predicts attraction between partners more strongly than their actual similarity does.

entries.title: Stats we refused to chart
entries.synopsis: Myth "82% of women want relationships, 18% want casual." Often attributed to a single platform's self-reported marketing stat (Bumble) — Tier 3 — and it treats wanting a relationship and being open to casual as mutually exclusive, which the Pew data in the first group shows they aren't.
boundaryConditions: This section exists to record refusals; a number appearing here has been examined and rejected, not left unexamined.
commonMisreadings: The 82% relationship versus 18% casual split is a solid figure about what women want.

entries.title: Is the extra-friendly barista flirting with you?
entries.synopsis: Men systematically over-read warmth as romantic interest — the sexual overperception bias — and service-industry friendliness is occupational, which inflates the false-positive rate further. The discriminating cue is the one Mika names: differential treatment and effort to extend the interaction, not baseline warmth.
phrases: Complimenting a customer and keeping the conversation going is not standard barista behavior. Girls don’t put in that kind of effort with customers unless they enjoy their company — she was most likely at least a little interested.

Girls in customer-service jobs are trained to be chatty, and some are just naturally social. If she were actually flirting she’d be flirting with dozens of guys every single day — real flirting is selective and treats you differently from everyone else.
boundaryConditions: Ani regraded from the earlier proposed Backwards to Oversimplified: Hall shows real flirting is also frequently MISSED, so “you’re missing signals” has partial support — her error is ignoring base rates in occupational-warmth contexts, not inverting reality.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: Complimenting a customer and keeping the conversation going is not standard barista behavior. Girls don’t put in that kind of effort with customers unless they enjoy their company — she was most likely at least a little interested.

sourceLinks.label: Sexual overperception bias — emotion projection & desire study (2021, replicating the bias)
Hall, Xing & Brooks (2014), Communication Research — flirting detection accuracy and base rates

entries.title: How obvious are women when they’re actually interested?
entries.synopsis: Interested women do emit identifiable cues — the ones Mika lists are the documented ones — but detection is genuinely bad: in lab interactions, actual flirting was correctly recognized only about a third of the time, and observers did no better than participants. Signals exist and get missed at high rates. Each camp holds half the picture.
phrases: Most girls will give you signals and wait to see if you do something. They’re not going to risk rejection by being super obvious — listen to what they do, not what they say.

Most girls who are actually interested give multiple hints that are pretty obvious if you’re paying attention — laughing at unfunny jokes, staying in the conversation longer than needed, personal questions. If she’s truly interested she doesn’t make it nearly that hard.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: Most girls will give you signals and wait to see if you do something. They’re not going to risk rejection by being super obvious — listen to what they do, not what they say.

oversimplified: Most girls who are actually interested give multiple hints that are pretty obvious if you’re paying attention — laughing at unfunny jokes, staying in the conversation longer than needed, personal questions. If she’s truly interested she doesn’t make it nearly that hard.

sourceLinks.label: Hall, Xing & Brooks (2014), Communication Research — two-study flirting detection design
University of Kansas summary — detection rates (38% when flirting occurred; women’s flirting read more accurately)

entries.title: If you take rejection gracefully, does shooting your shot cost you anything?
entries.synopsis: The pursuit literature puts the damage where Ani puts it: across 241 people's dual pursuer/target accounts, targets' negative reactions attached to persistence after explicit rejection — and pursuers, especially men, over-reported reciprocation signals and under-reported the no. No study shows a polite, once-and-done ask costing reputation.
phrases: Girls don’t give guys a bad reputation for politely asking for a number when the vibe is good. Bad reputations come from being pushy, entitled, or bitter after rejection — most girls respect a guy who makes a clean move and takes no well.

Perception matters more than how nicely you take the rejection. If she never gave real signals, your advance is unwanted attention no matter how polite it is — and repeatedly misreading friendliness as flirting damages your reputation, because girls talk.
boundaryConditions: No study directly measures reputational fallout from a single graceful approach — that gap caps this at evidence tier, and Ani's "most girls respect a clean move" is inference from the persistence literature, not a measured approval rate.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: Perception matters more than how nicely you take the rejection. If she never gave real signals, your advance is unwanted attention no matter how polite it is — and repeatedly misreading friendliness as flirting damages your reputation, because girls talk.

entries.title: What counts as a crush?
entries.synopsis: Definitionally both miss, in opposite directions. Crush research treats a crush as an attraction-based, usually unilateral and uncommunicated longing that ranges from light to intense (O'Sullivan et al. 2022, n=3,585). That sinks Ani's “any positive thought counts” — fondness, or a laughed-at joke with no attraction behind it, isn't a crush.
phrases: [Reported — paraphrase] Anyone who thinks anything positive of you — finds you cute, laughs at your jokes, has you on their mind — has a crush.

A crush is romantic interest with emotional investment — someone excited or nervous to be around you who wants your attention. Finding someone cute or enjoying their company is basic attraction, not a crush.

entries.title: Does cold-approaching women in everyday places actually work?
entries.synopsis: Where couples actually form: friends, family, coworkers, school and — now the leading channel — online dating account for the bulk of matches; meeting cold in a public place is a small and shrinking share. Initiative matters within a context, but as a strategy, venue beats volume.
phrases: Average guys who consistently shoot their shot on any sensed interest get rejected a lot but also get far more yeses than the overthinkers — many girls are open to dating and just don’t want to be the one who initiates. The bold guy wins more often than people admit.

The polite refusal wins by a huge margin — cold flirting in public has a very low success rate, and the numbers game burns confidence and reputation. High-quality contexts (apps, social circles, hobbies) beat high-quantity approaches.

entries.title: Do women prefer the guy who takes it slow and waits to make a move?
entries.synopsis: On long-term outcomes the claim inverts: among 2,035 married individuals, later sexual timing predicted better communication, satisfaction, perceived stability, and sexual quality — controlling for religiosity, education, partner count, and relationship length. Decisiveness may help short-term attraction, but “death sentence” depends entirely on which finish line you’re measuring.
phrases: Those stories are extremely rare — usually she was already strongly attracted, or she friend-zoned the slow guy and is retelling it kindly. For every girl who liked that he waited, hundreds lost interest because he never tried.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: Those stories are extremely rare — usually she was already strongly attracted, or she friend-zoned the slow guy and is retelling it kindly. For every girl who liked that he waited, hundreds lost interest because he never tried. For average guys, waiting too long is usually a death sentence.

entries.title: Should you build confidence before dating, or through it?
entries.synopsis: Mastery experiences are the strongest of the four sources of self-efficacy, and the founding formulation is nearly verbatim the claim: persistence in activities that feel threatening but are in fact safe builds efficacy and reduces defensive avoidance. Confidence is downstream of reps, not a prerequisite for them.
phrases: Get-confident-first is a fantasy and a common form of procrastination. Confidence with women only develops through repeated exposure — you can lift, read, and meditate, but until you’re across the table under pressure it doesn’t fully form.
boundaryConditions: Mastery experiences and vicarious ones differ in strength, so which source of confidence is being built matters.
commonMisreadings: A man must finish building confidence before he starts dating, or he wastes the attempt.

sourceLinks.label: Bandura (1977), Psychological Review — self-efficacy theory; APA overview of the four sources

entries.title: She’s flirting with you in front of her boyfriend — what does it mean?
entries.synopsis: Deliberate jealousy induction is a documented behavior with validated scales; flirting with others in front of a partner is one of the recognized techniques, and the measured motives cluster on attention, validation, security-testing, and relational power — essentially the two readings both AIs gave. The convergence entry survives its own audit.
phrases: Either she’s a natural tease who enjoys feeling desired — her boyfriend being there may make it more exciting — or she’s testing the waters in an unhappy relationship. Either way it’s mostly about her validation, not about you.

She was most likely flirting for attention, not interest — girls who do this with their boyfriend right there are enjoying the ego boost. A genuinely interested girl tries to be discreet and catches you when he’s not around.
boundaryConditions: Inducing jealousy and signalling availability are distinct behaviours with distinct scales, and one episode rarely separates them.
commonMisreadings: A woman flirting with another man in front of her boyfriend wants to leave him.

entries.title: Opposites attract.
entries.synopsis: Similarity — actual and perceived — strongly predicts attraction: r =.47 and.39 across 313 studies. One wrinkle: in established relationships it is perceived similarity that carries the effect, not measured similarity. Evidence for complementarity (“opposites”) is weak and trait-specific.
boundaryConditions: Verified. The stability half of the original mockup claim was trimmed — Montoya covers attraction, not longitudinal stability; add a homogamy/marital-quality source if the ruling should speak to stability.

entries.title: Never go to bed angry.
entries.synopsis: Forcing resolution while physiologically flooded escalates conflict, and sleep-deprived partners fight worse: couples short on sleep behaved more hostilely and showed stronger inflammatory responses to conflict discussions. A structured timeout beats a forced 2 a.m. settlement.

entries.title: Who cares more about looks?
entries.synopsis: In stated preferences the traditional gap is real and replicated: men rate looks as more important, women rate earning prospects higher. But in live speed-dating behavior the sex differences disappear — both sexes’ actual romantic interest tracked partners’ attractiveness about equally. The stated gap exists; the behavioral gap is a fraction of what either camp believes.
phrases: Men are visual. Women barely care about looks at all.
Everyone weighs looks the same. The gap is a myth.
boundaryConditions: E&F 2008 verified; a 2015 direct replication reached consistent results. NOTE: “The classic” regraded from the mockup’s Backwards to False — the direction of the stated difference is real, so the claim isn’t inverted, just wrong in magnitude. “The leveler” is closest to right on revealed preferences and could arguably land higher — Jason’s call.
commonMisreadings: false: Men are visual. Women barely care about looks at all.
oversimplified: Everyone weighs looks the same. The gap is a myth.

entries.title: Does being direct about wanting sex get a man rejected where the indirect route succeeds?
entries.synopsis: The outcome asymmetry is real and repeatedly replicated: in Clark and Hatfield's field experiments, 69–75% of men accepted a stranger's "go to bed with me tonight," zero women did — yet roughly half of women in the same experiments accepted a date request. The lesson drawn is wrong, though.
phrases: A guy who just says "wanna have sex" gets shut down immediately, but a guy who goes on three pretend dates gets it. Same goal, opposite outcome. The market rewards the guy willing to play the long game — the pretend dates, the slow-built vibe, the gradual escalation over multiple…

When a man is direct and honest about wanting you, it often kills the spark — and when he plays it cool, teases, and keeps you guessing, it pulls you in. Multiply that across millions of women and you get a training program: men learn that honesty gets them rejected and games get…

Blurting "I want to have sex" out of nowhere reads as low-effort and a little gross — like she's just a hole you're trying to use. No romance, no buildup, no seduction. Most women want to feel desired, not just needed for sex, and the wording is where that lives.
boundaryConditions: The "three dates gets it" half is script-consistent but not directly quantified in this literature, and the lab-parity results (Conley; Baranowski & Hecht) measure hypothetical consent under manufactured safety, not real-world behavior — so the mechanism evidence is softer than the outcome data.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: A guy who just says "wanna have sex" gets shut down immediately, but a guy who goes on three pretend dates gets it. Same goal, opposite outcome. The market rewards the guy willing to play the long game — the pretend dates, the slow-built vibe, the gradual escalation over multiple conversations — and punishes the guy who's honest about what he…

oversimplified: When a man is direct and honest about wanting you, it often kills the spark — and when he plays it cool, teases, and keeps you guessing, it pulls you in. Multiply that across millions of women and you get a training program: men learn that honesty gets them rejected and games get them results.

entries.title: Is sexual directness received differently from a woman than from a man?
entries.synopsis: Yes — this is a repeatedly replicated result. In the Clark–Hatfield paradigm, a woman's direct sex offer to a male stranger typically gets a yes, while the identical offer from a man got zero acceptances from women — a gap that held on campus, in nightclubs, and in a 2025 pair of naturalistic replications.
phrases: If a woman says "I want to have sex" to a guy, most guys find it hot as hell — bold, confident, sexy. A guy says the exact same words to a woman and she's usually turned off or uncomfortable. Same sentence, opposite reception.
boundaryConditions: The original 1989 percentages (commonly cited as ~69-75% of men vs 0% of women) could not be re-verified verbatim this session — the original article and the 2025 full text both 403'd — so the ruling uses the abstract-level magnitudes confirmed on PubMed ("men quite likely to accept, women never did").
commonMisreadings: A man who propositions a stranger directly gets the reception a woman would, so directness attracts equally.

sourceLinks.label: Conley (2011), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — the Clark–Hatfield gap (men quite likely to accept a stranger's casual-sex offer, women never) disappears with attractive, famous, or friend proposers; perceived sexual skill predicts acceptance for both sexes

entries.title: Do women reward the same player behavior they complain about?
entries.synopsis: At first contact, partly yes: narcissists are more popular at first sight, and the charming traits are precisely the toxic ones — exploitativeness and entitlement (Back et al. 2010). But the reward is front-loaded: across three weeks of real contact the advantage decays as arrogance and untrustworthiness surface (Leckelt et al., n=311).
phrases: A lot of the same people who complain loudest about fuckboys and players are the ones who keep rewarding that behavior and rejecting the honest guys. They author the outcome they complain about.

If you're endlessly frustrated by fuckboys and players, look honestly at the pattern in who you actually give your time, attention, and chances to. A lot of the heartbreak comes from rewarding the exact behavior you complain about while writing off the steadier men as "boring."
boundaryConditions: No study directly tests the within-person claim — that the loudest complainers are the same individuals rewarding players — so that part rests on inference from population-level first-impression effects.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: A lot of the same people who complain loudest about fuckboys and players are the ones who keep rewarding that behavior and rejecting the honest guys. They author the outcome they complain about.

oversimplified: If you're endlessly frustrated by fuckboys and players, look honestly at the pattern in who you actually give your time, attention, and chances to. A lot of the heartbreak comes from rewarding the exact behavior you complain about while writing off the steadier men as "boring."

But the claim's "even knowing he's dishonest" clause fails: describing a target as honest raises attractiveness ratings (replicated at n=457), and narcissists' popularity decays precisely as they…

entries.title: When women say they want an honest guy, is that the real preference?
entries.synopsis: Partly. In live speed dating, ideals stated beforehand failed to predict who actually inspired desire — the stated/revealed gap is real and replicated at first attraction. But "branding" overreaches: stated ideals prospectively predicted the traits of partners singles ended up with five months later (N=763), and across 43 countries, partners matching one's own ideals were rated better (corrected β=.19, N=10,358).

"I just want a nice, honest guy" sounds good and makes you look like you've got your priorities straight — but if the men who actually make you feel something are the confident, cocky, smooth ones, then "honest guy" is branding, not your real preference.
boundaryConditions: Also verified the Eastwick, Luchies, Finkel & Hunt (2014) Psychological Bulletin meta-analysis (k=97, PMID 23586697): both sexes' live evaluations tracked attractiveness at r≈.40 with nonsignificant sex differences, backing the stated/revealed split at first attraction.

entries.title: Are men checking out of dating?
entries.synopsis: The checkout is measurable: only 50% of single U.S. men were looking for a relationship or dates in July 2022, down from 61% in 2019 (Pew, n=6,034); 63% of men under 30 are single; and past-year sexlessness among men 18–24 rose from 19% to 31% between 2000–2002 and 2016–2018 (GSS).
phrases: A lot of guys just say "fuck this" and check out entirely. Some go monk mode and pour everything into money and themselves; others swallow their pride and learn to become players too.

For a long time dating ran on an unspoken default: men approach, women select. That arrangement is quietly breaking. A growing share of younger men are opting out of approaching altogether — worn down by the apps, the rejection, and years of being told they're the problem.
boundaryConditions: The withdrawal trend itself is solid across two independent representative datasets, but the claim's motive story (bitter honest men going monk mode or turning player) is untested — Pew's self-reported reasons read as indifference/priorities, not lost hope, and self-reports may under-capture bitterness.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: A lot of guys just say "fuck this" and check out entirely. Some go monk mode and pour everything into money and themselves; others swallow their pride and learn to become players too. For the ones who only ever wanted to be decent and honest, it really is a raw deal, and a lot of them are losing hope.

oversimplified: For a long time dating ran on an unspoken default: men approach, women select. That arrangement is quietly breaking. A growing share of younger men are opting out of approaching altogether — worn down by the apps, the rejection, and years of being told they're the problem.

entries.title: Does arrogance attract, even when women say they can't stand it?
entries.synopsis: At first sight, yes — this paradox is a replicated finding. Narcissists were more popular at zero acquaintance (73-person round-robin, 2,628 dyads), the entitled, exploitative facet was the most attractive of all, and narcissism predicted real courtship success. But the decomposition matters: the pull runs through confidence, boldness, and appearance — when observers read a man as arrogant per se, desirability drops.
phrases: That mix of confidence and game is magnetic to a lot of women — even when the guy is genuinely a dick or full of it. So the very traits women say they can't stand — arrogance, being full of yourself — are often the ones that get rewarded most.

The cocky, arrogant, slightly-too-confident man often gets you in a way the kind, humble one doesn't — even when you can see he's a bit of a jerk. That confidence reads as high value, and it's genuinely magnetic.
boundaryConditions: The reward is front-loaded: Carlson & DesJardins (2015, PSPB, fetched and verified this session) found narcissists initially gained status but lost it with repeated exposure and overestimated their own popularity, so the paradox is strongest where acquaintance is thinnest. Converging support left out under the 3-source cap: Jauk et al.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: That mix of confidence and game is magnetic to a lot of women — even when the guy is genuinely a dick or full of it. So the very traits women say they can't stand — arrogance, being full of yourself — are often the ones that get rewarded most.

oversimplified: The cocky, arrogant, slightly-too-confident man often gets you in a way the kind, humble one doesn't — even when you can see he's a bit of a jerk. That confidence reads as high value, and it's genuinely magnetic.

entries.title: Does charisma make red flags disappear?
entries.synopsis: Temporarily, yes — and not just on women. In a 73-person round-robin of first meetings (2,628 dyads), the most exploitative, entitled narcissism facets were exactly the most charming at first sight. But the spell decays: across three weeks of group contact, narcissists were increasingly read as untrustworthy and their popularity sank.
phrases: Women will ignore massive red flags if the guy has enough charisma and confidence. They convince themselves "he'll change for me" or "I'm different," then act shocked when the guy who slept with 300 women behaves exactly like a guy who slept with 300 women.

The smoother and more confident he is, the more you'll be tempted to wave off the warning signs — the inconsistency, the history, the way he treats other people. "He's different with me" and "he'll change for me" are the famous last words here.
boundaryConditions: The lab evidence measures narcissism-driven first-impression charm, not literal "red flag ignoring," and Back 2010's mixed-sex round-robin plus Knopp's gender-consistent infidelity odds undercut the women-specific framing; the "he'll change for me" persistence is better explained by investment-model commitment research than by charisma.

A man becomes more attractive the moment you can tell other women want him — it's why the taken guy, the popular one, the one with options pulls harder than the equally-good man nobody's noticed. It feels like taste; a lot of it is just social proof.

Seeing that you have options — that you're genuinely chosen and pursued — spikes interest, because it triggers competition and the instinct that "if all these women want him, there must be something good here."
