Kreager, Cavanagh, Yen & Yu (2014), Journal of Marriage and Family — both sexes send messages to the most socially desirable partners regardless of their own desirability; women initiate 4x less than men.
Epley & Whitchurch (2008), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin — people recognize an attractively enhanced version of their own face as their true face (self-enhancement).

entries.title: Do men and women avoid commitment for the same reason?
entries.synopsis: The sex-typed split is half-real. Schmitt's 48-nation study (N=14,059) confirms men score reliably higher on unrestricted sociosexuality — the 'variety' motive is well-founded and cross-culturally robust. Apostolou et al. (2020) likewise found men more often single to 'flirt around' or avoid family life.
phrases: A lot of women stay uncommitted because they're holding out for a better option: they'll keep a decent "good enough" guy around as a backup while they keep looking, never fully locking in because they're always wondering if someone higher-value is a swipe away.
boundaryConditions: Schmitt's sociosexuality sex difference is robust and cross-cultural, but the specific 'women optimize/keep a backup vs men seek variety' dichotomy rests on single studies (Apostolou; Dibble) that partly conflict — back-burner counts run opposite to the claim's gendering. Regrade risk if stronger reasons-for-single sex-difference data emerges.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: A lot of women stay uncommitted because they're holding out for a better option: they'll keep a decent "good enough" guy around as a backup while they keep looking, never fully locking in because they're always wondering if someone higher-value is a swipe away.

sourceLinks.label: Schmitt (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences — 48 nations, N=14,059; men's higher unrestricted sociosexuality is large and cross-culturally universal.
Apostolou, O & Esposito (2020), Frontiers in Psychology — N=648 singles; men more often single to 'flirt around'/avoid family life, women more often 'too picky'/fearing hurt.
Dibble & Drouin (2014), Computers in Human Behavior — N=374; men reported more 'back burners' (alternative partners kept in reserve) than women.

entries.title: How much is a woman's explicit first move worth?
entries.synopsis: Rarity and weight check out; the 'men ignore it' half is shakier. Kreager et al. (2014) found women send first messages four times less often than men — and those who do initiate connect with more desirable partners, so an explicit move is both rare and a costly, informative signal.
phrases: A woman making the first explicit move — not a covert signal, but actually saying it — is genuinely rare, so when it happens it tends to carry more weight than men give it.
boundaryConditions: Kreager's 4x initiation gap is one large study; female-initiation rarity is widely observed but only this source was verified here. Haselton & Buss concerns overperception of ambiguous cues, not dismissal of explicit stated moves, so the tension with 'men wave it off' is suggestive rather than decisive.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: A woman making the first explicit move — not a covert signal, but actually saying it — is genuinely rare, so when it happens it tends to carry more weight than men give it. When a woman compliments your looks unprompted, asks for your number, or says something like "you smell nice," she's usually spent real social risk to do it.

sourceLinks.label: Kreager, Cavanagh, Yen & Yu (2014), Journal of Marriage and Family — women send first messages 4x less often than men; women who initiate connect with more desirable partners.
Haselton & Buss (2000), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — men overperceive women's sexual intent; women underperceive men's commitment (error management theory).

entries.title: Should men wait for a choosing signal before approaching?
entries.synopsis: Choosing signals are useful evidence, not an admission ticket. Moore’s field observations found that women who signaled more were approached more often, so repeated, person-specific cues raise the odds that an opening is welcome. But Hall’s two studies found actual flirting harder to identify than nonflirting; making a detectable green light mandatory would turn ordinary uncertainty into paralysis.
phrases: Men should wait for a woman to give a choosing signal before approaching. Women commonly initiate indirectly, and approaching without that green light mostly creates low-yield or unwanted attention.
boundaryConditions: No direct head-to-head outcome study comparing a strict signal-required strategy with a respectful once-and-done approach was found, which prevents a hard-data grade and makes a synthetic truth percentage inappropriate.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: Men should wait for a woman to give a choosing signal before approaching. Women commonly initiate indirectly, and approaching without that green light mostly creates low-yield or unwanted attention.

sourceLinks.label: Moore (1985), Ethology and Sociobiology — field observations: women who displayed solicitation signals more often were approached more often across four social contexts
Hall, Xing & Brooks (2014), Communication Research — two studies found actual flirting harder to identify than nonflirting for participants and outside observers
Sinclair & Frieze (2005), Sex Roles — 241 pursuer/target accounts: pursuers over-reported reciprocation and under-reported rejection as courtship became unwanted persistence

entries.title: Do women regret casual sex while men regret passing it up?
entries.synopsis: The mirror pattern is robust, not destiny. Galperin et al.’s three studies (Ns = 200, 395, and 24,230) found more casual-sex action regret among women and more missed-opportunity regret among men; the Norwegian replication and later two-wave study reproduced the average sex-linked pattern. “Tendency” is essential: it does not predict any individual, and it does not mean women usually regret casual sex.
phrases: Women have a tendency to regret casual sex they had more than men do.
Men have a tendency to regret casual sex they passed up more than women do.
boundaryConditions: Hard-data grades the replicated descriptive direction, not a proven evolutionary mechanism. Galperin’s three studies and the Norwegian replication rely on retrospective self-report; the authors’ sexual-strategies interpretation is one proposed distal explanation, not an experimental result.
commonMisreadings: Women who have casual sex regret it, so regret predicts which women date casually.

sourceLinks.label: Galperin et al. (2013), Archives of Sexual Behavior — three descriptive studies (Ns = 200, 395, 24,230) found the casual-sex action/inaction regret pattern across methods and a diverse online sample
Kennair, Bendixen & Buss (2016), Evolutionary Psychology — Norwegian replication (N = 263) plus tests of gratification, worry, reputation, and sociosexuality as competing proximate correlates
Kennair, Grøntvedt & Bendixen (2021), Evolutionary Psychology — two-wave longitudinal test found no clear evidence that regret produced the predicted later mating-behavior shifts

Sagioglou & Dick (2026), Archives of Sexual Behavior — international cross-sectional study (N = 1,044): most one-night stands neutral-to-positive; heterosexual regret gap mediated chiefly by satisfaction and orgasm

entries.title: Do romance scammers mostly prey on lonely older women?
entries.synopsis: The stereotype survives on exactly one axis: check size. FTC median losses climb steeply with age — $750 per report at 18–29 up to $9,000 at 70 and over — so when older adults are taken, they are taken hardest. Targeting cuts the other way: 52% of online daters say they’ve come across a suspected scammer, and men under 50 top the table at 63%, against 44% of women of any age.
phrases: The romance-scam victim is the lonely grandma wiring her savings to a fake soldier overseas. Young men grew up online — they can smell a catfish a mile away, and scammers don’t waste time on them.
boundaryConditions: Axes kept honest: Pew measures self-reported encounters with SUSPECTED scammers (perception, not completed victimization); the FTC counts voluntary reports, and only ~4.8% of mass-market fraud victims complain to any authority (Anderson 2021, cited in both spotlights), so age differences in reporting propensity shade every count — the report mix by age is…
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: The romance-scam victim is the lonely grandma wiring her savings to a fake soldier overseas. Young men grew up online — they can smell a catfish a mile away, and scammers don’t waste time on them.

sourceLinks.label: Pew Research Center (Feb 2023), “Key findings about online dating in the U.S.” — 52% of users encountered a suspected scammer; men under 50 highest at 63% (men 50+: 47%; women of any age: 44%); n = 6,034
FTC Data Spotlight (Feb 2022) — 2021 romance scams: record $547M reported; median individual loss by age from $750 (18–29) to $9,000 (70+); 18–29 reports up more than tenfold since 2017
FTC Data Spotlight (Feb 2023) — 2022: nearly 70,000 reports, $1.3B reported losses, median $4,400; sextortion reports over six times as likely from 18–29 as from 30+, population-normalized

entries.title: The Black Pill
entries.synopsis: The Black Pill is constraint awareness pushed toward terminal certainty. It notices that looks, early impressions, social sorting, and fixed traits matter more than polite society admits. Its useful part is realism about hard floors. Its failure is turning disadvantage into destiny.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: use Black Pill insight to identify real constraints, then return to the remaining agency. Do not confuse clear sight with a death sentence.
LE preserves constraint awareness while rejecting terminal certainty, moral ranking, and the claim that every outcome is fixed.
commonMisreadings: Total fatalism: A model that makes you less alive, less warm, and less capable has started eating the person using it.
A lens that identifies hard constraints is not itself proof that effort, context, exposure, or probability no longer matter.
pressureTests: What observable outcome would falsify the terminal version of the claim without denying the underlying constraint?

entries.title: The Height Pill
entries.synopsis: Height is the Black Pill’s favorite exhibit, and not by accident: it is a real, measurable advantage you genuinely cannot change. Women pull toward taller men more than men pull toward shorter women, and the male-taller norm shows up in almost every couple — far beyond what chance alone would produce. The lens is right that it matters and right that it’s fixed.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: count height honestly as a fixed input you can’t move — then stop relitigating it and spend the effort on the four factors you can. See the height-preference data and the Looks factor.
commonMisreadings: “It’s over under six feet” is fatalism: The premium is a window, not a ladder. The height–success curve is curvilinear: the very shortest men are penalized, but the optimum is only moderately above average — and extremely tall men get screened out too, by shorter women.

entries.title: The Face Pill
entries.synopsis: The Black Pill’s deepest fixation is the face — and its core mistake is treating it as one thing: bone. But a face is a stack of layers. The skull is the bottom one; on top sit skin and soft tissue, then framing and grooming, then the harmony of the whole — plus a side profile a front photo never shows. Raters integrate the stack, not the cephalogram.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: count the bone honestly as the one fixed layer — then stop relitigating it and work the three that move. And remember even the bone mostly prices the first glance. See The Bone Pill, checked and the Looks factor.
commonMisreadings: “Your bone-score is your fate”: The looksmaxxing pill collapses all four layers into the skull, freezes it, and scores it to a PSL decimal that “ends” you. Three of the four layers are improvable, single bones explain little alone, and the shared score itself dissolves once someone actually knows you. A real input is laundered into a sealed verdict.

entries.title: Sort the constraint before you obey it
entries.synopsis: The Black Pill is most useful as a diagnostic pass, not a permanent residence. When an outcome keeps repeating, separate what is fixed from what is trainable and what belongs to the environment. That prevents two equal-and-opposite mistakes: trying to self-improve your way through a hard limit, or calling a changeable bottleneck destiny.
boundaryConditions: The useful sentence: “This channel exposes a constraint.” The fatalistic sentence: “This result explains my whole future.” The first invites a decision; the second erases every variable the test never measured.
commonMisreadings: A repeated bad outcome reveals a fixed limit that explains how the rest will go.

entries.title: The Black Pill makes predictions. Here is the scoreboard.
entries.synopsis: A lens earns its authority by predicting things. The Black Pill does make claims specific enough to check — which is more than most dating advice manages, and worth crediting. So check them. Three of its four load-bearing claims land in the same place: the direction is right, the magnitude is inflated, and the fourth one is not a claim at all.
aliases: Black Pill makes predictions. Here is the scoreboard.
boundaryConditions: Read the scoreboard honestly in both directions. The Black Pill is not wrong about the world; it is wrong about the size of the world. It found four real effects and rounded every one of them up to infinity. And the fourth line is the reason the first three never get corrected from the inside: the lens ships with a clause that immunizes it. Take the effects.
commonMisreadings: The Black Pill gets its dating predictions right, so its whole model of attraction holds.

entries.title: Just Be First
entries.synopsis: A timing exploit that can override normal SMV matching. The person who arrives before comparison pressure and full market calibration can form a bond that the open market might never have produced.
boundaryConditions: Important: this is not a moral ideal or a seduction recommendation. It is a structural story about timing, calibration, and why some mismatches survive because they formed before the open market could price them.
LE states outright that this is not a moral ideal or a seduction recommendation, but a structural story about timing and calibration.
The mechanic depends on a low-feedback environment before full market calibration, and explains why some mismatches survive rather than predicting that they will.
commonMisreadings: Just be first is the strategy: lock a woman in before she learns her own dating value.
pressureTests: Did the pairing form before comparison pressure was salient, or is "we met young" explaining a match that would have formed anyway?

entries.title: “It’s over”
entries.synopsis: The verdict phrase. It converts a measured penalty into a finished sentence. Every study behind it reports a slope or a shifted distribution — never a closed door.
commonMisreadings: A man below average in looks has his dating future closed permanently by that measurement.

entries.title: “Cope”
entries.synopsis: The thought-terminating rebuttal. Anything that contradicts the model gets reclassified as denial, which makes the model unfalsifiable — and an unfalsifiable model has stopped describing the world.
commonMisreadings: Anyone disputing the looks verdict is coping, so disagreement itself proves the dating model correct.

entries.title: LMS
entries.synopsis: Looks, Money, Status — attraction reduced to three things you supposedly cannot move. Two of the three are movable over a decade, and the reduction quietly deletes charm and exposure entirely.
commonMisreadings: Three fixed traits settle who gets picked, so a man's dating outcome is decided at birth.

entries.title: The Red Pill
entries.synopsis: The Red Pill treats dating as a market shaped by incentives, asymmetry, self-presentation, leverage, and strategic behavior. Its useful part is agency: improve the offer, read signals, understand incentives. Its failure mode is contempt dressed up as realism.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: use Red Pill insight to become more effective, not less humane. If it makes you sharper but colder, you are losing part of the game.
Descriptive patterns and strategies remain probabilistic and cannot override autonomy, consent, safety, or individual variation.
commonMisreadings: Contempt as doctrine: Strategy becomes poison when it loses empathy and starts treating people as enemies instead of people with incentives.
A strategy that improves odds does not create entitlement to another person's response.
pressureTests: Would the strategy still be defensible if the other person's agency and full information were made explicit?

entries.title: The Dread Pill
entries.synopsis: Dread is the Red Pill’s most operational instruction: if your partner has stopped trying, make them feel replaceable and the effort comes back. It is worth taking seriously precisely because the observation underneath it is correct — comfort is not desire, and a partnership where one side has quietly stopped competing does decay. The failure is not the diagnosis.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: treat dread as a diagnostic, never a tactic. If the thought “they’d panic if I had options” is appealing, the real finding is that you have no options and have been coasting on their inertia. Fix that — honestly, out loud, and where they can see it.
commonMisreadings: Engineering the fear is a measured tactic with a measured cost: Deliberate jealousy induction has its own research literature, and the results are not ambiguous. Fleischmann et al. (2005) found the tactic’s goals split into seeking rewards and seeking revenge, and that the partner responses it produces include aggression and withdrawal, not just renewed…

entries.title: Turn observation into an ethical loop
entries.synopsis: The Red Pill becomes constructive when strategy means noticing feedback and improving your side of the interaction. It becomes theater when every conversation is a dominance test and every person is reduced to a predictable opponent. A clean strategy loop keeps agency while leaving the other person fully free to say yes, no, or not yet.
commonMisreadings: Every conversation with a potential partner is a dominance test you either pass or fail.

entries.title: Six tells that clarity has turned into contempt
entries.synopsis: The dossier says the Red Pill’s failure mode is contempt dressed up as realism. That is easy to agree with and useless as a warning, because nobody experiences their own contempt as contempt — from the inside it feels like finally seeing straight. So here are the observable symptoms instead. These are behavioural tells, not thoughtcrimes: the test is what you do, not what you have read.
boundaryConditions: The repair is not to become naive again. Keep every accurate observation and re-attach it to an action you could still respect if it failed. Contempt is what strategy decays into once it stops producing anything — and the honest question is not “am I bitter?” but “what has this analysis actually got me in the last six months?”
commonMisreadings: Anyone who has turned contemptuous in a romance can feel it happening and self-correct.

entries.title: Hypergamy
entries.synopsis: The tendency to seek upward in status, resources, desirability, or perceived mate value. Useful as a pressure concept; dangerous when treated as a cartoon law.
boundaryConditions: LE indexes hypergamy as a useful pressure concept and a dangerous cartoon law — a directional pull over status, resources, desirability, and perceived mate value, not a threshold.
The Red Pill dossier's operating rule caps it: strategy stops being useful when it turns into blanket claims about women or men.
commonMisreadings: Hypergamy is a law with zero exceptions: a woman always leaves her man to date someone richer.
pressureTests: Is the claim stated as a tendency with variation, or as a law no counterexample can touch?

entries.title: Preselection
entries.synopsis: Interest can rise when other people visibly want you. Social proof does not create all attraction, but it can change how value is read.
boundaryConditions: LE's claim is that visible wanting changes how existing value is read, not that social proof creates all attraction or manufactures value on inspection.
LE grades the mate-specific reading Contested: preselection may be domain-general social learning, since people copy others' choices about many things.
commonMisreadings: Social proof creates attraction outright, so women want any man other women were seen with.
pressureTests: Is the effect being attributed to mate-specific copying, or is domain-general social learning a sufficient explanation?

entries.title: Frame
entries.synopsis: The ability to hold your center without begging the room to validate you. At its best, calm self-command; at its worst, performative dominance.
boundaryConditions: LE indexes frame as calm self-command at its best and performative dominance at its worst; citing only the healthy reading drops half the entry.
The Red Pill dossier names manipulation as its distortion and caps the technique: sharper but colder counts as losing part of the game.
commonMisreadings: Frame means dominating every exchange and staying cold, so a woman wants a man who dominates.
pressureTests: Is the frame being described self-command, or a performance staged for an audience?

entries.title: Shit test
entries.synopsis: A provocation read as a covert stability check. People genuinely do probe for steadiness before trusting someone. Reading every friction as a rigged exam is how a partner stops being a person and becomes an examiner.
commonMisreadings: Every argument a woman starts while dating is a covert test of your steadiness.

entries.title: Dread
entries.synopsis: Deliberately raising a partner’s fear of losing you to restore their effort. The most operational advice the lens gives, and the one that has actually been measured — badly. See the case below.
commonMisreadings: Making a romantic partner feel replaceable reliably restores their effort and strengthens the relationship.

entries.title: Abundance
entries.synopsis: Having enough going on that no single outcome owns you. Real as a life; fake as a posture. Built abundance changes your behaviour; performed abundance only changes your messaging.
commonMisreadings: Performing abundance while dating attracts partners just as well as actually having options.

entries.title: The Blue Pill
entries.synopsis: The Blue Pill treats romance as sincere, fair, moral, and personality-driven. Its useful part is warmth: love is not just sorting math, and people need trust, affection, kindness, and safety. Its failure is denying the thresholds that decide who gets considered in the first place.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: keep the heart. Drop the denial. The synthesis needs romance, but it also needs eyes.
Hope, character, and compatibility can matter without erasing attraction thresholds, market structure, or timing.
commonMisreadings: Fair-world comfort: Kindness is not a substitute for attraction. Personality matters, but usually after a first filter has been passed.
Rejecting fatalism does not require pretending that every preference is negotiable or that effort guarantees selection.
pressureTests: What observed rejection or selection pattern would the optimistic account need to explain rather than dismiss?

entries.title: The Soulmate Pill
entries.synopsis: The Blue Pill’s deepest article of faith is that somewhere there is the person, and that finding them is what a good relationship is made of. Psychologists have measured this belief for decades under two names — destiny beliefs, that a pairing either is right or is not, versus growth beliefs, that a relationship is built out of effort over time (Knee, 1998; Franiuk, Cohen & Pomerantz, 2002).
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: feel destiny, run growth. Let chosenness be the story you tell about your partner, and never the instrument you use to evaluate a bad week. The practical form is one substitution: when something goes wrong, the question is “what does this need?” — never “does this mean they’re not the one?”
commonMisreadings: Fit as a verdict instead of a project: The trapdoor is the theory of trouble, not the theory of love. Once difficulty counts as evidence against the match, every relationship reaches the point where the belief tells you to leave — and the searching it sends you back to is for a person with whom nothing goes wrong. Nobody has ever met them.

entries.title: Kindness is not the key to every door. It is what makes a room livable.
entries.synopsis: Blue Pill advice often fails because it puts relationship virtues at the first-impression stage. Kindness, loyalty, patience, and communication are enormously valuable, but much of their value can only be observed after contact repeats. The correction is not to discard them. It is to place them at the stages where they can do their real work.
commonMisreadings: Being kind and loyal enough is what earns attraction from someone you just met.

entries.title: Just be yourself
entries.synopsis: Healthy when it means authenticity. Harmful when it means refusing to improve presentation, social skill, standards, or exposure.
boundaryConditions: LE rates this healthy when it means authenticity and harmful when it means refusing to improve presentation, social skill, standards, or exposure — not wrong outright.
It says nothing about the first filter: the Blue Pill dossier's own discard is that kindness is not a substitute for attraction.
commonMisreadings: Improving your style and social skills is fake, so a man just being himself attracts women.
pressureTests: Is "be yourself" protecting a real self, or protecting an untouched presentation, social skill, standard, or exposure level?

entries.title: Personality matters
entries.synopsis: True but incomplete. Personality can deepen, convert, and sustain attraction. It does not always create initial consideration from nothing.
boundaryConditions: LE marks this true but incomplete: personality can deepen, convert, and sustain attraction, but does not always create initial consideration from nothing.
The claim is scoped to what happens once attraction has opened the door; the dossier's failure mode is reading rejection as a moral failure of the market.
commonMisreadings: A good personality creates attraction from scratch, so any man with one makes women want him.
pressureTests: Is personality being credited with converting and sustaining attraction, or with creating it from nothing?

entries.title: The right person
entries.synopsis: Useful as patience, dangerous as passivity. The right person still has to meet you, notice you, want you, and choose you.
boundaryConditions: Patience and passivity produce the same visible behaviour, and only one of them keeps meeting new people.
commonMisreadings: The right person arrives without being met, so a man who waits patiently will marry.

entries.title: Chemistry
entries.synopsis: Real, and a poor forecaster. It reports how the first hours felt, not whether two people can run a decade together. Treated as a verdict, it screens out slow-burn matches and waves through volatile ones.
commonMisreadings: Instant chemistry on a date forecasts whether a romance will last for a decade.

entries.title: “Love conquers all”
entries.synopsis: Affection is not a solvent. It does not dissolve incompatible plans about children, money, geography, or faith. Feeling strongly about someone tells you the stakes, never the answer.
commonMisreadings: Loving someone enough settles every practical disagreement, so a romance survives on strength of emotion.

entries.title: “Don’t settle”
entries.synopsis: Sound as a floor, corrosive as a ceiling. It correctly refuses contempt and neglect; it wrongly licenses rejecting a real person for failing to match a composite who does not exist.
commonMisreadings: Holding out for a flawless partner is always right, so rejecting real dating prospects costs little.

entries.title: SMV (Sexual Market Value)
entries.synopsis: Your desirability as priced by the dating market — looks, money, status, charm, exposure, scaled by timing and competition. A market read, not a measure of human worth.
boundaryConditions: Pricing by a market and judging a person are separate operations, and only the first is what a score reports.
commonMisreadings: A man's market value measures his human worth, so a low score means he deserves less.

entries.title: Assortative mating
entries.synopsis: The tendency to pair with someone of similar overall value. On looks alone the average couple matches (r ≈ 0.4) rather than one side relentlessly trading up.
boundaryConditions: The r of roughly 0.4 is observer-rated physical attractiveness; similarity on education or income is a separate correlation.
It describes who ended up paired, not who received attention — app attention skews far harder than pairing does.
commonMisreadings: Assortative mating is a law: couples always match on looks, so mismatched couples break up.
pressureTests: Is this measuring who actually paired, or who received attention?

entries.title: The Wall
entries.synopsis: The claim that a woman’s value falls off a cliff around 30. Real as a slope, false as a cliff — and it measures stranger-attention, not whether she actually pairs.
boundaryConditions: Stranger attention and actual pairing move differently with age, so a curve drawn on one mispredicts the other.
commonMisreadings: A woman's attractiveness collapses at thirty, so men stop wanting to date her after that.

entries.title: Looks Rating (support & resistance)
entries.synopsis: Every looks score carries a support floor and a resistance ceiling — a band inside which familiarity, bias, and behavior move perception, and outside which they don’t. First reads are accurate; the band is how much drift that accuracy leaves room for.
boundaryConditions: The band bounds how far perception travels; where the first rating came from is a separate question.
commonMisreadings: A looks rating drifts freely, so any partner will eventually find you attractive.
pressureTests: Is the lift inside one observer's band, or is it a fresh rating by a different observer?

entries.title: The Matching Curve
entries.synopsis: Within-sex looks matching among couples that already formed: the further from average you sit, the harder your partner regresses toward the middle. One curve for both sexes — not a discovered sex-difference but a consequence of scoring within sex. Read the column as the average partner, not the typical one.
boundaryConditions: The curve describes couples that already formed, so it cannot be read as who pairs at all.
commonMisreadings: A top-rated woman dates a partner rated exactly as high as herself.
pressureTests: Is the number an average partner or a typical one, and how wide is the spread around it?

entries.title: The Option Pool
entries.synopsis: Who can be converted from attention into a date or a commitment — a different question from who reacts. Options are asymmetric; pairings are not. A woman’s raw pool usually reaches above her looks line with commitment gated; a man’s sits at or below his unless status, competence, or familiarity lifts it.
boundaryConditions: Reach into a partner tier and conversion into a couple are separate measurements on the same ladder.
commonMisreadings: A woman's option pool is the set of men she will actually date and keep.
pressureTests: Is this access to a tier, or an outcome recorded with one?

entries.title: The Supply-and-Demand Rule
entries.synopsis: When one side of a local dating pool is scarcer, that side can be more selective while the more numerous side competes harder. The rule changes bargaining conditions, not anyone’s worth — and it only works after age, location, eligibility, economic filters, and who is actually searching are counted.
commonMisreadings: The sex ratio where you live decides your dating results before you even try.

entries.title: Conversion Ladder
entries.synopsis: The stage model separating being seen, noticed, desired, chosen, and kept. It keeps attention, attraction, commitment, and retention from being confused.
boundaryConditions: The ladder names where a person stalls, not why; the same stall can come from exposure, presentation or fit.
Stage order is the typical sequence, not a requirement — social-circle markets routinely collapse being seen and being known.
commonMisreadings: Attention is attraction, attraction is selection, so a woman who likes your photo has chosen you.
pressureTests: Which rung is this evidence actually drawn from — visibility, attraction, selection or retention?

entries.title: The Interaction Gate
entries.synopsis: Use profiles and scores to screen out known incompatibility; use richer interaction to learn pair-specific chemistry, ease, and reciprocity. A hard boundary stays hard, and nobody is owed a meeting.
boundaryConditions: A hard incompatibility and an unknown chemistry need different tests, and only the first can be screened in advance.
commonMisreadings: Screening on a profile alone settles whether two people will actually get along dating.

entries.title: The Readiness Gate
entries.synopsis: For a commitment goal, interest and present willingness to build are separate gates. “Not ready” is a current boundary, not a delayed yes or a renovation project.
boundaryConditions: Interest and present willingness are separate gates, so one can run high while the other stays closed.
commonMisreadings: A woman who wants him but delays commitment will marry him once he waits longer.

entries.title: The Good-News Rule
entries.synopsis: Celebrate before you evaluate: notice a partner’s win, recognize why it matters, ask a genuine follow-up, then celebrate in a form they can receive. Practical caution can follow without swallowing the moment.
boundaryConditions: Celebrating first and evaluating later are ordered steps, so practical caution can follow without displacing the moment.
commonMisreadings: Leading with caution instead of celebration builds attraction and the relationship stability that keeps couples together.

entries.title: Attention
entries.synopsis: Market signal before selection: views, likes, messages, glances, replies. Attention can be abundant and still low-intent; scarce and still high-quality.
boundaryConditions: Attention is market signal, not selection, and says nothing about whether anyone was chosen or kept.
Attention volume is platform-shaped; a skew measured inside a swipe app does not transfer to social-circle markets.
commonMisreadings: A woman's pile of dating-app likes proves she is desired, because attention and selection are the same.
pressureTests: Is the number a count of attention received, or of relationships formed?

entries.title: Desire
entries.synopsis: The felt pull toward someone. It may arrive spontaneously or emerge responsively inside a willing, rewarding context; neither sequence is consent, commitment, or long-term fit.
boundaryConditions: Desire says nothing about long-term fit; the traits that spike the pull and those that sustain a bond are not the same list.
Desire is warmer and narrower than attention and does not aggregate into a market rate the way attention counts do.
Responsive describes the timing of desire inside a willing context; it does not turn reluctance into consent.
commonMisreadings: A man she desires is a man she will choose, so desire and commitment are the same.
Responsive desire means willingness can be assumed before it appears.
pressureTests: Would the person doing the desiring actually pay an opportunity cost for it?
Is there genuine willingness and room to stop before responsive desire is invoked?

entries.title: Commitment
entries.synopsis: Selection over alternatives. Someone can desire you without choosing you; commitment is where attraction starts paying opportunity cost.
boundaryConditions: Commitment is a present willingness, not a forecast; a stated intention that has never cost anything has not been tested.
It describes selection against alternatives, so where alternatives are absent the same behavior carries far less information.
commonMisreadings: A man who keeps showing up is committed, so he already chooses you over everyone else.
Wanting predictability is wanting commitment, so a person who prefers the same partner every week has already paid the opportunity cost.
pressureTests: What alternative was actually forgone here, and what did forgoing it cost?

entries.title: Pairing
entries.synopsis: The outcome where two people actually form a couple. Pairing data answers a different question than app attention, casual access, or fantasy preference.
boundaryConditions: Pairing counts couples formed and does not measure whether they lasted or whether either side was satisfied.
Pairing rates are slow-moving and cohort-bound, so a rate from one country or decade does not transfer without argument.
commonMisreadings: The top twenty percent of men pair with every woman worth dating, so pairing is winner-take-all.
pressureTests: Is this a count of couples formed, or of likes, matches and hypothetical preferences?

entries.title: Stranger market
entries.synopsis: The arena where people judge with little or no exposure: apps, cold approach, first glance. It prices looks and status hardest because almost nothing else has time to compound.
boundaryConditions: The concept stops applying wherever repeated exposure exists; inside a social circle, charm and familiarity modify the first read.
Findings drawn from dating apps are stranger-market findings and do not license claims about how couples form in shared workplaces.
commonMisreadings: The stranger market is the whole dating market, so app data explains how every couple formed.
pressureTests: How much exposure did these people have to each other before rating one another?

entries.title: Social-circle market
entries.synopsis: The arena where repeated exposure lets charm, trust, competence, and familiarity modify the first read. Slower, less scalable, and often more forgiving than the stranger market.
boundaryConditions: The advantage is access-gated, not value-gated: it requires a circle to be inside and does not scale the way app exposure does.
The model assumes genuinely repeated contact; a single second meeting is not the exposure it depends on.
commonMisreadings: Inside a social circle enough familiarity makes looks stop mattering, so any man can date anyone.
pressureTests: Did these people have repeated contact, or were they rating a photo?

entries.title: Sex recession
entries.synopsis: The rise in young adults reporting no sex in the past year, especially visible among young men. It is the attention deficit made measurable, not proof that everyone is doomed.
phrases: no sex in the past year
boundaryConditions: The measure is self-reported and bounded to the past twelve months; it does not separate involuntary celibacy from choice or life stage.
The effect is concentrated among young men — extending the slope across ages or both sexes overstates it.
commonMisreadings: The sex recession means most young men and women are sexless and want a partner desperately.
pressureTests: Does the source separate involuntary sexlessness from deliberate withdrawal?

entries.title: Cope
entries.synopsis: Any comforting story used to dodge a hard truth. A useful scalpel — but “that’s cope” is itself often used to wave away evidence that complicates the blackpill.
boundaryConditions: The label describes a motive for holding a belief, not the belief's truth value; motive and accuracy are independent.
It only does work where a hard truth has been established; where the underlying claim is contested, the accusation begs the question.
commonMisreadings: Calling it cope settles the argument, so a comforting claim about dating is automatically worthless.
pressureTests: If this belief were true, would the person still be accused of coping for holding it?

entries.title: The 7–7 Rule
entries.synopsis: The long-term qualification gate: looks ≥ 7 and personality composite ≥ 7, scored independently — a high score on one never buys back the other. A rule about frequency, not a law.
boundaryConditions: Both scores are graded independently, which is what stops a high mark on one from buying back the other.
commonMisreadings: A woman scoring nine on looks clears the gate, so men will date her regardless of personality.

entries.title: Sub-5 (Auto Disqualification)
entries.synopsis: One important component under 5 trips the floor no matter how strong the rest is — averages launder weak points. Binds only if you clear 5 yourself; below that, Parity overrides it.
boundaryConditions: The floor binds only on someone who clears five themselves, and below that parity overrides it.
commonMisreadings: One weak component disqualifies a partner outright, whatever the person doing the scoring rates himself.

entries.title: The Parity Rule
entries.synopsis: Your realistic ideal is your own coordinates: a 6–6 pairs with a 6–6. The 7–7 is the universal aspiration; parity is the attainable one. You don’t marry the gate — you marry your tier.
boundaryConditions: A universal aspiration and an attainable target are different numbers, and this one is the second.
commonMisreadings: Everyone should hold out for a seven on looks and seven on personality when dating.

entries.title: The Spiderman Effect
entries.synopsis: To another 6–6 you read as their 7–7, and they as yours. Mutual belief makes the subjective upgrade function as real — the humane resolution of parity’s cap.
boundaryConditions: Mutual belief works inside the band that bounds how far perception moves, so it lifts the reading rather than the rating.
commonMisreadings: Mutual belief raises two partners' actual market ratings, so the upgrade shows up to strangers dating them.

entries.title: Treatment Markup
entries.synopsis: How you treat a partner earns a real markup on top of base value — enough to clear a parity bracket, never enough to turn a 4 into an 8. Behavior is value-add, not décor.
boundaryConditions: The markup applies on top of a base value that already cleared consideration and does nothing at the stranger-market stage.
Its size is a modeled magnitude, not a measured one — roughly one parity bracket, by judgment rather than a published effect size.
commonMisreadings: Treating a partner well overrides any looks gap, so good treatment alone makes a woman want you.
pressureTests: Is the claimed uplift within one bracket of base value, or being asked to carry two?

entries.title: The Sham
entries.synopsis: A relationship that persists without the thing it appears to be about — motive holding it up (hard sham) or a mismatch nobody names (soft sham). Not a bad relationship: one the attraction model can’t account for.
boundaryConditions: A hard sham held up by motive and a soft sham nobody names are separate diagnoses, and neither means the pairing is bad.
commonMisreadings: A couple staying together for motive rather than desire have a relationship anyone would call bad.

entries.title: The Ownership Load
entries.synopsis: The invisible household work before and around a task: anticipating, deciding, arranging, remembering, and checking. Doing what was assigned is execution; carrying what happens without a reminder is ownership. Lab find · 2026-07-31 · Petts et al. 2025
boundaryConditions: Execution and ownership can be divided differently; the term names the anticipating, deciding and monitoring layer, not every unpleasant feeling about housework.
commonMisreadings: Doing the chores a partner assigns means the ownership load is already equal.
pressureTests: Would the task still be noticed and completed if the usual manager stopped reminding anyone?

entries.title: Clock, Market, Context
entries.synopsis: The three multipliers that scale all five levers: your timing, the market you’re standing in, and what that market selects for. Raise the levers; respect the multipliers.
boundaryConditions: The three scale the levers rather than adding to them; a zero on the levers stays a zero however favourable the market.
The multiplier framing is a modeling convention for how timing and venue scale value, not a measured coefficient.
commonMisreadings: A strong five-lever score wins in any dating market, so timing and venue are irrelevant.
pressureTests: Would this claim still hold in a different age band and a different market?

entries.title: The Great Unbundling
entries.synopsis: The historical arc: marriage once bundled sex, children, residence, economics, care, and adult standing into one contract — and the last two centuries pulled the functions loose one by one.
boundaryConditions: The functions came loose one at a time across two centuries, so which one is being counted decides the date.
Residence, property, care and commitment can move separately; one is not a safe proxy for the others.
Sleep and intimacy can be routed through different times or spaces, but the evidence does not rank separate or shared sleep for couples generally.
Separate sleep can solve a practical sleep conflict without solving relationship conflict; mutuality and a replacement channel for intimacy remain relevant.
commonMisreadings: Marriage still bundles sex, children, money and adult standing, so couples who marry get all four.
Partners who do not share a household cannot be committed to each other.
Couples who sleep separately are less intimate, while couples who share a bed have healthier relationships.
pressureTests: Is bed-sharing being used as a proxy for intimacy, commitment or relationship quality that the source did not measure?

entries.title: Living apart together (LAT)
entries.synopsis: Intimate partners maintaining separate households: a clean specimen of the Great Unbundling, where partnership stays joined while residence and property stay separate. It is not automatically casual, and the evidence does not say living apart is better. Lab find · 2026-07-31 · Hu + Coulter 2025
boundaryConditions: The mental-health evidence is longitudinal but specific to UK adults aged 60 to 85; it does not show that separate households are better for couples generally.
LAT separates partnership from residence; it does not by itself reveal commitment, exclusivity, care or financial integration.
commonMisreadings: Partners who keep separate homes are casual, less committed or not a real couple.
pressureTests: Is co-residence being used as a proxy for a relationship feature that was never measured?

entries.title: Third places
entries.synopsis: The venues that weren’t home or work — church, club, league, corner bar — where couples used to form for free. They emptied out before the apps won; the apps won partly by default.
boundaryConditions: The venue decline is measured mostly on US civic, religious and associational participation and is not automatically the same elsewhere.
The concept covers where people meet, not who they choose — restoring a third place changes exposure, not standards.
commonMisreadings: The dating apps emptied the third places where couples used to meet before them.
pressureTests: Does the timeline put the venue decline after the apps, or before them?

entries.title: Situationship
entries.synopsis: Relationship behavior without the relationship title — intimacy real, terms undefined, exit costless. Tried on the Mythbuster: real and rising, short of “the dominant form.”
boundaryConditions: The label describes the absence of defined terms, not the presence of dysfunction; some are honestly negotiated by both sides.
Prevalence figures come from self-labelling surveys, so they track how far the word spread as much as the arrangement.
commonMisreadings: A situationship is dysfunction by definition, so dating in one always wastes both people's time.
pressureTests: Is the source measuring the arrangement, or how many people now use the word for it?

entries.title: Post-wall
entries.synopsis: Manosphere shorthand for a woman past 30, spoken of as expired. The site’s read of the actual curves: a slope everyone walks at different grades, not a cliff one sex falls off.
boundaryConditions: The age effect is steepest in low-exposure settings where a photograph is the whole signal, and flattens where exposure carries.
It is an aggregate slope that makes no prediction about any individual, and men walk their own version of it.
commonMisreadings: She is post-wall at thirty, so men reject her and her dating life is over.
pressureTests: Is the evidence a drop in attention received, or a drop in relationships formed?

entries.title: Pick-me
entries.synopsis: The label thrown at a woman who says out loud how women tend to behave. Rarely a rebuttal — usually social policing that reframes honesty as betrayal.
boundaryConditions: The term describes a rhetorical move inside female social enforcement; it does not establish that the accused woman was correct either.
The site's read is about how the label functions, not a measured claim about how often it is deployed.
commonMisreadings: A woman who admits how women date is just a pick-me, so her point is worthless.
pressureTests: If a man had said the same sentence, would it have drawn a rebuttal instead of a label?

entries.title: Abundance blindness
entries.synopsis: The flood of low-effort attention women receive hides how scarce attention is for average men — each side generalizes its own inbox and misreads the other’s market.
boundaryConditions: The blindness runs both ways; treating it as a one-sided female failure to notice is the same generalization the concept names.
It describes stranger-market attention, mostly on apps — inside a social circle neither inbox is the relevant signal.
commonMisreadings: Women get flooded with attention on dating apps, so they have it easy and men suffer.
pressureTests: Whose inbox is this generalizing from, and would it survive being stated from the other side?

entries.title: The Abundance Trap
entries.synopsis: What visible abundance does to the chooser: with the whole distribution on screen, evaluation replaces connection and standards drift without the market moving. Choice overload survives replication only as a conditional effect — and dating sits where the conditions concentrate. Lab find · 2026-07-26 · Pew 2023
boundaryConditions: Standards drifting and the market improving are different explanations for the same visible rise in what someone expects.
commonMisreadings: Seeing more options raises a chooser's standards because the market genuinely improved around her dating.

entries.title: 4B
entries.synopsis: The Korean women’s refusal movement — no dating, sex, marriage, childbirth. Cited as the women’s strike, but the timing undercuts the causal story: Korea went sub-replacement in 1983, decades before the hashtag.
boundaryConditions: Korea went sub-replacement in 1983, decades before the movement existed, so the timing puts 4B downstream of the trend.
It is a South Korean phenomenon with its own labor-market conditions; exporting it as a general model of Western withdrawal is unsupported.
commonMisreadings: The 4B movement made Korean women refuse dating and marriage, which caused the birth-rate collapse.
pressureTests: Does the trend this is blamed for start before or after the movement did?

entries.title: Halo effect
entries.synopsis: The “beautiful is good” bias: one strong trait — usually looks — colors how every other trait gets read. Real and replicated, and a big slice of why the looks lever leaks into all the others.
boundaryConditions: The halo is strongest at low exposure and on rated first impressions; sustained acquaintance supplies the evidence that dissolves it.
It explains why the looks lever leaks into the others; it does not mean the other levers are only looks in disguise.
commonMisreadings: The halo effect is accurate — attractive people really are kinder and make better dating partners.
pressureTests: Were the other traits measured independently, or rated by people who could see the face?

entries.title: Friend zone
entries.synopsis: Where one-sided desire gets parked and the friendship is the consolation prize. Real as an asymmetry; toxic when treated as a debt owed — see the emotional harem for the exploitative version.
boundaryConditions: The concept covers unreciprocated desire inside a genuine friendship; knowing extraction of support is the emotional harem instead.
It describes a state, not a cause — landing there is not by itself evidence about either person’s value.
commonMisreadings: Being in the friend zone for years means a woman owes you a chance at dating.
pressureTests: Is the complaint that desire was not reciprocated, or that reciprocation was owed?

entries.title: Heteropessimism
entries.synopsis: Performed despair about straight life — regret, embarrassment, hopelessness — that almost never comes with actually leaving it. Named by Asa Seresin (2019), who called it an anesthetic: it numbs the feeling instead of changing the conditions. The site’s read: the mainstream mirror of the black pill.
boundaryConditions: Performed despair and an actual exit are separate measurements, and most speakers produce only the first.
commonMisreadings: Heteropessimists have actually stopped dating men, so the despair predicts who leaves the market.
pressureTests: Would this speaker's dating behaviour over the next year differ from someone who never said any of it?

entries.title: Search cost
entries.synopsis: What being in the market charges you to stay in it — time, money, attention, and a running dose of rejection. Matters because a model that prices only the people can read a stopping rule as a preference: someone who accepts a partner after a long search may have revalued nobody and simply run out of budget.
boundaryConditions: Search theory shows costly looking can tier a market; it does not establish that search cost tiers this one.
commonMisreadings: Someone who settles in dating after a long search has revalued the partner they accepted.

entries.title: Costly signal
entries.synopsis: A claim you can believe because it would have been expensive to send falsely. The theorem is narrower than the slogan — separation needs a cost that differs across senders, not merely a high one — but the working question is blunt: what would this have cost if it were false? Nothing means decoration. A body someone has to arrive in, a reputation, two years of training: evidence.
boundaryConditions: Separation requires a cost that differs across sender types, so absolute expense alone settles little.
commonMisreadings: An expensive display in dating is reliable evidence about the person sending it.

entries.title: Network approval
entries.synopsis: What the friends and family around a couple think of it — and it travels with whether the couple lasts. The famous opposite claim, the Romeo and Juliet effect (parental interference deepens love), was re-tested and did not appear; interference tracked poorer quality on every measure. Correlational throughout, and mostly one partner’s guess at what everyone else thinks, so the causal arrow stays open.
boundaryConditions: The evidence is correlational and mostly records one partner's perception of what the network thinks.
commonMisreadings: Family opposition to a romance pushes the couple closer together and strengthens their bond.

entries.title: The re-entry discount
entries.synopsis: The claim that the market you return to after a relationship ends is not the one you left — the cohort thinned, constraints grew, and the exchange rate you last transacted at went stale. Runs in both directions; the discourse only ever aims it at women, and the divorced man rediscovering that his twenties-era approach no longer clears is the same mechanism without a catchphrase.
boundaryConditions: No study measures the three components as a combined effect on re-entrant outcomes.
commonMisreadings: A woman returning to dating after divorce faces a thinner market than a man does.

entries.title: Substitute good
entries.synopsis: What someone leaving the dating market leaves for — gaming, pornography, parasocial media, synthetic companionship — delivering part of the reward at a fraction of the cost with the rejection risk removed. The economics are describable and the causal arrow is not: substitution and complementarity look identical in cross-section, so whether substitutes start a withdrawal, prolong it, or merely occupy the freed time is…
boundaryConditions: Substitution and complementarity are observationally identical in cross-section, so the direction stays unresolved.
commonMisreadings: Pornography and video games are why young men stopped dating and pursuing relationships.

entries.title: The calibration error
entries.synopsis: The gap between how you rate your own looks and how strangers rate them — about r ≈ 0.24, close to orthogonal. It is also bottom-heavy: measured against stranger ratings, the low-rated group over-places itself while the top rates itself accurately or slightly low. Fences every instrument on this site, because they all take a self-supplied number.
boundaryConditions: The correlation does not convert into a point-scale margin of error, and none is published here.
commonMisreadings: A dating self-rating is close enough to a stranger's rating to argue about single points.

entries.title: The consumer unit
entries.synopsis: Coupling read as an economic arrangement rather than only a romantic one. For most of the twentieth century the couple was the primary consumer unit — the household advertising was aimed at, and marital consumption was the shape the promised “good life” took. Seresin (2019) argues that dyad has been replaced by a smaller one: the individual consumer and her phone.
aliases: the couple as a consumer unit
boundaryConditions: This describes consumption incentives around coupling, and says nothing about how much any individual wants a partner.
commonMisreadings: Marriage is purely an economic arrangement, so romance and attraction are marketing invented to sell households.
pressureTests: If the couple stopped being the unit advertisers target, which measured dating or marriage behaviour changed with it?

entries.title: The Marriage Bar
entries.synopsis: A socially defined economic-readiness threshold that gates marriage specifically — a third gate that neither interest nor willingness measures. Among U.S. cohabiters who want to marry someday, about three-in-ten name their partner’s (29%) or their own (27%) lack of financial readiness as a major reason they are not engaged; interview work finds the household already working while the wedding waits on savings, debt…
boundaryConditions: The figures describe U.S. cohabiters who say they want to marry someday, not all unmarried couples.

About three-in-ten name a partner's (29%) or their own (27%) financial readiness as a major reason they are not engaged, which leaves it unnamed by most of that sample; the household-already-working picture comes from interview work, not a rate.
commonMisreadings: If two people actually wanted to be married they would be — an unmarried couple that has been together for years is telling you one of them isn't interested.
Money is an excuse people give; the real gate is always commitment.

entries.title: The Meeting Channel
entries.synopsis: Where the looking happens, treated as a variable rather than as weather. The apps, friends, work, school, a bar, a congregation, a hobby — each channel draws a different pool, reads a different trait first, and bills a different cost; meeting online passed friends around 2013 and reached roughly 39% of U.S. heterosexual couples by 2017, disintermediating the people who used to vouch.
boundaryConditions: The roughly 39% figure is U.S. heterosexual couples as of 2017, with online passing friends around 2013 — it is a share of couples formed, not a share of people searching.
The entry names what each channel draws, reads first and bills; it does not rank the channels against each other.
commonMisreadings: Where you meet is just weather — it has no bearing on who you end up with or what it costs you.
Everyone meets online now, so the apps simply are the dating market.

entries.title: The Market-Maker’s Cut
entries.synopsis: The dominant venue is a business, and the business is paid by the search, not the match — a subscription market-maker collects for every month a search continues and nothing extra when it succeeds. Match Group and Bumble clear most of the U.S. market on subscription revenue, and consumer-group audits in several countries found the same tier priced differently by age, with personalized pricing on no disclosed basis.
boundaryConditions: The incentive claim rests on the subscription model: Match Group and Bumble clear most of the U.S. market on subscription revenue, where the fee recurs for every month a search continues.
The price findings are consumer-group audits in several countries showing the same tier priced differently by age, on no disclosed basis — the audits establish the variation, not the reason for it.
commonMisreadings: The apps are paid to pair people off, so their incentives point the same way yours do — a happy couple is their best advertising.
Pricing on a dating app is one published number and everybody pays it.

entries.title: The Costless Exit
entries.synopsis: When two people share no network, ending contact carries no reputational bill — and the same repeal that makes exit without notice (ghosting) nearly free makes retention without intent (breadcrumbing) nearly free too. Roughly a fifth to a quarter report each, not the universal the discourse claims, and in the one sample that separated them, breadcrumbing predicted lower life satisfaction and more loneliness while…
boundaryConditions: Roughly a fifth to a quarter report each, which is well short of the universal the discourse claims.

The comparison between them comes from the one located sample that separated the two behaviours, where breadcrumbing predicted lower life satisfaction and more loneliness — an association within that sample.
commonMisreadings: Everyone ghosts now — it is simply what dating is, so there is no point reading anything into it.
Ghosting is the harm and breadcrumbing is the harmless version, since at least the person is still around.

entries.title: The Support Portfolio
entries.synopsis: Emotional support and social connection held as a portfolio across a partner, friends, family and community — three variables the discourse collapses into one: how many channels exist, how concentrated support is in the relationship, and who does the work of keeping the other channels alive.
boundaryConditions: The entry separates three variables — how many channels exist, how concentrated support is in the relationship, and who maintains the other channels — and does not set a correct number or concentration for any couple.
It describes the shape of a support portfolio, not what any given distribution produces.
commonMisreadings: Your partner should be your best friend and your whole support system; needing anyone else means the relationship is falling short.

entries.title: The Delegation Boundary
entries.synopsis: Courtship assistance sits on a gradient of transferred agency: feedback leaves the seeker authoring and deciding, co-authorship shares the presentation, and substitution lets a proxy present, screen, select or converse as the seeker.
boundaryConditions: The gradient is defined by transferred agency — whether the seeker still authors and decides — not by how well the assistance works.
It names three positions (feedback, co-authorship, substitution) and does not rule on which of them succeeds.
commonMisreadings: Help is help — having a friend read your profile and having someone else run your conversations are the same thing with different labels.

entries.title: The Replaceability Asymmetry
entries.synopsis: What keeps someone satisfied with the partner they have is not how well that partner matches their stated ideals — across three studies, ideal-partner fulfilment barely moved satisfaction once mate value discrepancy entered the model.
boundaryConditions: The finding is about satisfaction with the partner someone already has, not about who they select in the first place.
It comes from three studies in which ideal-partner fulfilment barely moved satisfaction once mate value discrepancy entered the model.
commonMisreadings: Find someone who matches your list and satisfaction follows — how closely a partner fits your stated ideals is what keeps you happy with them.

entries.title: Attention to Alternatives
entries.synopsis: Interdependence theory long ago named the comparison level for alternatives — your running estimate of how you’d do if you left. The addition here is treating attention to that comparison as its own variable: how much a partnered person notices, seeks out and gets distracted by other candidates.
boundaryConditions: Interdependence theory supplies only the comparison level for alternatives, the running estimate of how you would do if you left; the addition here is treating attention to that comparison as its own variable.
The entry defines that variable — noticing, seeking out, being distracted — and does not state how much of it predicts what.
commonMisreadings: Noticing anyone else means you are already halfway out — a committed person does not see other candidates at all.

entries.title: Mate Retention Intensity
entries.synopsis: How much retention behaviour someone deploys — the range from compliments and attention through vigilance and guarding — treated as an output of satisfaction rather than a mood. In the source dataset, mate value discrepancies moved satisfaction and satisfaction predicted retention effort, while the same discrepancies also moved trust, which predicted retention behaviour in the opposite direction.
boundaryConditions: The paths come from the source dataset: mate value discrepancies moved satisfaction, and satisfaction predicted retention effort.
The same discrepancies also moved trust, which predicted retention behaviour in the opposite direction, so a single intensity score does not carry one sign.
commonMisreadings: Retention effort is a mood, and more of it means more love — a partner who guards and checks is a partner who cares.

entries.title: The Desire-Maintenance Split
entries.synopsis: “Desire fades with familiarity” is said as one claim and is actually three, unequally supported. That desire, sexual satisfaction and frequency decline over relationship duration has real prospective support. That attachment orientation regulates the decline failed the only located instrumented test — anxious attachment-related needs correlated positively with desire and neither orientation moderated the…
boundaryConditions: Only part of the compound claim carries prospective support: that desire, sexual satisfaction and frequency decline over relationship duration.

The regulation claim failed the only located instrumented test — anxious attachment-related needs correlated positively with desire and neither orientation moderated the decline — which is one test, not a settled negative.
commonMisreadings: Desire fades with familiarity, and your attachment style is what decides how fast it goes.

entries.title: The Satisfaction Flywheel
entries.synopsis: Across eight waves of 207 newlywed marriages, sexual satisfaction predicted changes in relationship satisfaction and relationship satisfaction predicted changes in sexual satisfaction at roughly equal strength — a genuine two-way loop rather than one domain quietly driving the other, with frequency of sex sitting inside it.
boundaryConditions: The two-way loop is measured across eight waves of 207 newlywed marriages, so it describes early marriage rather than long-duration or non-marital relationships.
The two directions ran at roughly equal strength in that sample, with frequency of sex sitting inside the loop.
commonMisreadings: Sex is downstream of the relationship — fix how the couple is doing and the sex takes care of itself.

entries.title: The Agreement Surface
entries.synopsis: The set of boundaries two people have actually made mutually legible — as distinct from the label on the relationship. “Monogamous,” “open” and “polyamorous” leave the material questions unanswered: what counts as sex or romance, what is disclosed and when, whether any bond has priority, how time and money are allocated, and how an agreement gets revised.
boundaryConditions: The surface is only what two people have actually made mutually legible; the label on the relationship is a separate thing and does not stand in for it.

The entry lists the material questions — what counts as sex or romance, what is disclosed and when, whether any bond has priority, how time and money are allocated, how an agreement gets revised — without saying which answers are correct.
commonMisreadings: Once you have both said 'monogamous', the rules are settled and both of you know what they are.

entries.title: The Financial Architecture Split
entries.synopsis: A couple’s account topology and its financial fidelity are separate variables. Joint, separate and hybrid describe where the money sits; fidelity describes whether conduct stays inside the couple’s disclosed and accepted rules — so separate accounts can be fully transparent and a joint account can coexist with hidden debt, income, spending or transfers.
boundaryConditions: Account topology and financial fidelity are separate variables: separate accounts can be fully transparent and a joint account can coexist with hidden debt, income, spending or transfers.
Fidelity here means conduct staying inside the couple's own disclosed and accepted rules, so it is defined against those rules rather than a general standard.
commonMisreadings: A joint account means nothing is hidden, and keeping separate accounts means somebody is hiding something.

entries.title: Co-Transition
entries.synopsis: When one partner undertakes a gender transition, the identity and body belong to that person while the relationship changes for everyone inside it — a partner may have to revisit attraction, orientation language, intimacy, public presentation, family roles and the future they thought they had.
boundaryConditions: The identity and the body belong to the person transitioning; what the entry adds is that the relationship changes for everyone inside it.

It names the domains a partner may have to revisit — attraction, orientation language, intimacy, public presentation, family roles, the expected future — and does not predict how any particular relationship resolves.
commonMisreadings: The transition belongs to one person, so nothing about it is the partner's to work through.
If the relationship changes at all, the partner was never really committed.

entries.title: The Care Role Split
entries.synopsis: Chronic illness can place two relationships inside one dyad: partners with a shared life, and caregiver with care receiver. The care role can organize medication, mobility, appointments, money and daily tasks while the couple role still carries reciprocity, privacy, desire and mutual choice — and trouble begins when one ledger silently consumes the other, either because every interaction becomes care or because…
boundaryConditions: The split applies where chronic illness places a care role alongside the couple role in one dyad — the care role organizing medication, mobility, appointments, money and daily tasks while the couple role still carries reciprocity, privacy, desire and mutual choice.
The entry names the failure mode as one ledger silently consuming the other; it gives no rate at which that happens.
commonMisreadings: When a partner gets sick you become their caregiver, and the couple part waits until they are better.

entries.title: The Constraint–Dedication Split
entries.synopsis: A relationship can continue because the people in it want it to (dedication: desire for a future, couple identity), because leaving has become costly (constraints: a lease, shared possessions, financial dependence, children, lost alternatives), or both — and persistence by itself identifies neither.
boundaryConditions: Persistence by itself identifies neither dedication nor constraint, and the entry allows for both being present at once.
It names examples of constraints — a lease, shared possessions, financial dependence, children, lost alternatives — without ruling on what any of them should mean for a decision.
commonMisreadings: They are still together, so they must want to be — a relationship that lasts is a relationship that is chosen.

entries.title: The Attention Boundary
entries.synopsis: Technoference is technology use that interrupts a shared conversation or activity; partner phubbing is the phone-specific case where a partner experiences the device as receiving attention the interaction was supposed to get. The relationship variable is not device ownership or total screen minutes — it is whether use displaced expected partner attention, what meaning the pair assigned to it, and whether either…
boundaryConditions: The relationship variable is not device ownership or total screen minutes; it is whether use displaced expected partner attention and what meaning the pair assigned to it.
Technoference covers interruption of a shared conversation or activity generally, while partner phubbing is the phone-specific case where the partner experiences the device as taking the attention.
commonMisreadings: Phones are the problem — cut the screen time and the relationship problem goes with it.

entries.title: The Repair Sequence
entries.synopsis: After harm, four different states get compressed into “forgive and move on”: the person who caused it can acknowledge it, make proportionate amends, and change future conduct; the injured partner can become less retaliatory or avoidant, which forgiveness research treats as a motivational shift. Whether the pair restores trust, access or the relationship is a further and separate decision.
boundaryConditions: Forgiveness research treats the injured partner's change as a motivational shift, becoming less retaliatory or avoidant — that is a different state from the other person acknowledging, making amends, or changing future conduct.
Whether the pair restores trust, access or the relationship is a further and separate decision the sequence does not settle.
commonMisreadings: Once you have forgiven them it is settled — forgiveness means the trust is back and the relationship carries on as before.

entries.title: The Stress Transmission Split
entries.synopsis: External stress enters a relationship by different routes, and the route decides what the evidence means. Spillover carries one person’s load from work, health or money into their own behavior at home; crossover is the cross-partner path where one person’s load changes the other’s experience; shared exposure means both face the same event at once.
boundaryConditions: The entry distinguishes three routes: spillover carrying one person's load into their own behavior at home, crossover where one person's load changes the other's experience, and shared exposure where both face the same event at once.
It states that the route decides what the evidence means; it does not attach effect sizes to any route.
commonMisreadings: Stress is stress — outside pressure hits a relationship the same way no matter where it came from or who is carrying it.

entries.title: The Sleep-Interaction Loop
entries.synopsis: Sleep and relationship functioning move in both directions, but the arrows are not interchangeable — name the direction, the person, the sleep measure and the time scale before interpreting anything. Randomizing couples to a night of total sleep deprivation before a recurrent-conflict discussion lowered positive affect and raised cortisol, yet produced no difference in agreement reached, discussion satisfaction,…
boundaryConditions: The experimental evidence covers one manipulation: randomizing couples to a night of total sleep deprivation before a recurrent-conflict discussion, which lowered positive affect and raised cortisol yet produced no difference in agreement reached or discussion satisfaction.
Because the arrows run both ways, the direction, the person, the sleep measure and the time scale have to be named before any result is interpreted.
commonMisreadings: Bad sleep makes couples fight, so sleeping better is what fixes the conflict.

entries.title: The Stock–Flow Error
entries.synopsis: A stock counts who is in a state right now; a flow counts who enters or leaves it over time — and almost every famous number in this subject is a stock read as a flow, a photograph of one moment presented as the shape of a life. “Half of marriages end in divorce” divides this year’s divorces by this year’s marriages, two groups that by construction share no members; the observed cohort figure is 46%, from people who…
boundaryConditions: The famous ratio divides this year's divorces by this year's marriages, two groups that by construction share no members, so it is a stock read as a flow.
The cohort figure of 46% is a different quantity, drawn from people who have already married rather than from one year's counts.
commonMisreadings: Half of marriages end in divorce — that is the number, everybody knows it.

entries.title: The Gray Divergence
entries.synopsis: Since 1990 the aggregate U.S. divorce rate has fallen, and that fall is a composite of two components moving in opposite directions: divorce among married adults past fifty roughly doubled (4.9 to about 10 per 1,000 married) while the rate for 25–39s fell from 30 to 24.
boundaryConditions: The composition is U.S. and dated from 1990: divorce among married adults past fifty roughly doubled, from 4.9 to about 10 per 1,000 married, while the rate for 25-39s fell from 30 to 24.
The aggregate fall is the net of those two components, so it describes neither group on its own.
commonMisreadings: The divorce rate has been falling since 1990, so marriages are getting more durable across the board.

entries.title: Residual Pool Dynamics
entries.synopsis: Every model that draws candidates treats the pool as a fixed urn, and it is not: people pair off and leave, others divorce and return, and a group’s average can fall while every person in it improves, purely from who left. That composition effect is real and is the most abused fact in this subject.
boundaryConditions: The composition effect means a group's average can fall while every person in it improves, purely from who left — it explains a moving average, not any individual.
The entry establishes that the pool is not a fixed urn, since people pair off and leave and others divorce and return; it does not size the effect in any particular pool.
commonMisreadings: The people still single at that age are what is left over, and the falling average of the pool tells you what is wrong with them.

entries.title: The Clearing Order
entries.synopsis: People do not leave the market at random, so time in it is not neutral — but the order is not the one the discourse assumes, and for the first decade it runs backwards. 27% of women without a high-school diploma had married by 20 against 3% of graduates; the order flips around 30, and by 40 graduates lead 89% to 77%.
