boundaryConditions: For the first decade the order runs the other way: 27% of women without a high-school diploma had married by 20 against 3% of graduates.
The order flips around 30, and by 40 graduates lead 89% to 77% — so the pattern is age-dependent and stated here by education among women.
commonMisreadings: The best partners get taken first, so the longer you wait the more you are picking through what nobody else wanted.

entries.title: The Effective Sex Ratio
entries.synopsis: When one side of a market is scarcer it can hold out for more and the abundant side concedes — established by four instrumented natural experiments (U.S. immigrant arrivals, the French war dead, post-1945 Soviet losses, China’s missing daughters) rather than by the out-of-print framework book this site used to lean on.
boundaryConditions: The support is four instrumented natural experiments — U.S. immigrant arrivals, the French war dead, post-1945 Soviet losses, China's missing daughters — that is, large exogenous shocks to one side of a market.
The site no longer leans on the out-of-print framework book for this claim, so the framework's wider extensions are not carried along with the finding.
commonMisreadings: Sex ratio is the master variable — count the men and women in any pool and you can read off who sets the terms.

entries.title: The Counting Correction
entries.synopsis: Two hidden choices sit under “there are more single men than single women” — which pool you count, and whether you count people actually in the market — and each is large enough to reverse the answer. The never-married pool runs male-surplus at every age from 18 to 64; the famous reversal exists only in the wider unmarried pool and is produced entirely by the divorced and widowed.
boundaryConditions: Which answer you get depends on two hidden choices: which pool you count, and whether you count people actually in the market.
The never-married pool runs male-surplus at every age from 18 to 64; the reversal exists only in the wider unmarried pool and is produced entirely by the divorced and widowed.
commonMisreadings: There are more single men than single women, full stop — the census says so.
The single-women surplus is a plain demographic fact you can apply at any age.

entries.title: The Ideological Filter
entries.synopsis: Political identity applied as a first-pass screen, which works exactly like a smaller pool. The measured identification gap is 15 points, not the 30 in circulation — 40% of women aged 18–29 identify as liberal against 25% of men — and the filter runs at sharply different rates: 60% of liberal young women call shared politics very important, against 47% of liberal young men and about 36–37% of conservatives of both…
boundaryConditions: The measured identification gap is 15 points, not the 30 in circulation: 40% of women aged 18-29 identify as liberal against 25% of men.

The filter is applied at sharply different rates — 60% of liberal young women call shared politics very important, against 47% of liberal young men and about 36-37% of conservatives of both sexes — so the gap and the screening are separate quantities.
commonMisreadings: Young women are 30 points more liberal than young men, and that gap is why the two of them can no longer date each other.

entries.title: The Local Market
entries.synopsis: Nobody participates in “the dating market” — people participate in a metro, a campus, a workplace, and those differ far more than the national average moves. Markets vary nearly twofold between U.S. metros, and one covariate flips the sign: nationally 115 single men per 100 single women aged 25–34 on a raw headcount, 84 counting only the employed.
boundaryConditions: Markets vary nearly twofold between U.S. metros, so the national average does not describe a metro, a campus or a workplace.
The 115 figure is a raw headcount of U.S. singles aged 25-34; counting only the employed turns the same measure into 84 per 100, so one covariate flips the sign.
commonMisreadings: The national ratio is 115 single men per 100 single women, so men are in surplus wherever you happen to live.

entries.title: The Border Bundle
entries.synopsis: What happens when a pairing joins two containers: mobility, legal status, language, employment, family separation and access to another social network enter the relationship’s terms, expanding the migrating partner’s options and creating leverage inside the relationship at the same time.
boundaryConditions: The entry names what enters the relationship's terms when a pairing joins two containers — mobility, legal status, language, employment, family separation, access to another social network.
It holds that these expand the migrating partner's options and create leverage inside the relationship at the same time, without saying which way that leverage falls in any given pairing.
commonMisreadings: A cross-border pairing is an immigration transaction with a relationship attached.
The migrating partner gains everything from the move and gives up nothing.

entries.title: The Saturation Rule
entries.synopsis: Edges decay, and not for the reason everyone gives. Published stock-market predictors returned 58% less after publication — but the same knowledge reached 39 markets and killed the edge in exactly one, unpublished data-mined strategies decayed just as much, and plain replication halves psychology effects with nobody arbitraging anything.
boundaryConditions: The evidence against the arbitrage story comes from finance and psychology: published stock-market predictors returned 58% less after publication, yet the same knowledge reached 39 markets and killed the edge in exactly one.

Unpublished data-mined strategies decayed just as much, and plain replication halves psychology effects with nobody arbitraging anything — so decay is established, the mechanism the discourse names is not.
commonMisreadings: An edge dies because everyone learns it and arbitrages it away — that is what saturation means.

entries.title: The Survivorship Channel
entries.synopsis: Dating advice is produced almost entirely by people selected for having succeeded or for being able to sell, and the coachable-tactic genre has essentially never been tested — not tested and failed, tested at all. The sharper finding is where the failures go: they sit in the source and get stripped in transit.
boundaryConditions: The coachable-tactic genre has essentially never been tested — not tested and failed, tested at all — so this is an absence of evidence rather than a measured failure rate.
The selection runs on who produces the advice: people selected for having succeeded or for being able to sell, with failures sitting in the source and getting stripped in transit.
commonMisreadings: He got the result, so the method works — his own outcome is the proof that the advice is sound.

entries.title: The Virality Filter
entries.synopsis: Every claim you hold about dating arrived through a filter that was not selecting for accuracy — it selected for novelty, out-group targeting, negative framing and above all confidence. False stories were 70% more likely to be retweeted, and each additional out-group word raised the odds of a share by 67%.
boundaryConditions: The measured quantities are about spread, not truth: false stories were 70% more likely to be retweeted, and each additional out-group word raised the odds of a share by 67%.
The filter selected for novelty, out-group targeting, negative framing and confidence, which says what travels rather than whether any particular claim is wrong.
commonMisreadings: If a claim about dating is everywhere, there must be something to it — that many people would not be repeating it otherwise.

entries.title: The Diagnostic Turn
entries.synopsis: What happens when clinical vocabulary becomes the dating vernacular — attachment styles, boundaries, gaslighting, trauma, narcissist — and a partner stops being described and starts being diagnosed, usually at a distance, by the other party to the dispute, and in the direction that exports the blame.
boundaryConditions: The entry is about what happens to the vocabulary in a dispute — applied at a distance, by the other party to the argument, and in the direction that exports the blame. It does not say the clinical terms are empty, only that this is not the setting in which they are being used to describe.
commonMisreadings: My ex is a narcissist and this was gaslighting — I know the attachment style and the diagnosis, so the argument is settled.
Clinical words are just more precise words: calling a partner's behaviour trauma or a boundary violation is describing them accurately, not accusing them.

entries.title: The Surplus
entries.synopsis: A pairing produces something neither person could produce alone — and how big that something is and how it gets divided are two different questions, with nearly every argument answering the second while borrowing the first’s authority.
boundaryConditions: How big the surplus is and how it gets divided are two separate questions; the concept names both and answers neither. Nearly every argument that invokes it is answering the division question while borrowing the authority of the size question.
commonMisreadings: This pairing produces a lot that neither of us could produce alone, so the way we currently split it is the right split.
I created most of the value here, which settles what share I am owed.

entries.title: The Outside Option
entries.synopsis: What each party could get elsewhere shapes what they get inside, without anyone renegotiating out loud — Spain’s 2005 collapse in divorce costs was followed by roughly a 30% fall in spousal conflict among couples who stayed married, and instrumenting women’s relative wages off industry composition cut female assault admissions.
boundaryConditions: The evidence is Spain's 2005 collapse in divorce costs, followed by roughly a 30% fall in spousal conflict among couples who stayed married, plus a study instrumenting women's relative wages off industry composition that cut female assault admissions. Those are conflict and assault outcomes in particular settings, not a general law.
commonMisreadings: Nothing inside a relationship changes unless the two people actually renegotiate it out loud.
Making exit cheaper only breaks marriages up; it cannot improve the ones that stay together.

entries.title: The Commitment Problem
entries.synopsis: What makes a promise believable is not how much someone means it but the destruction of their own ability to renege — Schelling’s move, which is a definition rather than a finding. The sharper version, “a promise that costs nothing to break carries no information,” was falsified by free virtual roses: a scarce but monetarily costless signal raised acceptance 3.3 points, a 20% increase, and over 50% for offers made…
boundaryConditions: Schelling's move — that credibility comes from destroying your own ability to renege — is a definition rather than a finding, and inherits no empirical support from being stated. The sharper cost-only version was falsified by free virtual roses: a scarce but monetarily costless signal raised acceptance 3.3 points, a 20% increase.
commonMisreadings: A promise that costs nothing to break carries no information, so a signal the sender did not pay for is worthless.
How believable a promise is depends on how sincerely the person means it.

entries.title: The Courtship Buffer
entries.synopsis: Alcohol sits underneath much of early courtship, and the discourse treats removing it as a reveal — meet sober and you finally see what someone is really like. The measured effects are real, small, and land on three different rungs, none of which is whether two particular people wanted each other.
boundaryConditions: The measured effects are real but small, and they land on three different rungs — none of which is whether two particular people wanted each other. The entry describes alcohol's place underneath early courtship, not the content of any specific pairing.
commonMisreadings: Meet sober and you finally see what someone is really like — the drinking was the only reason two people wanted each other.
Alcohol manufactures attraction, so an attraction that started over drinks was never real.

entries.title: The Ambiguity Tax
entries.synopsis: The interpretive price of running a courtship interaction — hints have to be caught, tone weighed, a soft answer graded, an outcome classified as a refusal or as nothing much — and the bill is not the same size for everyone at the table.
boundaryConditions: The concept names the interpretive cost of running the interaction — catching hints, weighing tone, classifying an outcome as a refusal or as nothing much — and its point is that the bill is not the same size for everyone at the table. It does not assign fault for any particular misread.
commonMisreadings: Reading a hint or grading a soft answer is the same job for everybody, so someone who misreads a signal simply was not paying attention.
There is nothing to interpret in courtship — people either say what they mean or they do not.

entries.title: The Typology Shortcut
entries.synopsis: A folk type — a star sign, a four-letter code, a love language — begins as vocabulary and becomes an instrument the moment it is used to rank or delete somebody. Matching on love languages added virtually nothing once personality and attachment were accounted for; what did track satisfaction was the continuously measured gap between what a person preferred and what they felt their partner expressed, which registers…
boundaryConditions: Matching on love languages added virtually nothing once personality and attachment were accounted for. What did track satisfaction was the continuously measured gap between what a person preferred and what they felt their partner expressed — a gap, not a type.
commonMisreadings: Match on love languages and satisfaction follows, so a mismatch on the four-letter code or the sign is a reason to rule someone out.
A folk type is a measuring instrument: it tells you who is worth ranking above whom.

entries.title: The Authority Firewall
entries.synopsis: Where two people met and whether the institution will tolerate the pairing are separate questions, and the second has an owner. The trigger is not the workplace or the campus but evaluative authority running one direction — one person holding the other’s assignments, pay, references, funding or promotion.
boundaryConditions: The trigger named here is evaluative authority running one direction — one person holding the other's assignments, pay, references, funding or promotion — not the venue. Where two people met and whether the institution will tolerate the pairing stay separate questions, and the second has an owner.
commonMisreadings: The problem is dating at work or on campus at all, so any relationship between two colleagues or two people on the same campus is the violation.
If both people say it is consensual, the institution has no claim on it.

entries.title: The Attribution Fork
entries.synopsis: Before anyone acts on a desire gap, somebody decides where it lives — in a body (medication, an endocrine condition, recovery after birth), in a person (a trait, an orientation, a diagnosis worn as identity), in the relationship (resentment, an unrepaired fight, touch that stopped) or in the situation (an infant, a night shift, a hard year).
boundaryConditions: The entry names four places the gap can be located — a body, a person, the relationship, or the situation — and covers the step where somebody decides between them. It does not rank which location is most common or say which one applies to any given couple.
commonMisreadings: A desire gap has one real cause and it is the person — low desire is a trait, an orientation, or a diagnosis they carry.
Where the gap lives is obvious, so you can skip straight to acting on it.

entries.title: The Distance Discount
entries.synopsis: Separation gets read as a defect in a bond rather than a feature of its arrangement, and the discount is applied before anyone looks at the bond. The measurement declines to cooperate: people separated by geography rate their relationships at least as warmly as those living at one address, reached through more adaptive self-disclosure and more idealised perceptions.
boundaryConditions: What the measurement covers is how people rate their own relationships: those separated by geography rate them at least as warmly as those at one address, reached through more adaptive self-disclosure and more idealised perceptions. Those are the named routes, and idealisation is one of them.
commonMisreadings: Long distance is a weaker version of a relationship, so a couple living apart is a couple with something wrong with it.
Living at one address is what makes a bond close, and distance dilutes it.

entries.title: Synthetic Reciprocity
entries.synopsis: A companion chatbot can be attentive, validating and always available while the party on the other side has no needs, no welfare and no independent claim on the user — a bond with one side of the ledger removed. Coded against an established support taxonomy, four functions arrived (companionship, emotional, informational, appraisal) and tangible support, the one made of resources rather than attention, did not appear…
boundaryConditions: One side of the ledger is removed by construction: the party on the other side has no needs, no welfare and no independent claim on the user. Coded against an established support taxonomy, four functions arrived — companionship, emotional, informational, appraisal — and tangible support, the one made of resources rather than attention, did not.
commonMisreadings: A companion chatbot gives you what a relationship gives you — it is attentive and always available, so it is a straight substitute for a person.
The bond runs both ways; the thing on the other side has something at stake too.

entries.title: Ghosting
entries.synopsis: Exit without notice — ending contact with no explanation and no closing move. The page reads it as a price change, not a character change: inside a shared network a silent exit was billed by mutual friends and reputation, and the app channel strips that graph, so the same conduct costs nothing. Around a fifth to a quarter of adults report it, not everyone.
boundaryConditions: The page reads it as a price change rather than a character change: inside a shared network a silent exit was billed by mutual friends and reputation, and the app channel strips that graph, so the same conduct costs nothing. Around a fifth to a quarter of adults report it — not everyone.
commonMisreadings: Ghosting shows what a person is really like — people got crueler, and the ones who do it are a type.
Everyone ghosts now; it is just how dating works.

entries.title: Breadcrumbing
entries.synopsis: Sporadic signals that keep an option warm without intent to close it — retention without intent, priced by the same repealed exit fee that makes ghosting cheap. The page’s own finding runs against the discourse: in a Spanish sample of 626 adults, breadcrumbing alone or combined with ghosting predicted lower life satisfaction and more loneliness and helplessness, while ghosting alone showed no significant association…
boundaryConditions: The finding rests on a Spanish sample of 626 adults, where breadcrumbing alone or combined with ghosting predicted lower life satisfaction and more loneliness and helplessness, while ghosting alone showed no significant association. Those are associations in one sample, on self-reported wellbeing.
commonMisreadings: Ghosting is the damaging one and breadcrumbing at least keeps the door open, so being strung along is the gentler outcome.
Sporadic contact means they intend to close eventually.

entries.title: Mankeeping
entries.synopsis: The discourse’s name for unreciprocated work compensating for deficits in a man’s other social ties — curating his social contact, becoming his concentrated support channel. The page insists this names one gendered instance, not the mechanism: the underlying variable is how a support portfolio spreads across partner, friends, family and community.
boundaryConditions: The page insists the term names one gendered instance and not the mechanism. The underlying variable is how a support portfolio spreads across partner, friends, family and community; the unreciprocated work is what a thin portfolio elsewhere pushes onto one channel.
commonMisreadings: Mankeeping is a fact about men as such — men need managing, women do the managing, and naming the gender is the whole finding.
If a woman is her partner's main emotional support, that is mankeeping by definition.

entries.title: Technoference / partner phubbing
entries.synopsis: Two terms the page keeps apart. Technoference is technology use that interrupts a shared conversation or activity; partner phubbing is the phone-specific case in which a partner experiences the device as receiving attention the interaction was supposed to get. The relationship variable is displaced expected attention, not device minutes.
boundaryConditions: The page keeps the two terms apart: technoference is technology use that interrupts a shared conversation or activity, and partner phubbing is the phone-specific case where a partner experiences the device as receiving attention the interaction was supposed to get. The relationship variable is displaced expected attention, not device minutes.
commonMisreadings: Technoference and phubbing are the same thing, and the damage is screen time — cut the device minutes and the problem goes away.
Any phone use in a partner's presence is phubbing.

entries.title: Covenant marriage
entries.synopsis: A real, legally binding, harder-to-exit marriage contract offered by three American states at the same price as the ordinary one — the cleanest test there is of whether people want commitment technology. Between 98% and 99% of couples declined it: Louisiana ran about 1% through the 2000s, its best year 609 licences at 1.55%; Arizona managed 0.25–1%.
boundaryConditions: What is measured is uptake, in three American states, where the harder-to-exit contract was offered at the same price as the ordinary one: between 98% and 99% of couples declined it, Louisiana running about 1% through the 2000s with a best year of 609 licences at 1.55%, and Arizona 0.25-1%. Uptake is not a measurement of how those marriages fared.
commonMisreadings: People would sign up for binding commitment if the law offered it — the reason nobody locks the door is that there is no lock.
Covenant marriage is a symbolic or religious label rather than an enforceable contract.

entries.title: Operational sex ratio
entries.synopsis: A term this site has retired. In its technical sense it counts individuals actively competing to mate; every study the entry rests on measures a plain headcount of adults, so the page dropped the word here and on the Five Levers page — its own correction reads “We also used the wrong term,” and calls borrowing a stricter term than your data supports a way of overclaiming quietly.
boundaryConditions: In its technical sense the term counts individuals actively competing to mate, and every study the entry rests on measures a plain headcount of adults instead. The site retired the word here and on the Five Levers page, its own correction reading "We also used the wrong term."
commonMisreadings: The operational sex ratio in a city is the number of single men divided by the number of single women there.
Counting adults in a population tells you how many people are competing to mate.

entries.title: Beer goggles
entries.synopsis: The claim that alcohol makes other people look better. Measured, it is real and small: a meta-analysis of 16 studies (n = 1,811) put it at d = 0.19, rising to d = 0.30 for opposite-sex targets and falling to a non-significant d = 0.04 for same-sex ones.
boundaryConditions: Measured, the effect is real and small: a meta-analysis of 16 studies (n = 1,811) put it at d = 0.19, rising to d = 0.30 for opposite-sex targets and falling to a non-significant d = 0.04 for same-sex ones. That is a shift in attractiveness ratings of that size, nothing larger.
commonMisreadings: Alcohol makes other people look dramatically better, which is why people go home together.
Beer goggles are a folk myth with nothing behind them.

entries.title: Length-biased sampling
entries.synopsis: Sampling a population by who is in a state right now over-represents whoever stays in it longest. An app population is a sample of people currently searching, and everyone who pairs off leaves — so measuring the singles pool at an instant and calling it the population will always look worse than the underlying reality.
boundaryConditions: The point is about sampling a state at an instant: an app population is a sample of people currently searching, and everyone who pairs off leaves, so whoever stays longest is over-represented. It explains why the instantaneous snapshot always looks worse than the underlying reality; it is not a claim that the pool is fine.
commonMisreadings: The app pool is what single people are like, so if the pool looks bad the dating population is bad.
Whoever you keep seeing in the pool is representative of everyone who was ever in it.

entries.title: The lemons market (adverse selection)
entries.synopsis: Akerlof’s 1970 mechanism: where only the seller knows quality, the bad drive out the good, because both sell at the same price. Carried as Tier 1 economic theory about markets in general — and the page is blunt that he never said a word about dating, so applying lemons logic to a dating pool is the site’s own extension and inherits none of his authority.
boundaryConditions: Akerlof's 1970 mechanism is carried as Tier 1 economic theory about markets in general — where only the seller knows quality, the bad drive out the good because both sell at the same price. He never said a word about dating, so applying lemons logic to a dating pool is the site's own extension and inherits none of his authority.
commonMisreadings: Akerlof showed that dating is a lemons market, so the good people get driven out of the pool.
The lemons result carries Nobel-grade authority wherever it is applied, dating included.

entries.title: Composition effect
entries.synopsis: The average of a group can fall while every single person in it improves, purely because of who left. The pool is genuinely not a random sample of your cohort — but the page’s verdict is that it is over-claimed as an exclusive explanation: consensus on desirability is only about 2% of romantic evaluation, so exits thin the pool close to randomly; men were degraded in place by trade shocks rather than sorted out; and…
boundaryConditions: The pool genuinely is not a random sample of a cohort, but the page's verdict is that composition is over-claimed as an exclusive explanation: consensus on desirability is only about 2% of romantic evaluation, so exits thin the pool close to randomly, and men were degraded in place by trade shocks rather than sorted out.
commonMisreadings: Everyone good is already taken and what is left is the leftovers — that alone explains why the pool looks the way it does.
If the average of the remaining pool fell, the people in it must have gotten worse.

entries.title: Disintermediation
entries.synopsis: Rosenfeld’s term for what the apps did to the meeting channel. Online became the top channel for U.S. heterosexual couples around 2013 and reached roughly 39% by 2017 while meeting through friends fell in step; the authors titled the finding “disintermediating your friends,” and the title is the mechanism.
boundaryConditions: The figures cover U.S. heterosexual couples: online became the top channel around 2013 and reached roughly 39% by 2017 while meeting through friends fell in step. Top channel at 39% is not most couples, and the mechanism named is the one in the authors' title, "disintermediating your friends."
commonMisreadings: Online is simply how couples meet now, so friends have dropped out of the picture entirely.
The apps only added a channel alongside the old ones and displaced nothing.

entries.title: The principle of least interest
entries.synopsis: The claim that whoever cares less sets the terms. The page grades the classic test Tier 3: it finds the less involved partner perceives more control, which is a survey of perceptions rather than a measurement of outcomes, and it sits beside campus sex-ratio findings that are cross-sectional and non-random.
boundaryConditions: The page grades the classic test Tier 3: it finds the less involved partner perceives more control, which is a survey of perceptions rather than a measurement of outcomes. It sits beside campus sex-ratio findings that are cross-sectional and non-random.
commonMisreadings: Whoever cares less sets the terms, so acting less interested hands you the power in a relationship.
The classic test measured who actually got their way.

entries.title: The suffocation model
entries.synopsis: Finkel’s term for what happens when one relationship is asked to supply what a whole network used to. The page cites it against boundary-maximalism rather than against high expectations: relationship science consistently finds partnerships need autonomy and interdependence, so a rule-set that optimises only the first builds the suffocation model from the other side — a connection so defended it cannot sustain the…
boundaryConditions: The page cites Finkel's term against boundary-maximalism rather than against high expectations. Relationship science consistently finds partnerships need autonomy and interdependence, so a rule-set optimising only autonomy builds the same model from the other side.
commonMisreadings: The suffocation model says people expect too much from a partner, so the fix is to want less.
A relationship suffocates when the two people are too involved with each other, so more distance and firmer rules always help.

entries.title: Propinquity
entries.synopsis: Physical proximity as the quiet filter on who you ever meet. Bossard’s 5,000 consecutive Philadelphia marriage licences from 1931 are the baseline: a third of couples lived within five blocks of each other, one in six on the same block, one in eight in the same building.
boundaryConditions: The baseline is Bossard's 5,000 consecutive Philadelphia marriage licences from 1931 — one city, one year — showing a third of couples living within five blocks of each other, one in six on the same block, one in eight in the same building. It describes who you ever meet, the filter upstream of choosing.
commonMisreadings: Proximity decides who you end up with — people marry whoever is nearest and the rest is decoration.
Where you live has nothing to do with who you meet.

entries.title: The male marital wage premium
entries.synopsis: The folk claim that marriage makes men earn more — which the page sets aside rather than banks. The cross-sectional premium is about 19% and a 280-pair twin study raises it to roughly 26%, but that is a five-page proceedings piece from a convention-recruited sample.
boundaryConditions: The page sets this aside rather than banks it. The cross-sectional premium is about 19%, and the 280-pair twin study that raises it to roughly 26% is a five-page proceedings piece from a convention-recruited sample.
commonMisreadings: Marriage makes men earn more, so getting married raises a man's income by around a quarter.
The twin study settled the causal question.

entries.title: The Love Hierarchy
entries.synopsis: The site’s gate model of qualification, short- or long-term: three tiers passed in sequence — Primary decides whether attraction can start, Secondary whether the dynamic has energy, Tertiary whether it has a base to last. Honest about its own status: four versions sit side by side (Jason’s, a generic male, two reads of the generic female), and the weights are sensible defaults, not measured coefficients.
boundaryConditions: The model is honest about its own status: four versions sit side by side — Jason's, a generic male, and two reads of the generic female — and the weights are sensible defaults, not measured coefficients. It is a gate model of qualification, short- or long-term, with three tiers passed in sequence.
commonMisreadings: The Hierarchy is a measured model — the weights are fitted coefficients, so scoring someone returns their actual value.
There is one Hierarchy and it applies to everybody the same way.

entries.title: Primary, Secondary & Tertiary factors
entries.synopsis: The three tiers of the Love Hierarchy. Primary failure blocks everything above casual interest; Secondary weakness caps the thing at short-term; Tertiary weakness rarely kills attraction but weakens the relationship’s ability to last. It ranks what disqualifies — it is not a scorecard you average.
boundaryConditions: The tiers rank what disqualifies rather than totalling what qualifies: Primary failure blocks everything above casual interest, Secondary weakness caps the thing at short-term, and Tertiary weakness rarely kills attraction but weakens the relationship's ability to last. It is not a scorecard you average.
commonMisreadings: Score the three tiers, average them, and a strong Tertiary makes up for a failed Primary.
Tertiary factors are the ones that decide whether someone is attracted to you.

entries.title: Sequential gates
entries.synopsis: The Hierarchy read as advancement rather than attributes: Desire, then Attachment (or Trust), then Life Fit — each one cleared before the next is even reached. Fail Gate 1 and warmth, loyalty, or shared values can’t manufacture what was missing. Strong as structure; the gate names themselves are two AI proposals, arbitrated — not a measured finding.
boundaryConditions: The structure is the strong part — each gate cleared before the next is reached, and a failed Gate 1 is not manufactured later by warmth, loyalty or shared values. The gate names themselves are two AI proposals, arbitrated, not a measured finding.
commonMisreadings: Desire, Attachment and Life Fit are the established, measured stages a relationship moves through.
Enough warmth, loyalty and shared values will eventually produce the attraction that was not there at the start.

entries.title: Exposure
entries.synopsis: The fifth lever, and the one nobody romantic wants to admit is decisive: how many qualified people actually encounter you. It’s the denominator sitting under every other factor — the best profile scores nothing if it’s never seen — and it’s both the most neglected and, for most people, the most movable. Its mirror-image cope is treating low exposure as proof the market is rigged.
boundaryConditions: Exposure is the fifth lever and the denominator under the others: how many qualified people actually encounter you, with the best profile scoring nothing if it is never seen. The entry calls it the most neglected and, for most people, the most movable — not a claim that volume substitutes for the other four.
commonMisreadings: I am not matching with anyone, which proves the market is rigged against people like me.
Exposure is the shallow lever — if you are actually worth meeting, you will be found.

entries.title: Manosphere
entries.synopsis: The loose online ecosystem the pill language comes from — men’s-rights politics, pickup technique, evolutionary storytelling, gym-and-career self-help, and open hostility to feminism sitting side by side under one metaphor. A computational history of 28.8 million posts across six forums and 51 subreddits found those communities increasingly overlapping: a real map of traffic and language, not proof that any…
boundaryConditions: The ecosystem is loose: men's-rights politics, pickup technique, evolutionary storytelling, gym-and-career self-help, and hostility to feminism side by side under one metaphor. The computational history of 28.8 million posts across six forums and 51 subreddits is a map of traffic and language, and it found those communities increasingly overlapping.
commonMisreadings: The manosphere is one movement with one doctrine, so anyone using pill language holds all of it.
The communities overlap, which shows every user travelled the same path to the same politics.

entries.title: Outcome laundering
entries.synopsis: Counting the response a tactic produces and reporting it as the result you wanted. Jealousy induction reliably produces something — pursuit, reassurance, surveillance, anger, withdrawal, exit — and the advice banks the pursuit and drops the rest. Movement is not improvement, and the gap between the two is where most of the tactical layer of the manosphere lives.
boundaryConditions: Jealousy induction reliably produces something — pursuit, reassurance, surveillance, anger, withdrawal, exit — and the laundering is banking the pursuit and dropping the rest. Movement is not improvement; the entry names the accounting error, not a measurement of how often each response follows.
commonMisreadings: She responded, so the tactic worked — jealousy induction gets results.
If a move reliably produces a reaction, the reaction is the result you were after.

entries.title: Just Be First
entries.synopsis: A timing exploit that can override normal SMV matching: arrive before comparison pressure and full market calibration, and a bond can form that the open market might never have produced. Attachment, habit and shared story get built before a clean comparison becomes salient, and commitment can lock it in.
boundaryConditions: The synopsis describes a window before comparison pressure and full market calibration, not a permanent exemption from matching: the bond can form and commitment can lock it in, both hedged.
It says nothing about what happens once a clean comparison does become salient, and names no rate at which the exploit works.
commonMisreadings: Getting there first is all it takes — be her first real relationship and she is locked in for good, whatever you bring to the table.

entries.title: Lens, not identity
entries.synopsis: The site’s operating stance on all three pills: they are ways of seeing, not tribes to join. Every lens sees something real and every lens also distorts, so the useful question is never “which pill is true” but “which one is answering this situation.” A lens that has become an identity has stopped returning you to reality with more options and started replacing reality with a team.
boundaryConditions: The stance covers the site's three pills as ways of seeing, and holds that every lens sees something real and also distorts.
It ranks lenses only by which one answers the situation in front of you — it does not rule any of them true or false in general.
commonMisreadings: One of the three pills is the true one and the other two are for people who cannot handle it.
Picking a lens means picking a team, and once you are on it you read everything through it.

entries.title: The Great Emptying
entries.synopsis: The site’s name for the post-1960 collapse of the venues that used to do introductions for free — lodges, unions, congregations, leagues, the department-store social world. The load-bearing claim is sequencing: the rooms emptied years before the apps arrived, so the app inherited a vacancy rather than causing one.
boundaryConditions: The load-bearing claim is sequencing: the venues emptied years before the apps arrived, so the app inherited a vacancy rather than causing one.
It covers the post-1960 decline of those specific venues and does not say what, if anything, replaced their introductions.
commonMisreadings: Dating apps destroyed the places people used to meet — before the apps, the lodges and congregations and leagues were still doing introductions.

entries.title: Coverture
entries.synopsis: The English common-law doctrine that folded a wife’s legal identity into her husband’s: no property in her own name, no wages of her own, no contracts. It matters here because it ran alongside the love match rather than before it — a marriage could be freely chosen and a legal erasure at once, until the Married Women’s Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 undid it.
boundaryConditions: This is English common law, undone by the Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882; nothing here extends it past those Acts or to other legal systems.
Its point of contact with the love match is that the two ran alongside each other, not that one caused or preceded the other.
commonMisreadings: Coverture proves marriage back then was never freely chosen — a wife legally erased into her husband cannot also have been a love match.

entries.title: Companionate marriage
entries.synopsis: Marriage grounded in the couple’s own consent, close in age, light on parental control, and set up in a household of its own — the form that emerged in the early modern West well before industrialization made it affordable. The honest caveat is that the feeling ran ahead of both the doctrine and the law: the 1662 Book of Common Prayer still ranked companionship last of three reasons to marry, and coverture was still…
boundaryConditions: The form described is Western and early modern, emerging before industrialization made it affordable.
The synopsis is explicit that feeling ran ahead of doctrine and law: the 1662 Book of Common Prayer still ranked companionship last of three reasons to marry, and coverture was still in force.
commonMisreadings: Companionate marriage is an industrial-era invention: consent, closeness in age and a household of your own only became the norm once wages made it possible.

entries.title: Bundling
entries.synopsis: The colonial New England custom of letting a courting couple spend the night in bed together under the girl’s parents’ roof. It is the single sharpest fact against the “puritanical past”: an estimated 30 to 40% of New England brides were pregnant at marriage, and a resulting pregnancy simply carried the expectation that the couple would wed.
boundaryConditions: Bundling is a colonial New England custom, and the 30 to 40% of brides pregnant at marriage is an estimate for that population, not a figure for the past in general.
commonMisreadings: The colonial past was puritanical: courting couples were kept apart, premarital sex was rare, and a pregnancy before the wedding was a scandal.

entries.title: Courtly love
entries.synopsis: The eleventh-century troubadour code of idealized, consuming passion aimed deliberately outside marriage — adulterous by design, because marriage was business. Its rulebook, De Amore (c. 1184), opens with “Marriage is no real excuse for not loving.” It is the cleanest proof that love and marriage were two systems that only occasionally overlapped, not one system under two names.
boundaryConditions: The reference points are the eleventh-century troubadour code and its rulebook De Amore, c. 1184.
The claim is that love and marriage were two systems that only occasionally overlapped — not that marriages of the period contained no affection.
commonMisreadings: Courtly love is where romantic marriage comes from — the troubadours invented the idea that you marry the person you are consumed by.

entries.title: The Hajnal line
entries.synopsis: John Hajnal’s 1965 line from Trieste to Leningrad: west of it, women marrying in their mid-twenties, a tenth to a fifth never marrying, and newlyweds expected to fund their own household; east of it, early and near-universal marriage inside extended families. The site flags it honestly — repeatedly revised and criticized, partly for thin Eastern data — and treats it as an influential map, not a settled measurement.
boundaryConditions: The line is Hajnal's 1965 construction from Trieste to Leningrad, and the site flags that it has been repeatedly revised and criticized, partly for thin Eastern data.
It is treated as an influential map, not a settled measurement.
commonMisreadings: The Hajnal line settles it: Western Europe has always married late and by choice, and the East has always married young and universally.

entries.title: Serial monogamy
entries.synopsis: Successive exclusive pairings rather than one lifelong bond — routinely framed as a modern decay, and it is not. Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries about 30% of French marriages involved a widow or widower, and roughly half of widowers remarried. Only the exit mechanism changed: death churned the market then in much the way divorce does now.
boundaryConditions: The historical evidence cited is French marriages between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries — about 30% involving a widow or widower, roughly half of widowers remarrying.
The comparison is about the exit mechanism, death then and divorce now, not a claim that the rates match.
commonMisreadings: Serial monogamy is modern decay: people used to pair once for life, and now they churn through partner after partner.

entries.title: “Surplus women”
entries.synopsis: The Victorian panic over “surplus” or “redundant” women — roughly 9.1 million women to 8.6 million men in mid-nineteenth-century England, with perhaps 30% of women over twenty unmarried. Contemporaries read it as a moral crisis. Stripped of the moralizing it was a supply imbalance in a marriage market, the kind of shortage that leaves real people unpaired no matter how a culture prefers to explain it.
boundaryConditions: The counts are mid-nineteenth-century England: roughly 9.1 million women to 8.6 million men, with perhaps 30% of women over twenty unmarried.
Stripped of the moralizing it names a supply imbalance in that one marriage market, not a rule for other places or periods.
commonMisreadings: The Victorian panic over surplus women was pure moralizing about spinsters — there was no real shortage, only disapproval of women who did not marry.

entries.title: No-fault divorce
entries.synopsis: California’s 1969 law, signed by Ronald Reagan and copied by nearly every state within fifteen years, that ended the requirement for an accusation and let one spouse simply decide. The US divorce rate more than doubled behind it, 2.2 per 1,000 in 1960 to 5.2 by 1980 — then began the long decline it has been on ever since.
boundaryConditions: The figures are US rates per 1,000 — 2.2 in 1960 to 5.2 by 1980 — after California's 1969 law was copied by nearly every state within fifteen years.
The same series then enters the long decline it has been on ever since, and the synopsis places the doubling behind the law without isolating cause.
commonMisreadings: No-fault divorce broke marriage: it sent the divorce rate up and the rate has been climbing ever since.

entries.title: The Two-Parent Privilege
entries.synopsis: Melissa Kearney’s term for the fact that the married-parent home did not decline evenly — it held for the college class and eroded for everyone else. From 1980 to 2019 the share of US children living with married parents fell only 90% to 84% for children of college-graduate mothers, but 83% to 60% in the middle and 80% to 57% at the bottom. Marriage was not abandoned so much as it moved upmarket.
boundaryConditions: The shares are US children living with married parents from 1980 to 2019, split by the mother's education: 90% to 84% at the top, 83% to 60% in the middle, 80% to 57% at the bottom.
It measures where children live, not what marriage does for any individual child.
commonMisreadings: Americans across the board gave up on marriage — the married-parent home declined everywhere at about the same pace.

entries.title: The Moynihan Report
entries.synopsis: Daniel Patrick Moynihan’s 1965 Labor Department memo on the Black family, whose alarm bell was that “nearly one-quarter of Negro births are now illegitimate.” The site’s read is not vindication or dismissal but perspective: by 2023 the non-marital birth share was 26.8% among non-Hispanic white mothers — above the figure that read as a national emergency in 1965 — and 40.0% overall.
boundaryConditions: The comparison runs between the 1965 memo's quarter-of-births alarm and 2023 shares — 26.8% among non-Hispanic white mothers, 40.0% overall.
The site's read is perspective rather than a verdict; it issues neither vindication nor dismissal.
commonMisreadings: The Moynihan Report was vindicated: non-marital birth is a Black-family problem, and 1965 called it early.

entries.title: The West as pilot program
entries.synopsis: The site’s framing for the geography of the unbundling: the West was not the exception that broke the rule, it was the region that happened to reach the turn first. East Asia is furthest along, sub-Saharan Africa has barely begun, and mandatory-marriage and optional-marriage societies alike arrive at the same low-fertility destination.
boundaryConditions: The framing is about sequence across regions: East Asia furthest along, sub-Saharan Africa barely begun.
It says mandatory-marriage and optional-marriage societies reach the same low-fertility destination, not that they arrive at the same time or by the same route.
commonMisreadings: The unbundling is a Western cultural export, and societies that keep marriage mandatory will not go through it.

entries.title: Unión libre (free union)
entries.synopsis: The Latin American arrangement in which couples form households, raise children, and stay together without ever registering a wedding — socially accepted, with roots running back centuries. It produces the world’s highest non-marital birth shares (87% in Colombia, 78% in Chile). And it settles a common argument: the region that decoupled marriage from childbearing earliest still fell below replacement.
boundaryConditions: The arrangement described is Latin American, socially accepted with roots running back centuries, and produces the world's highest non-marital birth shares — 87% in Colombia, 78% in Chile.
The region that decoupled earliest still fell below replacement, so the case is about that region, not a transferable mechanism.
commonMisreadings: Unión libre shows that decoupling marriage from childbearing protects fertility: where people can have children without a wedding, they keep having them.

entries.title: Replacement rate
entries.synopsis: The total fertility rate at which a generation exactly replaces itself, about 2.1 births per woman. Global fertility has fallen along one long curve — roughly 5.0 in the 1960s, 3.3 by 1990, 2.2 in 2024 — with the UN projecting the crossing around 2050. More than half of countries are already below it, and the regional spread reads as one descent caught at different points, not as regions following different rules.
boundaryConditions: The rate is about 2.1 births per woman, and the global series runs roughly 5.0 in the 1960s, 3.3 by 1990, 2.2 in 2024.
The crossing around 2050 is a UN projection rather than a measurement, and the regional spread is read as one descent caught at different points.
commonMisreadings: 2.1 is a target countries either hit or miss, and the ones below it are following a different path from the ones still above.

entries.title: Love marriage
entries.synopsis: The South Asian term for a self-chosen match, set against the arranged marriage that remains the default. A 2016 Lokniti-CSDS survey of married Indians aged 15–34 across nineteen states found 84% arranged and just 6% love marriages.
boundaryConditions: The 84% arranged and 6% love figures come from one survey, Lokniti-CSDS 2016, of married Indians aged 15 to 34 across nineteen states.
The term is South Asian and is defined against arranged marriage as the default; the synopsis carries no later or wider measurement.
commonMisreadings: India has modernized into love marriage — the self-chosen match is the norm now and arranged marriage is basically over.

entries.title: The double standard of aging
entries.synopsis: England and McClintock’s finding from US marriage records 1970–1988: the older a man is when he marries, the further below his own age his bride tends to be, in first marriages and remarriages alike, across every education group. The market extends a man’s reach downward as he ages in a way it does not extend a woman’s.
boundaryConditions: The finding is England and McClintock's, from US marriage records covering 1970 to 1988, in first marriages and remarriages across every education group.
It measures the age gap of the bride relative to the groom, not desirability, offers received, or how those marriages turned out.
commonMisreadings: Men get more desirable with age and women get less, so an older man can have whichever much younger woman he wants.

entries.title: Advanced maternal age
entries.synopsis: The clinical label attached at 35, and the site is precise about what it is: a screening threshold, the point at which doctors monitor a pregnancy more closely, not an endpoint or a door swinging shut. ACOG puts the real turns at about 32 (gradual but significant decline) and about 37 (faster) — neither of them 30, the number the Wall reaches for. A genuine curve, on the body’s own clock, and not a cliff.
boundaryConditions: 35 is a screening threshold, the point at which a pregnancy is monitored more closely, not an endpoint.
ACOG puts the real turns at about 32, gradual but significant, and about 37, faster — neither of them 30 — and the shape described is a curve, not per-person odds.
commonMisreadings: Fertility falls off a cliff at 35 — past that the door has shut.

entries.title: Involuntary singlehood
entries.synopsis: Being unpartnered without having chosen it — the category self-report is worst at measuring. Among singles not looking, the flattering answers run high (47% bigger priorities, 44% like being single) and the stigmatized one runs low, so the involuntary share is almost certainly understated. The tell is the one reason that splits sharply by sex: “no one would be interested in me,” 26% of men against 12% of women.
boundaryConditions: The numbers are self-report among singles not looking: 47% bigger priorities, 44% like being single, and 'no one would be interested in me' at 26% of men against 12% of women.
The synopsis holds that the involuntary share is almost certainly understated — an inference from how self-report behaves, not a measured quantity.
commonMisreadings: Single people who are not looking are single by choice — they say so themselves, so the involuntary category is mostly imaginary.

entries.title: The female exit
entries.synopsis: The site’s name for the fact that among singles 40 and over, 71% of women say they are not looking to date against 42% of men — a large withdrawal that an app measuring only its active users cannot see. It is the reason a “men’s strike” lands on a market many women have already left, and the reason unpartnered women in that band are less “left behind” than the passive voice suggests.
boundaryConditions: The figures cover singles 40 and over: 71% of women say they are not looking to date against 42% of men.
An app measuring only its active users cannot see the withdrawal, so app data is not evidence about the women who have already left.
commonMisreadings: Unpartnered women over 40 are out there being passed over — they are on the market and nobody is choosing them.

entries.title: The sexual double standard
entries.synopsis: The claim that a man is praised for the sexual history a woman is shamed for. The site deliberately refuses to chart it with hard numbers: belief in it is widespread, but controlled studies find it weaker than expected — vignette designs detect a small effect, attitude scales find none. Where it does bite is behavior: anticipated stigma measurably lowers women’s stated willingness to accept casual sex.
boundaryConditions: Belief in it is widespread while controlled studies find it weaker than expected: vignette designs detect a small effect, attitude scales find none, and the site deliberately refuses to chart it with hard numbers.
Where it does show up is behavior — anticipated stigma measurably lowers women's stated willingness to accept casual sex.
commonMisreadings: A man is praised for the exact sexual history a woman is shamed for, and it is one of the best-documented asymmetries we have.

entries.title: The provider norm
entries.synopsis: The expectation that the husband is the household’s primary earner — the material base under hypergamy and the Status Trade. It fell from 85% of US opposite-sex marriages in 1972 to 55% in 2022: still the majority, but its dominance halved, with ~45% now equal- or female-earning. One asterisk from the same report: even in equal-earning marriages wives still do more housework and caregiving.
boundaryConditions: The measure is US opposite-sex marriages, 85% in 1972 to 55% in 2022, with roughly 45% now equal- or female-earning: dominance halved, still the majority.
The same report adds that wives in equal-earning marriages still do more housework and caregiving.
commonMisreadings: The male provider norm is finished — marriages are equal-earning now, so the material base under hypergamy is gone.

entries.title: Demand-withdraw
entries.synopsis: The conflict loop where one partner pushes harder to discuss or change and the other evades, shuts down, or leaves — each response intensifying the other. Across 74 studies (N = 14,255) it carries a moderate association with worse outcomes, r =.36.
boundaryConditions: The evidence is 74 studies, N = 14,255, and the association with worse outcomes is moderate at r =.36.
That is an association across studies, not a direction of cause or a prognosis for any one couple.
commonMisreadings: Demand-withdraw is what kills couples — if your fights run that way, the relationship is already finished.

entries.title: The cohabitation effect
entries.synopsis: The finding that couples who move in before any commitment to marry later report lower marital satisfaction and more proneness to divorce — while those who move in after getting engaged look no different from those who never cohabited. So it is about sequence, not about living together.
boundaryConditions: The split is by sequence: couples who moved in before any commitment to marry, versus those who moved in after getting engaged, who look no different from those who never cohabited.
The outcomes reported are marital satisfaction and proneness to divorce.
commonMisreadings: Living together before marriage raises your odds of divorce, so moving in first is a mistake.

entries.title: Friends first
entries.synopsis: Pairing with someone you already knew rather than a stranger, and it measurably changes the terms. Couples who paired off quickly were tightly sorted by looks; for couples who knew each other about nine months or longer before dating, attractiveness matching was no longer statistically distinguishable from zero.
boundaryConditions: The contrast is between couples who paired off quickly, who were tightly sorted by looks, and couples who knew each other about nine months or longer before dating.
For the latter, attractiveness matching was not statistically distinguishable from zero — an absence of detectable sorting, not proof that looks stopped mattering.
commonMisreadings: Couples match on looks, full stop — attractiveness sorting is how pairing works no matter how people met.

entries.title: On-again/off-again
entries.synopsis: Breaking up and reconciling with the same partner — common rather than rare: 37% of cohabiting and 23% of married couples report having done it at least once with their current partner. Cyclers reported more uncertainty about the future and lower satisfaction afterward, on both sides of the couple, and past cycling predicted more cycling.
boundaryConditions: The shares are self-reported and cover having cycled at least once with the current partner: 37% of cohabiting and 23% of married couples.
What is reported afterward is more uncertainty about the future and lower satisfaction on both sides, with past cycling predicting more cycling.
commonMisreadings: Breaking up and getting back together is a rare, doomed pattern, and a couple who reconciles has worked the problem out.

entries.title: Selection effect
entries.synopsis: When a gap between two groups is produced by who ends up in each group rather than by the thing being measured. It is the single most-used correction on this site: paid app users report better experiences, but they skew richer, older, and more intent; families that break differ from families that don’t before anything breaks; happier people are likelier to marry and stay married.
boundaryConditions: The correction names a gap produced by who ends up in each group — paid users skewing richer, older and more intent; families that break differing before anything breaks; happier people being likelier to marry and stay married.
It flags that a comparison may not be causal; it does not say how much of any gap is selection.
commonMisreadings: Paid app users report better experiences, so paying for the app gets you a better experience.

entries.title: The pool is not the population
entries.synopsis: The site’s correction to every aggregate sex-ratio argument. Headcount says 126 never-married men per 100 women aged 25–34. Apply one filter most women name — a job — and the surplus becomes a shortfall of 91. By education it flips hard: 67 employed men per 100 women at post-graduate level, 108 at high school or less. Same country, same year, two opposite markets.
boundaryConditions: The headcount is never-married men and women aged 25 to 34; applying one filter women commonly name, a job, turns the surplus into a shortfall of 91.
By education it flips: 67 employed men per 100 women at post-graduate level against 108 at high school or less — same country, same year.
commonMisreadings: There are 126 never-married men per 100 women aged 25 to 34, so the numbers are on women's side.

entries.title: Sexual overperception bias
entries.synopsis: The documented tendency for men to over-read warmth as romantic interest — the mechanism under “is the friendly barista flirting with me?” Occupational friendliness inflates the false-positive rate further. The honest other half, which the site keeps: real flirting is also frequently missed, so “you’re misreading everything” and “you’re missing signals” are both partly true.
boundaryConditions: The site keeps the other half: real flirting is also frequently missed, so 'you're misreading everything' and 'you're missing signals' are both partly true.
Occupational friendliness inflates the false-positive rate, which makes this a tendency in a context, not a rate you can apply to a single read.
commonMisreadings: Men imagine interest that is not there, so if you think she is into you, you are wrong.

entries.title: Fear of being single
entries.synopsis: A measured construct (Spielmann’s Fear of Being Single Scale), not just a taunt: across seven studies, people high on it stay in unsatisfying relationships and warm to less responsive, less attractive partners. The sex direction has support — single men are likelier to be looking (61% vs 38%) and less happy single.
boundaryConditions: It is a measured construct, Spielmann's Fear of Being Single Scale, with findings across seven studies: staying in unsatisfying relationships and warming to less responsive, less attractive partners.
The sex direction has support — single men likelier to be looking, 61% against 38%, and less happy single — which is support, not a settled magnitude.
commonMisreadings: Fear of being single is just a taunt for people who settle, not anything you could actually measure.

entries.title: Romance scam
entries.synopsis: Fraud run through a fabricated relationship, and the stereotype of the lonely older woman survives on exactly one axis: check size. FTC median losses climb from $750 per report at 18–29 to $9,000 at 70 and over. Targeting runs the other way — 52% of online daters report meeting a suspected scammer, with men under 50 highest at 63%, and the sextortion variant hits 18–29-year-olds at over six times the rate of everyone…
boundaryConditions: The age pattern the stereotype survives on is check size: FTC median losses per report climb from $750 at 18 to 29 to $9,000 at 70 and over.

Targeting runs the other way in the reported figures — 52% of online daters say they met a suspected scammer, men under 50 highest at 63%, and the sextortion variant concentrates on 18-to-29-year-olds.
commonMisreadings: Romance scams are a lonely-older-woman problem — that is who the scammers go after.

entries.title: The Black Pill
entries.synopsis: Constraint awareness pushed to fatalism: looks and fixed traits matter more than polite society admits (true), so it’s hopeless (false).
boundaryConditions: Constraints being real and outcomes being settled are separate propositions, and only the first survives the data.
commonMisreadings: Fixed traits settle romantic outcomes completely, so a man below the looks floor stays single.

entries.title: The Height Pill
entries.synopsis: Height as destiny. The premium is real and fixed — but “it’s over under six feet” is fatalism. The curve is a window, not a ladder.
boundaryConditions: A premium measured across a range and a threshold below which nothing works are different shapes.
commonMisreadings: Height works as a ladder, so every added inch buys a man proportionally more dates.

entries.title: Looksmaxxing
entries.synopsis: Maximizing physical attractiveness. Soft-maxxing (grooming, fitness, style) genuinely works; surgery-chasing and PSL despair is mostly cope.
boundaryConditions: The returns concentrate in the improvable layers; the further a protocol moves toward bone and surgery, the thinner the evidence gets.
It raises the looks lever only and does nothing for exposure, which is the lever most often actually binding.
commonMisreadings: Looksmaxxing has unlimited returns, so enough surgery will make any man attractive to women.
pressureTests: Is the intervention in the soft-maxxing band where the evidence is, or the surgical band where it isn't?

entries.title: Mogging
entries.synopsis: To visibly outrank someone on looks, height, or status in a shared space. A real perception effect, inflated into constant ranking anxiety.
boundaryConditions: Contrast effects require the comparison to be visible and simultaneous; they do not persist once the comparison leaves the room.
Mogging describes how a pair is perceived side by side, not who either person actually pairs with.
commonMisreadings: A taller guy walks in and mogs you, so the woman instantly loses attraction to you.
pressureTests: Does the claimed effect survive the comparison person leaving the room?

entries.title: LMS (Looks · Money · Status)
entries.synopsis: The blackpill’s claim that attraction reduces to three things you can’t change. They matter — but it drops charm and exposure, the two you can move.
boundaryConditions: Three fixed inputs mattering and two movable ones mattering are compatible, so dropping the movable pair is a choice.
commonMisreadings: Attraction reduces to looks, money and status, so charm and exposure move nothing in dating.

entries.title: PSL
entries.synopsis: The looksmaxxing forums’ 0–10 facial scale, graded to the decimal and treated as destiny. The site’s Face Calc scores in it — and rejects the fatalism it ships with.
boundaryConditions: The scale is a forum convention calibrated against forum consensus, not an instrument validated against pairing outcomes.
It rates a face at first glance and says nothing about how the same face is read after acquaintance.
commonMisreadings: Your PSL score to the decimal measures how much women want you and decides everything.
pressureTests: What was the scale validated against — pairing outcomes, or the agreement of its inventors?

entries.title: Chad & Stacy
entries.synopsis: The blackpill’s top-tier archetypes — the man and woman the market’s rules supposedly never touch. Useful shorthand for the top band; corrosive as a story that everyone below it lost.
boundaryConditions: The archetypes compress a distribution tail; treating them as a separate species you either are or are not is where the shorthand curdles.
Top-band advantages are largest in the stranger market, where the comparison is visible and instantaneous.
commonMisreadings: Chads and Stacys are a separate species, so women only want Chads and everyone else lost.
pressureTests: Does the argument still work if the top band is a continuous tail rather than a separate class?

entries.title: Incel / femcel
entries.synopsis: Involuntarily celibate. A real predicament at the market’s bottom band — and an identity that hardens the predicament into a life sentence the data doesn’t sign.
boundaryConditions: The term names an outcome, not being chosen, and does not establish the cause, which may be exposure or presentation rather than fixed traits.
It applies to a genuinely bottom-band predicament; stretching it to anyone currently single goes past the outcome data.
commonMisreadings: Being an incel is a permanent life sentence because the fixed traits women reject stay fixed forever.
pressureTests: Is this describing a current state or asserting a permanent one, and what makes it permanent?

entries.title: Normie
entries.synopsis: The ladder’s broad middle — unremarkable by PSL lights, which is most people. The insult quietly concedes the blackpill’s problem: the average face still pairs.
boundaryConditions: The label is a position on a rating scale, not a description of relationship outcomes.
It marks the middle of a forum grading convention, so its boundaries move with whoever is grading.
commonMisreadings: Being an average-looking normie means women reject you, so the average face loses at dating.
pressureTests: If the broad middle still pairs at ordinary rates, what is the ladder actually predicting?

entries.title: The Bone Pill
entries.synopsis: The claim that attraction is mostly face, face is mostly bone, and your skeleton is a verdict. The features are real and people agree at first glance — then the agreement dissolves on acquaintance.
boundaryConditions: Consensus at a glance and consensus after acquaintance are separate measurements, and they diverge as exposure grows.
commonMisreadings: Facial bone structure settles attraction, so agreement about a man's face holds as women know him.

entries.title: The Face Pill
entries.synopsis: The Bone Pill’s retail version: your face reduced to one scoreable verdict. Three of the four facial layers are improvable; the pill launders a real input into a sealed sentence.
boundaryConditions: Four facial layers are distinguished precisely because three of them respond to effort and one does not.
commonMisreadings: A face reduces to one score, so women reject a man on bone structure alone.

entries.title: Canthal tilt
entries.synopsis: The angle from inner to outer eye corner — PSL’s favorite millimeter. Its link to attractiveness is essentially unstudied: a load-bearing metric with no load-bearing evidence.
boundaryConditions: The angle is real and reliably measurable; what is missing is any published effect on attractiveness ratings or pairing outcomes.
The honest verdict is unstudied rather than disproven — a future finding either way would be news.
commonMisreadings: Negative canthal tilt is why women reject a man's face, and the tilt decides his attractiveness.
pressureTests: Which study measured canthal tilt against rated attractiveness, and what was the effect size?

entries.title: “It’s over”
entries.synopsis: The blackpill’s verdict-phrase: fixed traits already decided your romantic life. The data behind it shows penalties and slopes — windows, not verdicts.
boundaryConditions: Fixed-trait penalties are largest at the stranger market’s first glance and shrink wherever exposure accumulates.
The phrase is a verdict about the future, which no cross-sectional attractiveness study is designed to issue.
commonMisreadings: Bad bone structure means it is over: a man dealt that hand loses at dating forever.
pressureTests: Does the cited evidence report a probability shift, or an impossibility?

entries.title: Constraint triage
entries.synopsis: The Black Pill used as a diagnostic pass rather than a residence. Sort a repeating outcome into fixed (height, age already lived, basic bone), movable (fitness, grooming, photos, conversation, emotional regulation, income, introductions) and contextual (app versus in person, city, age band, subculture, whether your strengths are even visible there).
boundaryConditions: This is a diagnostic pass over a repeating outcome, not a residence — the sort has a movable column (fitness, grooming, photos, conversation, emotional regulation, income, introductions) and a contextual one.
Because the contextual column covers app versus in person, city, age band, subculture and whether your strengths are visible there, a triage done in one setting does not carry to another.
commonMisreadings: Triage just confirms the verdict: sort the causes honestly and they all land in the fixed column, so the only rational move is to stop.
If a constraint is on the list at all it is permanent, so grooming, conversation and fitness are cope.

entries.title: fWHR (facial width-to-height)
entries.synopsis: Bizygomatic width divided by upper-face height — a forum favorite the Face Calc displays but deliberately barely weights. What it actually tracks is perceived dominance and aggression, not attractiveness; larger is, if anything, less attractive to women (Geniole 2015). Popular online, thin in the literature: shown for completeness, not weight.
boundaryConditions: What fWHR tracks in the cited work is perceived dominance and aggression, not attractiveness; Geniole 2015 has larger being, if anything, less attractive to women.
It is popular online and thin in the literature, which is why the Face Calc displays it but deliberately barely weights it — shown for completeness, not weight.
commonMisreadings: A wide midface is a more attractive face, so a high fWHR raises your score and widening the midface is a looksmax.
fWHR is a core facial metric — the calculator underweights it because it is inconvenient.

entries.title: Averageness
entries.synopsis: Closeness to the population-mean face — counter-intuitively one of the two most replicated predictors of attractiveness (Rhodes 2006). It is the quiet rebuttal to the whole PSL project: the trait that most reliably reads as attractive is being typical, not being extreme on any single scoreable feature.
boundaryConditions: Averageness means closeness to the population-mean face, so which face reads as average depends on the population being averaged.
Rhodes 2006 places it as one of the two most replicated predictors of attractiveness — a strong predictor, not the whole of attractiveness.
commonMisreadings: An average face is a plain face, so attractiveness comes from being extreme on the scoreable features rather than typical.

entries.title: Sexual dimorphism
entries.synopsis: How strongly a face or body carries sex-typical cues — jaw, nose and shoulder breadth on the masculine side, softer features and a lower waist-to-hip on the feminine. With averageness it is the other most replicated driver of attractiveness, but the dose matters and the sexes are not symmetric: femininity reliably predicts attractiveness in women, while the preference for male masculinity is genuinely mixed.
boundaryConditions: The dose matters and the sexes are not symmetric: femininity reliably predicts attractiveness in women, while the preference for male masculinity is genuinely mixed.
With averageness it is one of the two most replicated drivers of attractiveness, which is a claim about replication, not about any single face.
commonMisreadings: More masculine is always more attractive on a man, so jaw and shoulder breadth pay off without limit.
Dimorphism works the same way in both directions — whatever femininity does for women, masculinity does for men.

entries.title: Golden ratio / phi mask
entries.synopsis: The “1.618 face” — the claim that beauty is a fixed set of divine proportions you can overlay on a photograph. A forum favourite the evidence does not support as a real predictor, carried in the Face Pill’s proportion layer only as a lens marker: a measure the forums oversell.
boundaryConditions: The evidence does not support the golden ratio as a real predictor of attractiveness; it is a forum favourite the site carries anyway.
It appears in the Face Pill's proportion layer only as a lens marker — a measure flagged as one the forums oversell, not a weighted input.
commonMisreadings: Beauty is 1.618: overlay the phi mask on a photograph and you have the actual measure of a face.
The divine proportions are fixed, so any deviation from them is a measurable flaw.

entries.title: Orbital vector
entries.synopsis: How far the under-eye rim sits ahead of the eyeball — a positive vector reads supported and youthful, a negative one exposes the under-eye. A genuine high-impact bone-layer feature, and one of the things a single front photo structurally cannot measure, which is why the Face Calc omits it instead of guessing. Real and fixed; routinely handed a verdict it cannot carry alone.
boundaryConditions: Orbital vector is a genuine high-impact bone-layer feature and it is fixed — but a single front photo structurally cannot measure how far the under-eye rim sits ahead of the eyeball, which is why the Face Calc omits it instead of guessing.
It is one feature among the bone layer; the synopsis notes it is routinely handed a verdict it cannot carry alone.
commonMisreadings: You can read orbital vector off a front photo, and a negative vector is the verdict on the whole face.
The calculator leaves it out because it does not matter.

entries.title: Facial thirds
entries.synopsis: The classical proportion check: hairline–brow, brow–nose, nose–chin in roughly equal thirds. A moderate-weight part of the gestalt raters actually integrate — and something the Face Calc refuses to report at all, because the hairline has no landmark to measure from. A real proportion, not a scoreable one.
boundaryConditions: Thirds carry moderate weight inside the gestalt raters actually integrate, not decisive weight on their own.
The Face Calc refuses to report them at all because the hairline has no landmark to measure from — a real proportion, not a scoreable one.
commonMisreadings: Thirds are the proportion test that settles a face: measure hairline to brow, brow to nose, nose to chin, and unequal thirds are a scored flaw.
The calculator skips thirds because the site does not believe in proportion.

entries.title: Waist-to-hip ratio (WHR)
entries.synopsis: The most replicated body cue there is — roughly 0.7 in women and 0.9 in men (Singh 1993). For women it is a true optimum rather than a lower-is-better slope, so both extremes cost. The Body Calc can only approximate it from a frontal silhouette: a front photo has no depth, and clothing, pose and camera angle redraw the outline. Real in principle, far softer in practice than the decimal suggests.
boundaryConditions: For women WHR is a true optimum rather than a lower-is-better slope, so both extremes cost; Singh 1993 puts it around 0.7 in women and 0.9 in men.

The Body Calc can only approximate it from a frontal silhouette — a front photo has no depth, and clothing, pose and camera angle redraw the outline, so it is far softer in practice than the decimal suggests.
commonMisreadings: 0.7 is the target, so for a woman lower is always better and a smaller waist keeps paying.
The ratio the calculator reads off a photo is her actual WHR.

entries.title: V-taper
entries.synopsis: Shoulder width over waist width — the dominant male body cue (Dixson), and on a woman the same ratio is what reads as the hourglass.
