The Black Pill’s body lens weights it above everything else, which is more defensible than its facial equivalent: unlike the bone layer, taper is largely built rather than inherited. The catch is that one frontal photo cannot separate a lean frame from a soft one.
boundaryConditions: Taper is largely built rather than inherited, which is what makes weighting it above everything else more defensible than the facial equivalent.
One frontal photo cannot separate a lean frame from a soft one, so the shoulder-over-waist read taken from a picture is limited.
commonMisreadings: Taper is the body's verdict and a frontal photo shows exactly who has it, so the ratio off one picture settles the read.
Like the bone layer, your frame is what you were born with.

entries.title: Waist-to-height ratio (WHtR)
entries.synopsis: The adiposity measure the literature actually uses — and Tovée and Cornelissen find body-fat is the single strongest cue for female bodies. The Body Calc shows a frontal width -to-height stand-in for it and pointedly refuses to score it: a front photo cannot see depth, so it does not convert to the waist circumference ratio the honest bands are built on.
boundaryConditions: Tovée and Cornelissen's finding that body fat is the single strongest cue is stated for female bodies.

The Body Calc shows only a frontal width-to-height stand-in and pointedly refuses to score it: a front photo cannot see depth, so it does not convert to the waist circumference ratio the honest bands are built on.
commonMisreadings: The width-to-height figure the calculator shows is your waist-to-height ratio, so you can read it straight against the published bands.
Body fat is the strongest cue for everyone, so the same threshold applies across the board.

entries.title: Frame (the body sense)
entries.synopsis: The word’s other meaning, and a standing source of confusion: not the Red Pill’s psychological composure but the literal skeleton and silhouette — shoulder span, taper, waist, leg-to-torso, symmetry. The Body Calc names its Black Pill profile after it because the looksmaxxing read on a body is exactly that: V-taper, broad shoulders and leanness weighted above everything else, with the softer, slower, health-shaped…
boundaryConditions: This entry is the body sense only — skeleton and silhouette: shoulder span, taper, waist, leg-to-torso, symmetry — not the Red Pill's psychological composure.
It names the Body Calc's Black Pill profile, where V-taper, broad shoulders and leanness are weighted above everything else; that weighting is the looksmaxxing read, not the whole of the page.
commonMisreadings: Frame is frame — the man told to hold his frame and the man told to build his frame are being told the same thing.
A body's frame is fixed skeleton, so nothing about it is buildable.

entries.title: The Red Pill
entries.synopsis: Dating as a market of incentives and leverage. Its gift is agency — build your value, read signals. Its poison is contempt dressed up as realism.
boundaryConditions: Reading incentives accurately and holding people in contempt are separable, and the second is what curdles the first.
commonMisreadings: Reading incentives and leverage correctly requires treating women with contempt while dating them.

entries.title: Solipsism
entries.synopsis: Philosophically, the doubt that any mind beyond one’s own can be known. Red-pill usage turns it into a sexed accusation: treating one’s own feelings as the whole map. Perspective failure is real; assigning it to women as a class is the solipsistic move the label claims to diagnose.
commonMisreadings: Women are solipsistic by nature and can only see relationships through their own feelings.

entries.title: Competition anxiety
entries.synopsis: Manosphere shorthand for making a partner or prospect feel that rivals could replace them. It splices two real effects — social proof and jealousy — into one tactic. Visible desirability can shift a first impression; deliberately manufacturing insecurity has no evidence of building durable desire.
commonMisreadings: Making your girlfriend jealous keeps her attracted because women want a man other women want.

entries.title: Hypergamy
entries.synopsis: The drive to “marry up” in status. Real as a tilt (women weight status more), false as an iron law (educational hypergamy has reversed).
boundaryConditions: The tilt is measured on stated and revealed preference for status and does not predict that any given pairing will be status-asymmetric.
The educational version has reversed across most developed countries, so evidence from an era of male educational advantage no longer transfers.
commonMisreadings: Hypergamy is an iron law: women always trade up and marry the highest-status man available.
pressureTests: Is the claim that women weight status more on average, or that women never pair downward?

entries.title: Body count
entries.synopsis: A partner’s number of prior lovers, claimed to wreck pair-bonding. Real as a confounded correlation with divorce; false as the “oxytocin runs out” mechanism.
boundaryConditions: The association is observational and confounded by religiosity and age at first marriage; controlling for those shrinks it.
It concerns a statistical association across populations and makes no prediction about any individual couple.
commonMisreadings: A high body count destroys a woman's oxytocin, so her marriage is doomed from the start.
pressureTests: Is the source claiming a correlation, or the biological mechanism the correlation does not support?

entries.title: AF/BB (Alpha Fucks, Beta Bucks)
entries.synopsis: The dual-mating claim that women take genes from hot men and provision from stable ones. The ovulatory-shift mechanism behind it fails to replicate.
boundaryConditions: A dual strategy existing and the ovulatory-shift mechanism working are separate questions, and replication bears on the second.
commonMisreadings: Women take genes from attractive men and provision from stable ones, cycling between them predictably.

entries.title: AWALT (All Women Are Like That)
entries.synopsis: The doctrine that women share one hidden nature. Where strategy curdles into contempt — a blanket claim that can’t survive contact with actual people.
boundaryConditions: An aggregate tendency and a universal rule are different strengths, and individual variation is what separates them.
commonMisreadings: Women share one hidden nature, so knowing it predicts how any individual woman dates.

entries.title: Frame
entries.synopsis: Holding your own center instead of begging the room to validate you. At its best, calm self-command; at its worst, performative dominance.
boundaryConditions: Frame is a disposition, not a technique that produces attraction; it removes a liability rather than adding value.
It says nothing about whether the interaction should continue — a well-held frame in a bad match is still a bad match.
commonMisreadings: Holding frame means hiding every feeling from her, so a man stays stone-faced while dating.
pressureTests: Is this describing self-possession, or a performance staged for someone else?

entries.title: Preselection
entries.synopsis: Being visibly wanted makes you more wanted. Real social proof — but it shifts how value is read, it doesn’t create attraction from nothing.
boundaryConditions: The effect requires the prior interest to be visible to the observer and does nothing where nobody can see who else wanted you.
Evidence for mate-choice copying is mixed and mostly from small lab studies; the direction is sound, the magnitude unsettled.
commonMisreadings: Looking wanted creates attraction from thin air, so women want a man other women already wanted.
pressureTests: Would the effect survive if the observer could not see who else was interested?

entries.title: Dread
entries.synopsis: Deliberately raising a partner’s fear of losing you so their effort returns. The diagnosis under it is sound — desire needs maintenance — but the tactic is one of the few here that has actually been measured, and jealousy induction tracks aggression, withdrawal, and partner violence.
boundaryConditions: The observation underneath it is sound and separable from the tactic: desire decays without maintenance, which argues for raising your own value rather than lowering their security.
commonMisreadings: Manufactured jealousy is a legitimate repair tool, so a romantic partner should stay slightly afraid.
pressureTests: Does this move raise your value, or only their fear?

entries.title: Shit test
entries.synopsis: A provocation read as a covert check on your steadiness. People genuinely do probe before trusting someone — but reading every friction as a rigged exam turns a partner into an examiner, which is the tell that the lens is running the relationship.
boundaryConditions: Probing for steadiness before extending trust is ordinary and mostly unconscious; the doctrine's addition is that it is deliberate, constant, and scored.
commonMisreadings: A woman's every complaint while dating is a covert exam, so calm defiance wins romance.
pressureTests: Is there a reading on which the other person meant exactly what they said?

entries.title: Statusmaxxing
entries.synopsis: Building status and resources as a man’s main lever. Sound — a man’s value is status-elastic — but prestige beats borrowed dominance theater.
boundaryConditions: Status elasticity is a male-side asymmetry; the same lever does not return the same amount on the female side.
Status is read locally — the status that prices well in one market prices at nothing in another.
commonMisreadings: Performing dominance is how a man raises his status, so acting alpha makes women want him.
pressureTests: Is the status earned prestige, or a dominance performance the audience is expected to score?

entries.title: The Charm Ceiling
entries.synopsis: How far “game” can carry you past looks. Access-gated, not value-gated: near-zero online, full-strength in a social circle.
boundaryConditions: Access and value are separate gates: the ceiling moves with how much exposure a venue allows, not with how much skill exists.
commonMisreadings: Learned social skill carries a man past his looks equally in every venue he dates in.

entries.title: Game
entries.synopsis: Learned social and seduction skill — the red pill’s answer to fixed looks. Real but access-gated: near-zero power online, full strength inside a social circle.
boundaryConditions: The skill needs an interaction to run in; where the filter is a photograph there is nothing for it to act on.
The ceiling is set by access, not by how good the practitioner gets — more skill does not buy the exposure it requires.
commonMisreadings: Enough game overcomes any face, so a man with tight game can attract any woman anywhere.
pressureTests: In this setting, is there enough interaction for social skill to act on at all?

entries.title: The 80/20 rule
entries.synopsis: The claim that female desire funnels to the top fifth of men. Real as app-attention skew; false as a pairing lock-out — tried on the Mythbuster, and the lock-out doesn’t hold.
boundaryConditions: App attention and actual pairing are measured on different populations, and the skew is far stronger in the first.
commonMisreadings: Twenty percent of men absorb every match, so the remaining men stay shut out of dating.

entries.title: High-value man
entries.synopsis: A man high on the SMV stack — looks, money, status, charm, exposure compounding. A market read; the trouble starts when “high-value” gets read as “high-worth.”
boundaryConditions: The read is market- and moment-specific: the same stack prices differently in another venue and age band.
It describes desirability as priced, not partner quality — nothing in the stack measures how someone treats a partner.
commonMisreadings: A high-value man is simply a better person, which is why women want him for a relationship.
pressureTests: Is high-value being used as a price, or as a verdict on the person?

entries.title: The Inversion
entries.synopsis: Past some SMV threshold the market flips: he stops offering and starts filtering, and women compete for access. Asserted constantly, measured never — the site files it as a Lens, not a fact.
boundaryConditions: A threshold being asserted and a threshold being measured are different states, and this one sits in the first.
commonMisreadings: Above a certain rating a man stops asking, and women start pursuing him to date.

entries.title: The Men’s Strike
entries.synopsis: The fantasy that coordinated male withdrawal would reset the market. The coordinated strike can’t hold (defection pays); the uncoordinated one is already here — and isn’t producing the reset.
boundaryConditions: A coordinated strike and a withdrawal already underway differ in whether anybody organised it, and defection pays in the first.
commonMisreadings: Men stopping together shifts the terms, so an organised refusal is what changes dating itself.

entries.title: MGTOW
entries.synopsis: Men Going Their Own Way — exit as ideology. The site’s read: a label for a withdrawal already underway, not its engine.
boundaryConditions: The ideology describes a stated exit; the measurable withdrawal it is credited with is uncoordinated and predates the label.
As a coordinated strategy it cannot hold, because defection pays, so the label describes individual exit rather than collective action.
commonMisreadings: MGTOW is why men quit dating; the ideology caused the withdrawal from the dating market.
pressureTests: Did the withdrawal this is credited with start before or after the label existed?

entries.title: The Status Trade
entries.synopsis: The model naming the real kernel in hypergamy: beauty traded against status. Tested against the data, the trade is eroding as women’s earnings rise — fading, not hardening.
boundaryConditions: A trade existing and a trade holding its exchange rate are separate questions, and earnings bear on the second.
commonMisreadings: Looks swap for rank at a fixed price, so the deal holds whatever a woman earns in dating.

entries.title: Simp
entries.synopsis: A man over-investing attention and resources in someone who prices him at zero. The insult overshoots — but the underlying exchange rate is worth auditing.
boundaryConditions: The term describes an exchange rate, not a personality; the same behavior inside a reciprocated relationship is not the phenomenon.
It is a rhetorical label with no measured prevalence behind it.
commonMisreadings: Any man who spends money on a woman he is dating is simping, full stop.
pressureTests: What did the other side actually return, and would this be called simping if it had been reciprocated?

entries.title: Emotional harem
entries.synopsis: The bench of “just friends” men kept for validation and support while romantic interest goes elsewhere. Being on the bench doesn’t make you special — it makes you useful.
boundaryConditions: It requires knowing extraction; friendship where interest is unrequited but not exploited is the friend zone instead.
The site's read describes a dynamic, not a measured prevalence — there is no count of how common it is.
commonMisreadings: Being an orbiter in her emotional harem makes you special, so she will start dating you eventually.
pressureTests: Is the support flowing both ways, or only inward?

entries.title: Monk mode
entries.synopsis: Withdrawing from the market to grind self-improvement — money, body, skills. Sound as a season; cope when it becomes a permanent excuse never to re-enter.
boundaryConditions: It targets the improvable levers — money, body, skills — and actively costs exposure while it runs.
It is a personal strategy with no outcome data behind it; the site files it as reasoned advice, not a measured effect.
commonMisreadings: Permanent monk mode fixes your value, so a man should stay out of dating indefinitely.
pressureTests: Is there an exit date and a measurable target, or has the season become the position?

entries.title: The feminine imperative
entries.synopsis: The claim that women in aggregate act on a shared drive toward status, security, and control of reproduction — and that laws, media, and courtship norms bend toward whatever serves it. Real as an incentive gradient; false as a committee — nobody convenes it, and reading every asymmetry as proof one does is how the model curdles into AWALT.
boundaryConditions: An incentive gradient and a committee are different mechanisms, and reading every asymmetry as design is how one becomes the other.
commonMisreadings: Women convene and coordinate a shared agenda, so laws and courtship norms follow a decision somebody made.

entries.title: The male imperative
entries.synopsis: The mirror claim: men in aggregate act on a shared drive toward status, provision, and reproductive access. The site names both because the two imperatives intersect and often align — treating only one sex as running an agenda is the tell that a model has curdled into a grievance.
boundaryConditions: Both imperatives are named here because they intersect, and treating only one sex as running an agenda is the tell.
commonMisreadings: Only women act as a bloc, so men pursuing rank and access approach dating as individuals.

entries.title: Fem-centrism
entries.synopsis: The claim that a culture’s operating default — what counts as normal, fair, or beyond debate — runs on the feminine imperative rather than on a neutral negotiation between the sexes. The site already described one slice of this without naming it: the one-sided commitment frame.
boundaryConditions: The claim is about which side’s terms count as neutral, not about who holds formal power.
Asymmetries running the other way exist and do not refute the claim, nor does the concept license reading every one of them as design.
commonMisreadings: Fem-centrism means women deliberately coordinate to set the rules about which men they date.
pressureTests: Is the asymmetry evidence of a default nobody set, or is the argument asserting somebody set it?

entries.title: The Operative Frame
entries.synopsis: The named mechanism under fem-centrism: whichever side holds more reproductive and social leverage sets the default the other gets measured against. The site’s read is that the post-1960 locus-of-control shift moved that default toward the feminine imperative — a structural argument, not a measured one.
boundaryConditions: Whose terms count as neutral and who holds formal power are separate questions, and this one is about the first.
commonMisreadings: Whoever holds formal power sets the default, so courtship norms follow whichever side writes the laws.

entries.title: Unplugging
entries.synopsis: Seeing the operative frame as a frame instead of as neutral reality — and noticing the conditioned shame that stops most men getting that far. A real cognitive shift; corrosive the moment “I’ve unplugged” hardens into an identity that forecloses re-examining the model itself.
boundaryConditions: The concept describes noticing a frame, not what follows from it, and licenses no particular doctrine about how the market works.
It is a described cognitive shift with no measurement behind it; the site treats it as a Lens, not a finding.
commonMisreadings: Once a man has unplugged he sees the dating market clearly and his model is settled.
pressureTests: Does the person claiming to have unplugged still allow the new model to be wrong?

entries.title: The locus-of-control shift
entries.synopsis: The claim that reliable hormonal birth control — available to women from 1960, with no male equivalent since — moved control over conception, and with it leverage over the whole market, toward women. The timing is settled history; how much of present-day fem-centrism it actually explains is a Lens, not a measurement.
boundaryConditions: Settled timing and measured causal weight are different standards of evidence, and only the timing is established.
commonMisreadings: Reliable contraception explains fem-centrism completely, so its arrival settles how women and men date now.

entries.title: The feminine reality
entries.synopsis: Tomassi’s term for the claim that men live inside a version of reality organized around women’s priorities and mistake it for reality itself. The Operative Frame is the mechanism; this is what living inside it is supposed to feel like. Real as a description of a default nobody voted on; empty the moment it turns unfalsifiable — if every counter-example is more proof of the frame, nothing could ever count against it.
boundaryConditions: A default favouring one side is compatible with nobody having chosen it, and with individual women resenting it.
commonMisreadings: Women consciously agreed among themselves on the terms men date under.
pressureTests: What observation would count against the frame instead of counting as one more instance of it?

entries.title: Feminization
entries.synopsis: The claim that culture, schooling, and media have been progressively remade around feminine norms — and that masculinity is now the thing boys get trained out of. Real as a shift in some institutions and in how men get written; useless as stated, because it reads every change as decline and never says what the right amount would have been. The testable version names an institution, a decade, and an outcome.
boundaryConditions: How men get portrayed in media and how boys get taught are separate measurements, and they often disagree.
commonMisreadings: Men who date now behave identically to the women they pursue.
pressureTests: Which institution, which decade, which outcome — and what would the correct amount of change have looked like?

entries.title: Negging
entries.synopsis: A backhanded compliment deployed as an opener, inherited from pickup-artist material. The page’s finding is precise and unflattering to both sides of the argument: it has never been tested for whether it works. The single empirical paper measured what people think of it — every variant was rated more harmful than an ordinary opening line — and nobody has run the efficacy study in either direction.
boundaryConditions: Negging has never been tested for whether it works: the single empirical paper measured what people think of it, not what it does.
In that paper every variant was rated more harmful than an ordinary opening line, and nobody has run the efficacy study in either direction.
commonMisreadings: Negging works — a backhanded compliment lowers her guard, which is why the technique spread.
The research has shown negging backfires, so the question is settled.

entries.title: Playing hard to get
entries.synopsis: Manufactured scarcity as a courtship tactic, and the coachable genre’s flagship. Its own founding 1973 paper ran five experiments that found nothing and a sixth that worked only for a selectively hard-to-get target — hard for others, available to you — a far narrower claim than the advice built on it.
boundaryConditions: The founding 1973 paper ran five experiments that found nothing; only the sixth worked, and only for a selectively hard-to-get target — hard for others, available to you.
That is a far narrower claim than the advice built on it, and it is the evidence base the entry rests on.
commonMisreadings: Manufactured scarcity works: make yourself unavailable and your value rises, and there is a 1973 study behind it.
Being hard to get is a general tactic that works on anyone.

entries.title: Market model vs. moral theory
entries.synopsis: The site’s cleanest cut through the Red Pill. A market model asks what is scarce, what is rewarded, and where a person has leverage; a moral theory decides what people deserve and what they are allowed to feel. The lens is strongest when it stays in the first column and weakest when it smuggles conclusions from the first into the second. An interpretive tool, offered as one — not a documented fact.
boundaryConditions: The model's own column is what is scarce, what is rewarded, and where a person has leverage; it is weakest exactly when conclusions from that column are smuggled into what people deserve.
The site offers it as an interpretive tool and marks it as one — not a documented fact.
commonMisreadings: If the market rewards it, that settles what people deserve — the numbers tell you who is owed what and what anyone is allowed to feel.
The market model is a documented fact about how mating works, not a lens.

entries.title: Branch-swinging
entries.synopsis: Manosphere shorthand for lining up the next partner before letting go of the current one. It is the textbook case of the leap the essay tracks: “people protect their options” is an ordinary human tendency, and “women always branch-swing” converts a distribution into a personality. Guarding your downside is real; a female essence built out of it is not.
boundaryConditions: Guarding your downside is an ordinary human tendency, and that is the real part; the leap is converting a distribution into a personality.
The entry is manosphere shorthand being audited as a textbook case of that leap, not a measured rate of the behaviour.
commonMisreadings: Women always branch-swing — lining up the next partner before letting go is simply what a woman is.
Because people protect their options, any woman with friends is already halfway out the door.

entries.title: Alpha / beta
entries.synopsis: The hierarchy of male types the lens sorts men into. A thematic analysis of 227 Red Pill and incel posts found it as one of three recurring pillars, beside gender essentialism and an informal psychology assigning women hidden motives.
boundaryConditions: The cited work is a thematic analysis of 227 Red Pill and incel posts, which found alpha/beta as one of three recurring pillars beside gender essentialism and an informal psychology assigning women hidden motives.
That is a finding about what the discourse repeats, not a measurement of whether the hierarchy exists.
commonMisreadings: Men sort cleanly into alphas and betas, and the tier you land in is a fixed fact about you.
Researchers studied the hierarchy and found it, so the categories are established.

entries.title: Hegemonic masculinity
entries.synopsis: The sociological name for the dominant, competitive template of manhood a culture holds up as the standard. A content analysis of 26 foundational Red Pill documents (~130,000 words) found the lens is that template fused to the language of self-optimization and markets: men instructed to treat themselves as improvable capital and relationships as strategic exchanges.
boundaryConditions: The term names the dominant, competitive template a culture holds up as the standard — a sociological description of a template, not of every man.

The evidence cited is a content analysis of 26 foundational Red Pill documents (~130,000 words), so it characterizes that corpus's fusion of the template with self-optimization and market language, not men in general.
commonMisreadings: Hegemonic masculinity is just an insult for masculinity itself — the term says being a man is the problem.
It describes how men actually are, since the culture's standard template is the natural one.

entries.title: Mate-choice copying
entries.synopsis: The measured construct sitting under “preselection”: social information about who else wants someone shifts how desirable they look. A 2018 meta-analysis found it real but narrow — women rated male targets higher beside an opposite-sex companion with no clear effect the other way, both sexes updated when the companion’s own desirability rose, and the literature carries high heterogeneity and moderate publication bias.
boundaryConditions: The 2018 meta-analysis found the effect real but narrow: women rated male targets higher beside an opposite-sex companion, with no clear effect the other way, and both sexes updated when the companion's own desirability rose.
That literature carries high heterogeneity and moderate publication bias, which bounds how firmly the effect can be read.
commonMisreadings: Preselection is a law: be seen with a woman and every woman wants you more.
Copying works the same in both directions, so men update on a woman's companion exactly as women update on a man's.

entries.title: Abundance
entries.synopsis: Having enough going on that no single outcome owns you. Real as a life, fake as a posture — built abundance changes your behaviour, performed abundance only changes your messaging. The useful version is friends, interests and several honest opportunities, so one stranger is not carrying your whole emotional future; the theater version is manufactured indifference and implied competition.
boundaryConditions: The split the entry draws is built versus performed: built abundance changes your behaviour, performed abundance only changes your messaging.

What is described is the composition of the useful version — friends, interests and several honest opportunities, so one stranger is not carrying your whole emotional future — not a measured effect on outcomes.
commonMisreadings: Abundance is a frame you project: act indifferent, imply competition, and the options follow.
Having options means never letting any single outcome matter to you.

entries.title: The fatherlessness statistic
entries.synopsis: The meme that 85% of imprisoned youth — or 90% of felons — grew up fatherless. It has no traceable source; fact-checkers chasing it land on decades-old, unlocatable citations. The measured figure is 57% of state prisoners raised in something other than a two-parent home: a real gap, nowhere near the claim.
boundaryConditions: The 85% and 90% versions have no traceable source; fact-checkers chasing them land on decades-old, unlocatable citations.
The measured figure is 57% of state prisoners raised in something other than a two-parent home — a real gap, nowhere near the claim, and a statement about household composition.
commonMisreadings: 85% of imprisoned youth grew up fatherless — the number is documented and it settles the argument.
The real figure is 90% of felons, and the only reason it gets disputed is discomfort.

entries.title: “Never date single mothers”
entries.synopsis: The manosphere rule, and the site audits both it and its mirror. It takes three true ledger entries — real time and money constraints, a 31.6% poverty rate for single-mother families, a custody split that prices four-fifths of the load onto women — and absolutizes them into a caste, turning a cost curve into a cliff. The blue-pill mirror, that noticing the ledger at all is bigotry, is the same dodge reversed.
boundaryConditions: The three ledger entries the audit accepts are real time and money constraints, a 31.6% poverty rate for single-mother families, and a custody split pricing four-fifths of the load onto women.
Those describe a cost curve, not a cliff — absolutizing them into a caste is the failure, and the blue-pill mirror is the same dodge reversed.
commonMisreadings: The costs are real, so the rule is right: single mothers are a category you rule out on sight.
Noticing the constraints at all is bigotry, so the ledger should not be read.

entries.title: “Ages like wine”
entries.synopsis: The Wall’s mirror claim — a man’s value climbs while a woman’s falls. Half of it holds: in the Bruch & Newman data men’s app desirability does rise through the thirties and forties. Then it peaks around 50 and turns down. The phrase describes the first half of a curve and quietly drops the second. The man on the favorable side of the double standard at 45 is on the far side of his own peak a decade later.
boundaryConditions: In the Bruch & Newman data men's app desirability does rise through the thirties and forties — then peaks around 50 and turns down.
The evidence is app desirability, and the phrase describes only the first half of that curve: the man favored at 45 is on the far side of his own peak a decade later.
commonMisreadings: Men age like wine: a man's value keeps climbing, so waiting costs him nothing.
The desirability data proves the double standard runs one way for life.

entries.title: Educational hypergamy
entries.synopsis: Marrying up in schooling — the credential version of the status trade, and the one place the trend has actually reversed. Esteve et al., across 120 countries, find wives are now more often the more-educated partner. Read alongside the provider norm halving from 85% to 55%, this is the site’s “fading, not hardening”: hypergamy’s material base thins as women’s earnings and degrees rise.
boundaryConditions: Esteve et al., across 120 countries, find wives are now more often the more-educated partner — this is the one place the trend has actually reversed.
Read alongside the provider norm falling from 85% to 55%, the site's read is 'fading, not hardening': hypergamy's material base thins as women's earnings and degrees rise.
commonMisreadings: Women always marry up in schooling, and as women collect more degrees hypergamy only hardens.
Educational hypergamy is a fixed rule, so a woman will not partner with a less-educated man.

entries.title: “The bar is in hell”
entries.synopsis: The complaint that women’s standards for men have collapsed. The ruling reframes it: the bar sits on the floor for men she isn’t attracted to and on the roof for the ones she is — selective, not low. Attraction really does bend the ruler (Langlois et al., 2000; attractiveness predicts live desire at r ≈.40, Eastwick et al., 2014).
boundaryConditions: The reframe is about selectivity, not level: the bar sits on the floor for men she isn't attracted to and on the roof for the ones she is.
The evidence cited is that attraction bends the ruler (Langlois et al., 2000; attractiveness predicts live desire at r ≈.40, Eastwick et al., 2014).
commonMisreadings: Women's standards for men have collapsed — the bar is on the floor, so anyone gets in.
If her standards were low she would be attracted to me, so being passed over proves the bar is high for everyone.

entries.title: Dark Triad
entries.synopsis: Narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy — the trait cluster the “women want jerks” argument leans on. The kernel holds at first sight: 128 women rated a high-Dark-Triad character as more attractive with looks held constant, and narcissists are more popular at zero acquaintance.
boundaryConditions: The kernel the synopsis grants holds at first sight: 128 women rated a high-Dark-Triad character as more attractive with looks held constant, and narcissists are more popular at zero acquaintance.
Zero acquaintance and first impressions are the conditions of that evidence; nothing here reaches past them.
commonMisreadings: Women want jerks: narcissism, manipulation and callousness are what actually attract, so decency is the mistake.
The Dark Triad advantage holds all the way through a relationship, not just at the start.

entries.title: The Blue Pill
entries.synopsis: Romance as sincere, fair, and personality-driven. Keeps the human center — warmth, trust — but denies the thresholds that decide who gets considered.
boundaryConditions: Warmth mattering and thresholds existing are compatible, so keeping the first does not require denying the second.
commonMisreadings: Sincerity and warmth decide romantic outcomes, so thresholds stay irrelevant to who gets considered for dating.

entries.title: Just be yourself
entries.synopsis: Healthy as authenticity; harmful when it means refusing to improve presentation, social skill, or exposure.
boundaryConditions: It is sound where the problem is pretense and does nothing where the binding constraint is exposure or presentation.
It says who to be, not who will meet you, and makes no prediction about outcomes.
commonMisreadings: Just be yourself and skip improving your style, because the right woman wants you as-is.
pressureTests: Is the person being told to stop pretending, or not to bother improving?

entries.title: There’s someone for everyone
entries.synopsis: Comforting, but not what the base rates show — especially for below-average men. Patience is wise; passivity isn’t.
boundaryConditions: The base rates that undercut the slogan concern the tail of the distribution, not the median person, who does pair.
Lifetime pairing rates are cohort-bound and shifting, so a rate from one generation is not a forecast for the next.
commonMisreadings: There is someone for everyone, so every man will meet someone eventually just by waiting.
pressureTests: Is this offering patience, or licensing doing nothing?

entries.title: Personality matters
entries.synopsis: True but incomplete. Personality deepens and sustains attraction — usually after a first physical filter is passed. In one nine-year study, a person’s own lower neuroticism and higher conscientiousness predicted their own satisfaction, while partner-personality effects were not detected. That actor–partner asymmetry is cohort-bound, not proof that a partner’s character never matters.
boundaryConditions: Personality's measured effect is largest on retention and satisfaction and smallest at the stranger market's first filter.
Ratings of personality taken after a face is visible are contaminated by the halo effect and overstate its independent contribution.
The nine-year actor-partner result concerns 486 different-sex German couples in three survivor cohorts and uses brief self-report instruments; it is not a universal null for partner effects.
Actor effects are associations with a person's own satisfaction, not proof that changing a trait will produce the measured relationship outcome.
commonMisreadings: Personality matters more than looks, so a great personality is what makes women choose a man.
A nine-year study found no partner effects, so a partner's personality cannot affect relationship satisfaction.
pressureTests: Was personality measured before the first physical filter, or after it?
Is an actor effect being confused with a partner effect, or a cohort-specific null being promoted into a universal law?

entries.title: The One / the right person
entries.synopsis: Useful as patience, dangerous as passivity. The right person still has to meet you, notice you, want you, and choose you.
boundaryConditions: Patience and passivity look identical from outside, and the difference shows up in whether anyone new is met.
commonMisreadings: One right person exists for everyone, so a man who waits will marry without ever approaching.

entries.title: “No good men left”
entries.synopsis: The female-side scarcity story. The men exist; the honest versions of the complaint are about the overlap — attraction, standards, and timing — not the census.
aliases: all the good men are taken
boundaryConditions: Local sex ratios and assortative constraints can make the complaint true inside one city or age band while the population census shows no shortage.
The claim concerns availability, not desirability, and makes no argument about whether the standards themselves are calibrated.
commonMisreadings: All the good men are taken, so a woman looking for a decent husband has zero options.
pressureTests: Is the shortage in the population, or in the overlap between one person's standards and their reachable market?

entries.title: The Soulmate Pill
entries.synopsis: The belief that a relationship is settled by finding the right person rather than built with one. Measured for decades as destiny versus growth beliefs, and the finding is stranger than “soulmates aren’t real”: the belief is an amplifier whose sign is set by fit — it supercharges a good match and becomes a trapdoor in a bad one.
boundaryConditions: The belief is an amplifier rather than an error: it raises satisfaction and commitment where perceived fit is good and accelerates exit where it is poor, so its sign is set by something outside itself.
commonMisreadings: Conflict in a romance proves a mismatch, so the destined partner produces effortless compatibility instead.
pressureTests: When something goes wrong, does the belief generate a task or a verdict?

entries.title: The spark
entries.synopsis: Butterflies read as destiny. Often the opposite: the flutter spikes on uncertainty and intensity — the exact things that make a bond unstable. Excitement and fit are not the same person.
boundaryConditions: Intensity and stability are separate properties, and the conditions that spike one often undermine the other.
commonMisreadings: Intense butterflies signal a stable match, so the flutter predicts which couples last together.

entries.title: “Love conquers all”
entries.synopsis: Affection is not a solvent. It does not dissolve incompatible plans about children, money, geography, or faith. Feeling strongly about someone tells you the stakes — never the answer.
boundaryConditions: The claim is about incompatible plans specifically: children, money, geography, faith.
Feeling strongly about someone tells you the stakes, never the answer — which is a statement about what affection cannot settle, not an argument against affection.
commonMisreadings: If we love each other enough, the disagreements about children, money, geography or faith will dissolve on their own.
Strong feeling is the answer — if it feels this big, we should go ahead.

entries.title: “Don’t settle”
entries.synopsis: Sound as a floor, corrosive as a ceiling. It correctly refuses contempt and neglect; it wrongly licenses rejecting a real person for failing to match a composite who does not exist.
boundaryConditions: As a floor the advice is sound — it correctly refuses contempt and neglect.
It goes corrosive only as a ceiling, where it licenses rejecting a real person for failing to match a composite who does not exist.
commonMisreadings: Never settle: if a real person misses anything on the list, holding out is the disciplined choice.
Any compromise at all is settling.

entries.title: “It happens when you stop looking”
entries.synopsis: Half right, and the half it gets wrong is the expensive one. Dropping desperation genuinely helps; dropping exposure cannot. The calmer version is to build a good life while keeping enough social surface area for luck to find you — communities, introductions, events, honest invitations.
boundaryConditions: Half of it holds: dropping desperation genuinely helps, while dropping exposure cannot.
The version that works keeps social surface area — communities, introductions, events, honest invitations — alongside a good life.
commonMisreadings: Stop looking and it will happen — the searching itself is what is keeping you single.
Wanting a relationship is the problem, so the fix is to want it less.

entries.title: The bond pathway
entries.synopsis: Notice → Explore → Trust → Build: the four stages at which different qualities become legible. Most Blue Pill advice fails by placing relationship virtues — kindness, loyalty, patience, communication — at the first-impression stage, where they cannot yet be observed. The correction is not to discard them but to put them where they do their work.
boundaryConditions: The four stages are Notice, Explore, Trust, Build, and the point is placement: relationship virtues cannot yet be observed at the first-impression stage.
The correction is to put those qualities where they do their work, not to discard them.
commonMisreadings: Kindness, loyalty and patience are what matter, so they are what should win the first impression.
The pathway says relationship virtues are overrated and should be dropped.

entries.title: Opposites attract
entries.synopsis: Staked at 10% true and graded Oversimplified. Similarity — actual and perceived — strongly predicts attraction: r =.47 and.39 across 313 studies. Evidence for complementarity is weak and trait-specific. One wrinkle worth keeping: in established relationships it is perceived similarity that carries the effect, not measured similarity.
boundaryConditions: The stake is 10% true, graded Oversimplified: similarity predicts attraction at r =.47 actual and.39 perceived across 313 studies, while evidence for complementarity is weak and trait-specific.
In established relationships it is perceived similarity that carries the effect, not measured similarity.
commonMisreadings: Opposites attract: difference is what generates the spark, and too much similarity goes flat.
Complementarity is as well supported as similarity, so it is a toss-up.

entries.title: Never go to bed angry
entries.synopsis: Graded Backwards. Forcing a resolution while physiologically flooded escalates the conflict, and sleep-deprived partners fight worse — couples short on sleep behaved more hostilely and showed stronger inflammatory responses to conflict discussions. A structured timeout beats a forced 2 a.m. settlement.
boundaryConditions: Graded Backwards: forcing a resolution while physiologically flooded escalates the conflict, and couples short on sleep behaved more hostilely and showed stronger inflammatory responses to conflict discussions.
What replaces the 2 a.m. settlement is a structured timeout — a deferral with a return, not indefinite avoidance.
commonMisreadings: Settle it before you sleep — going to bed angry is what lets resentment set in, so stay up until it is resolved.
A fight left open overnight is a fight that gets worse.

entries.title: “Like me for me”
entries.synopsis: The request to be accepted as-is, and the ruling is “runs both ways.” Nobody actually buys as-is acceptance: in Li et al.’s budget studies, under tight budgets women spend first on status and resources and men on physical attractiveness, while kindness and intelligence are necessities for both — necessary, not sufficient, which is the kind-but-awkward man’s exact problem.
boundaryConditions: The ruling runs both ways, and the evidence is Li et al.'s budget studies: under tight budgets women spend first on status and resources and men on physical attractiveness, while kindness and intelligence are necessities for both.
Necessary is not sufficient — which is the kind-but-awkward man's exact problem.
commonMisreadings: The right person takes you exactly as you are, so working on anything is a betrayal of who you are.
Being kind and intelligent is enough — those are the traits people actually select on.

entries.title: Relationships Throughout History
entries.synopsis: “Marriage as we know it is the anomaly, not the baseline.”
boundaryConditions: The hub card carries the essay's thesis in one line; the evidence and the qualifications live in the essay itself.
commonMisreadings: Marriage as we know it is the historical baseline that modern couples have drifted from.

entries.title: Third Spaces
entries.synopsis: “The apps didn’t win the courtship market. The places where people met were demolished first.”
boundaryConditions: The hub card states the claim; whether the emptying caused the apps or merely preceded them is argued in the essay.
commonMisreadings: Dating apps won the courtship market by outcompeting the places where couples used to meet.

entries.title: Relationships by Country
entries.synopsis: “The West didn’t invent the unbundling. It was just the pilot program.”
boundaryConditions: The hub card compresses a region-by-region comparison, so its one line is a summary rather than a finding about any country.
commonMisreadings: The West invented the unbundling of marriage and childbearing, and other countries are copying it.

entries.title: What the Wall Actually Is
entries.synopsis: “Not a cliff at 30 — a slope that everyone walks, at different grades.”
boundaryConditions: The card announces that three curves are being separated; which curve turns where is settled band by band in the essay.
commonMisreadings: The wall is a cliff at thirty where men stop wanting a woman altogether.

entries.title: Single Parenthood
entries.synopsis: “Death built it, divorce rebuilt it, choice runs it now — and America leads the world by three to one.”
boundaryConditions: The card's three-to-one comparison is against the global average, not against the next-highest country.
commonMisreadings: Divorce still runs the single-parent home, and American marriage sits close to other wealthy countries.

entries.title: The Red Pill
entries.synopsis: “The useful observations survive without the total theory. The contempt does not.”
commonMisreadings: Taking the red pill means finally seeing the truth that dating is rigged against men.

entries.title: Competition Anxiety
entries.synopsis: “Social proof can change a first read. Manufactured insecurity changes the relationship.”
commonMisreadings: Making sure your partner sees rivals chasing you is the fastest way to deepen attraction.

entries.title: Autism and Dating
entries.synopsis: “The advice assumes you missed a signal. The evidence keeps pointing at two people who missed each other.”
boundaryConditions: The hub card states the reframe in one line; the rates, the experiments and the two figures the essay could not confirm are all set out inside it.
commonMisreadings: Autistic people find dating hard because they do not really want relationships in the first place.

entries.title: Relationships Throughout History
entries.synopsis: Marriage as we know it is the anomaly, not the baseline. A Deep Dive tracing how alliance, religion, industry, and the modern love-match each rewrote what a relationship was for — from 3500 BC to now.
commonMisreadings: Alliance, religion and industry each refined one continuous idea of what marriage between two people was for.

entries.title: The Alliance Era
entries.synopsis: For most of recorded history, a wedding joined two families rather than two people. The couple stood at the center of a contract they had not written and could not easily break, closer to the terms of the deal than to the parties making it. Their assignment was to be joined, exchanged, and made to produce: an heir, an alliance, a claim on land.
boundaryConditions: This describes propertied and settled populations best, since they are the ones whose contracts survived to be read.
commonMisreadings: For most of history a wedding joined a man and a woman who chose each other freely.

entries.title: The Church Rewrites the Rules
entries.synopsis: When the Roman order gave way to the medieval Church, the institution inherited the alliance system intact and then, across centuries, quietly edited it. The Church’s strangest innovation was a single requirement: consent. It spent generations insisting that what actually made a marriage was the freely given “I do” of the two people, not the father’s signature and not the transfer of property.
boundaryConditions: Consent became the doctrinal test long before it became the practical one; families kept arranging matches throughout.
commonMisreadings: The medieval Church made a father's signature and the property transfer what created a marriage.

entries.title: The Early Modern Turn
entries.synopsis: If the Middle Ages carry an undeserved reputation for child brides, the early modern centuries carry one for prudishness, the buttoned-up world of stern sermons and unbroken chastity before the wedding. That reputation is just as false. In the rural English parishes of the late sixteenth century a startling share of brides walked to the altar visibly pregnant. The demographer P.E.H.
boundaryConditions: The bridal-pregnancy shares come from rural English parish registers, which are unusually well kept rather than representative of Europe.
commonMisreadings: Early modern brides walked to the altar chaste, since couples avoided sex before the wedding.

entries.title: The Love-Match Revolution
entries.synopsis: Then the ground moved, and it moved because of work. Industrialization pulled production out of the household and into the factory and the office, dismantling the economic logic that had underwritten marriage for five thousand years.
boundaryConditions: Industrialisation made the love-match affordable, which is a weaker mechanism than industrialisation having produced the romantic ideal.
commonMisreadings: Couples began to marry for love because romantic ideals spread across society.

entries.title: The Great Unbundling
entries.synopsis: The conclusion is worth stating bluntly, because so much modern argument is built on getting it backwards. The version of marriage nostalgia treats as timeless (the young couple, the single male breadwinner, the house full of children, the wife at home) was not history’s baseline but a brief, freakish dip.
boundaryConditions: Calling the mid-century pattern a brief dip is a claim about its duration, not a judgement of whether it worked.
commonMisreadings: The 1950s single-breadwinner household with a wife at home was marriage's long-standing historical baseline.

sourceLinks.label: Hu & Coulter (2025), The Journals of Gerontology: Series B 80(3):gbae192
Andersen et al. (2025), Journal of Health Psychology
Drews et al. (2020)
Keller et al. (2019)

entries.title: Third Spaces
entries.synopsis: The apps didn't win the courtship market — the third places where people used to meet were emptied out first. A Deep Dive tracing where courtship actually happened, from the well and the agora to the age of the app.
commonMisreadings: Couples moved courtship online because dating apps offered more than the well and the agora did.

entries.title: The Well and the Agora
entries.synopsis: Every settlement that has ever existed needed a place to draw water, and so every settlement had a place where, sooner or later, everyone turned up. The well, the spring, the public fountain: the young came to them alongside the old, because water admitted no exceptions, and in the coming and going a good deal of looking got done. Nobody built a well to make marriages.
boundaryConditions: The courtship function is a by-product of places built for water and trade, which is the section's whole point.
commonMisreadings: The well and the public fountain were built so young men and women could meet partners.

entries.title: Parish and Fair
entries.synopsis: When the classical city receded, its gathering places did not vanish so much as change management. For the thousand years between the fall of Rome and the Reformation, the two dependable venues of ordinary European life were the parish church and the seasonal fair, and between them they set the rhythm of courtship for most of the population that ever lived.
boundaryConditions: Parish and fair describe ordinary European life; elite courtship ran through household and dynasty instead.
commonMisreadings: The parish church and seasonal fair vanished with Rome, so medieval courtship lost its venues.

entries.title: The Coffeehouse Century
entries.synopsis: Then something genuinely new appeared: a gathering place you paid a small coin to enter, built for no purpose but company itself. The coffeehouse reached England in the 1650s and multiplied fast, and around it grew a whole ecology of commercial sociability — the tavern and the public house, the assembly room, the pleasure garden, the salon.
boundaryConditions: Commercial sociability was novel in being paid for and purposeless; most early coffeehouses were also largely male.
commonMisreadings: The coffeehouse was built for courtship, which is why couples paid a coin to enter.

entries.title: The Golden Age of Joining
entries.synopsis: By the last decades of the nineteenth century the gathering place had multiplied into something like a dense mesh laid over ordinary life. This was the golden age of joining: lodges and mutual-aid societies, unions and congregations, choirs and clubs and bowling leagues and fraternal orders, and above all the new commercial palaces of leisure — the dance hall, the department store, the amusement park.
boundaryConditions: The membership densities are strongest for the United States and Britain, where the joining statistics were actually collected.
commonMisreadings: The dance hall and bowling league did little to introduce men and women who would marry.

entries.title: The Great Emptying
entries.synopsis: The turn comes around 1960, and it is worth stating flatly: the third space drained. Suburbanization spread people thin across the map; the car privatized the journey that used to throw strangers together; the television, and then the screen in every pocket, privatized the evening. Membership in the joined institutions fell, decade over decade, in nearly every category at once.
boundaryConditions: Four mechanisms are named as simultaneous; the section does not apportion the decline between them.
commonMisreadings: Suburbanization, the car and television left third places full, and couples kept meeting partners there.

entries.title: Relationships by Country
entries.synopsis: The unbundling of marriage and childbearing is a wave crossing the whole world at different speeds, not a uniquely Western event. A Deep Dive comparing where the relationship transition has reached region by region — from ultra-low-fertility East Asia through Latin America, South Asia, and the Middle East to high-fertility sub-Saharan Africa.
commonMisreadings: The marriage transition reached East Asia, Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa at one uniform speed.

entries.title: East Asia
entries.synopsis: Begin where the wave has traveled furthest. More than half the countries on Earth, holding a clear majority of the world’s people, now have fertility below the level that replaces a generation, and the line keeps moving outward. East Asia is where it has moved farthest and fastest.
boundaryConditions: East Asia is the furthest along, not the only case: more than half the world's countries are already below replacement.
commonMisreadings: Fertility below replacement is confined to a few East Asian countries where couples marry late.

entries.title: Latin America
entries.synopsis: Latin America runs the experiment in almost the opposite order and arrives at the same place. Marriage here never held the monopoly it holds in East Asia. Across much of the continent, couples have for generations formed households, raised children, and stayed together without ever registering a wedding — the unión libre, the free union, a socially accepted arrangement with roots that run back centuries.
boundaryConditions: The free union is centuries old in much of the region, which is why Latin America reaches the same place in a different order.
commonMisreadings: Latin American couples always needed a registered wedding, so the unión libre is a recent invention.

entries.title: South Asia
entries.synopsis: India poses a harder question: what happens to the birth rate when the old marriage system does not loosen at all? Marriage in India remains close to universal and, for most people, arranged. Families still vet and select partners, weigh caste and community and dowry, and broker the match; the couple’s own preference has grown but still sits inside a decision the two families largely make together.
boundaryConditions: India is presented as the case where fertility fell while the marriage system held, so it works as a counter-example rather than a rule.
commonMisreadings: Indian marriage loosened into free choice, which is why the birth rate fell there.

entries.title: Middle East & North Africa
entries.synopsis: No country has fallen faster than Iran, and none makes the point more sharply, because Iran spent decades trying, with the full weight of the state, to steer its birth rate: first up, then down, then up again — and lost the wheel every time.
boundaryConditions: Iran is the sharpest case of state pronatalism failing; one country losing the wheel does not establish that every policy fails.
commonMisreadings: Iran steered its birth rate successfully whenever the state told couples to marry and reproduce.

entries.title: Sub-Saharan Africa
entries.synopsis: End where the wave has barely arrived. Sub-Saharan Africa holds the highest fertility on Earth and the youngest populations, and it is the one large region where marriage, children, and kinship still look roughly as they did across most of human history: early and near-universal marriage, bride-wealth passing between families, and, in a wide belt across the middle of the continent, polygyny that is still openly and…
boundaryConditions: The region is large and internally varied; the description fits the high-fertility belt better than the southern and coastal cities.
commonMisreadings: Sub-Saharan African marriage now looks Western: late, freely chosen, and without bride-wealth between families.

entries.title: What the Wall Actually Is
entries.synopsis: The wall isn't a cliff at 30 — it's three different curves the discourse fuses into one birthday: desirability, fertility, and marriage-market position. A Deep Dive that walks each one separately, band by band, and lets it peak where the evidence puts it. Extends the Wall card from the Frameworks page.
commonMisreadings: Desirability, fertility and marriage-market position are one curve turning on a woman's thirtieth birthday.

entries.title: 18 to 25
entries.synopsis: The wall is the most repeated claim there is about women and age, and it arrives as a single event on a single birthday. Youth is the asset, youth peaks in the early twenties, and somewhere around thirty the whole thing drops off a cliff, after which a woman is spoken of as post-wall. The picture is vivid and portable, which is most of why it travels as far as it does. It is also fused.
boundaryConditions: App-desirability curves measure attention inside one market, which is a narrower thing than being wanted.
commonMisreadings: A woman's desirability, fertility and marriage-market position all peak together in her early twenties.

entries.title: 26 to 31
entries.synopsis: By these years the app-desirability line has already tipped downward for women, and in the wall’s telling the window is closing fast. Set beside the actual timing of marriage, the alarm looks misplaced. The median American woman marries for the first time near the top of this band, not before it — and the median man a couple of years later still.
boundaryConditions: Median first-marriage age is a population median; it says where the middle sits, not when any individual window closes.
commonMisreadings: A woman in her late twenties has already missed the age when most women marry.

entries.title: 32 to 37
entries.synopsis: Here is the part of the wall that is not a myth, and it deserves a fair hearing before anything is subtracted from it. Fertility genuinely declines with age, and it does so on a schedule the other curves do not share. This is the one gradient that comes from the body rather than the market, and its real turn falls inside these years.
boundaryConditions: This is the one gradient the essay concedes to the wall; conceding it is not conceding the fused version.
commonMisreadings: Fertility decline between thirty-two and thirty-seven comes from the dating market rather than the body.

entries.title: 38 to 49
entries.synopsis: Past the fertility inflection comes the curve the culture watches hardest of all — the age gap between partners. It has been measured directly, and the measurement is unambiguous about its direction.
boundaryConditions: The age-gap measurement is unambiguous about direction and says nothing about whether either partner is satisfied.
commonMisreadings: The age gap between partners who marry runs in both directions about equally often.

entries.title: 50 and Up
entries.synopsis: The wall’s mirror claim is that men age like wine, their value climbing while a woman’s falls. The same Bruch and Newman curve that anchors the female slope carries the male one, and it does rise — for a while. Men’s app-desirability climbs through the thirties and forties and peaks around 50, and then it too turns down. “Ages like wine” describes the first half of a curve and quietly drops the second.
boundaryConditions: The male curve does rise for decades before turning; the section disputes where it ends, not that it climbs.
commonMisreadings: Men age like wine, so women want a man more as he passes fifty.

entries.title: Single Parenthood
entries.synopsis: The one-parent home is not new — it changed owners. Death built it, divorce rebuilt it, and the never-married route runs it now, with America leading the world at 23% of children in solo-parent households against a 7% global share. A Deep Dive that walks the century, the custody split, the class gradient, and what the outcome data actually survives scrutiny. Extends the single-parenthood charts on the Statistics page.
boundaryConditions: The essay separates a money line, an outcome line and a meme line precisely because they do not survive scrutiny equally.
commonMisreadings: The custody split and class gradient confirm the harshest outcome numbers about marriage and single mothers.

entries.title: 1900 to 1959: The Widow’s House
entries.synopsis: No figure in the gender discourse works harder than the single mother. One side reads her as the proof of male abandonment, the other as the price of female choices, and the statistics posters have her raising 85% of the youth in prison and most of the dropouts and runaways besides — numbers that close arguments precisely because nobody checks them. This essay checks them.
boundaryConditions: Pre-1968 figures predate the Census Bureau's modern series, so the early picture is assembled from less consistent sources.
commonMisreadings: Before 1960 the one-parent home came from divorce rather than the death of a husband.

entries.title: 1960 to 1979: Divorce Rebuilds It
entries.synopsis: When the Census Bureau first drew its modern series in 1968, the old world was still largely intact: 85% of American children lived with two parents, 11% with their mother only, 1% with their father only. Then the legal ground moved.
boundaryConditions: Legal change is named as the trigger; the section does not claim no-fault divorce alone produced the whole rise.
commonMisreadings: American children living with a husband and wife held their share steady through the 1970s.

entries.title: 1980 to 1999: The Route In Flips
entries.synopsis: The divorce boom crested around 1980 and receded. The single-parent share kept climbing anyway, because the route into the one-parent home was changing underneath it: children stopped arriving in marriages that later broke, and started arriving outside marriage in the first place.
boundaryConditions: The flip is about the route in, so the same household share can be reached by two different paths with different histories.
commonMisreadings: The single-parent share kept climbing after 1980 because divorce among married couples kept rising.

entries.title: 2000 to 2019: The World’s Highest
entries.synopsis: Where did the curve land? Higher than anywhere else on Earth. Not among the highest — the highest, of every country measured.
boundaryConditions: The ranking covers the 130 countries in one study, so highest means highest of those measured.
commonMisreadings: Several wealthy nations sit above America for children raised outside marriage by one parent.

entries.title: The 2020s: The Ledger
entries.synopsis: So what does the one-adult house actually cost? The honest answer has three entries: a money line that is brutal and undisputed, an outcomes line that is real but smaller than advertised, and a meme line that is mostly fabricated. They deserve to be kept apart.
boundaryConditions: Keeping the three lines apart is the section's method: the money line is undisputed, the outcome line is smaller than advertised, the meme line is mostly fabricated.
commonMisreadings: For the children of a couple who marry, the poverty gap and the memes are equal.

entries.title: The Red Pill
entries.synopsis: A sourced Deep Dive into the Red Pill: where the ideology came from, which observations about dating markets survive scrutiny, where its sexed theory outruns the evidence, and why agency does not require contempt.
commonMisreadings: The red pill is proven science about how women actually behave in the sexual marketplace.

entries.title: What It Is: A Lens Sold as an Awakening
entries.synopsis: The Red Pill borrows its name from The Matrix: swallow the pill and see the machinery hidden behind ordinary life. In its dating form, the hidden machinery is a sexual marketplace. Looks, status, scarcity, and leverage matter; stated ideals are treated as public relations; men are told to stop waiting to be chosen and improve the traits the market rewards. That package is why the label travels.
commonMisreadings: Swallowing the red pill reveals the hidden rules every woman follows in dating.

sourceLinks.label: Van Valkenburgh (2021), “Digesting the Red Pill: Masculinity and Neoliberalism in the Manosphere,” Men and Masculinities 24(1):84–103
Ribeiro et al. (2021), “The Evolution of the Manosphere Across the Web,” Proceedings of ICWSM 15

entries.title: What Survives: Markets Are Uneven and Agency Matters
entries.synopsis: The Red Pill’s durable appeal is not mysterious. It names facts polite advice often evades. Attraction is not awarded for moral effort. Looks matter strongly in first impressions. Men still do most initiating in heterosexual markets. Women, on average, weight a partner’s resources and status more than men do. Online attention is sharply unequal. A person can be kind, sincere, and lonely at the same time.
commonMisreadings: Every red pill claim about attraction holds because looks and money decide who men and women pick.

sourceLinks.label: Bruch & Newman (2018), Science Advances 4(8)
Walter et al. (2020), Psychological Science 31(4)

entries.title: The Leap: From Patterns to a Theory of Women
entries.synopsis: The break happens when a distribution becomes a personality. “Women weight status more on average” becomes “women are hypergamous.” “People protect their options” becomes “women always branch-swing.” A description of incentives becomes a claim that one sex is deceitful by nature and the other must manage it with permanent suspicion.
aliases: Leap: From Patterns to a Theory of Women
commonMisreadings: Hypergamy is female nature, so a committed woman upgrades to a richer man whenever possible.

sourceLinks.label: Vallerga & Zurbriggen (2022), “Hegemonic masculinities in the Manosphere,” Analyses of Social Issues and Public Policy 22(2):602–625

entries.title: The Verdict: Keep the Agency, Drop the Total Theory
entries.synopsis: The Red Pill solves a real emotional problem: it gives men who feel acted upon a sense that they can act. Train. Dress better. Earn more. Stop pleading with people who are not choosing you. Build enough of a life that rejection is information rather than annihilation. Those moves need no claim about women’s nature to work.
aliases: Verdict: Keep the Agency, Drop the Total Theory
commonMisreadings: Keeping the red pill's agency in dating means accepting its whole theory of women too.

sourceLinks.label: Dignam & Rohlinger (2019), “Misogynistic Men Online: How the Red Pill Helped Elect Trump,” Signs 44(3):589–612

entries.title: Competition Anxiety
entries.synopsis: A sourced Deep Dive into competition anxiety: the manosphere term is not a validated construct, but its ingredients are studied as mate-choice copying, social proof, jealousy induction, and mate retention.
commonMisreadings: Competition anxiety is a proven psychological law that jealous partners commit harder to the relationship.

entries.title: Name the Term Before Believing It
entries.synopsis: Competition anxiety is manosphere shorthand for making a romantic prospect or partner feel that other people want you and could replace them. The promised mechanism is urgency: perceived rivals certify your value, remove complacency, and make the other person invest. Sometimes the advice is passive — have a full social life and do not conceal that you have options.
commonMisreadings: A date who worries other people want you will chase harder and commit sooner.

entries.title: Social Proof: A Real but Narrow First-Read Effect
entries.synopsis: People do not evaluate potential partners independently of social information. Someone who appears accepted by desirable peers can look safer or more valuable than the same person shown alone. Relationship research calls this mate-choice copying. It is the strongest empirical piece beneath competition anxiety, and it is much narrower than the tactic built on top of it.
commonMisreadings: If other women flirt with a man, every woman who watches wants him for keeps.

sourceLinks.label: Gouda-Vossos, Nakagawa, Dixson & Brooks (2018), “Mate Choice Copying in Humans: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis,” Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology 4:364–386
Waynforth (2007), Human Nature 18:264–271
Jones et al. (2010), PLOS ONE 5(2):e9115

entries.title: Jealousy: The Tactic Works on Arousal, Not Necessarily the Bond
entries.synopsis: Once two people are involved, the mechanism changes. A visible alternative is no longer only information about desirability; it is information about possible loss. Jealousy can produce pursuit, reassurance, surveillance, anger, withdrawal, or exit. Counting only the extra attention and calling the tactic successful is outcome laundering.
commonMisreadings: Sparking jealousy in your girlfriend proves her love and pulls the relationship closer together.

sourceLinks.label: Fleischmann, Spitzberg, Andersen & Roesch (2005), “Tickling the monster: Jealousy induction in relationships,” Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 22(1):49–73
de Miguel & Buss (2011), “Mate retention tactics in Spain,” Journal of Personality 79(3):563–585
Tortoriello et al. (2017), Personality and Individual Differences 114:10–15
Degiuli, Andreis & Vucenovic (2023), European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education 13:2877–2890

entries.title: The Rule: Signal a Full Life; Do Not Manufacture a Threat
entries.synopsis: There is a clean, non-manipulative kernel here. A person with friends, standards, purpose, and the willingness to leave a bad fit is more attractive than a person performing dependence. Real options matter because they make choice voluntary. Hiding a full life to appear harmless is not intimacy.
aliases: Rule: Signal a Full Life; Do Not Manufacture a Threat
commonMisreadings: Flaunting invented rivals keeps a partner anxious enough to treat the relationship seriously.

entries.title: Autism and Dating
entries.synopsis: A sourced Deep Dive into autistic dating: what the evidence says about wanting and having relationships, the double empathy problem, the cost of masking, reading signals, sensory logistics, and when to disclose.
boundaryConditions: The essay rests on self-report and convenience samples throughout; it establishes mismatch and association, never the cause of any individual outcome.
commonMisreadings: Autistic dating difficulty is a deficit located inside the autistic person, and the remedy is better social technique.

entries.title: Start From What Has Actually Been Measured
entries.synopsis: Almost every piece of dating advice written for autistic adults opens with an inventory of what you are presumed to be missing. Eye contact. Small talk. The ability to tell a polite exit from an invitation. The inventory has a shape, and the shape is a verdict: the reason this is hard is located inside you, and the remedy is to become someone else quickly enough that nobody notices.
boundaryConditions: Desire and partnership rates come from self-selected surveys of adults without intellectual disability, and the milestone comparison rests on thirty boys.
commonMisreadings: Autistic adults seldom want romantic relationships, and their lower partnership rates are the proof.

sourceLinks.label: Strunz, Schermuck, Ballerstein, Ahlers, Dziobek & Roepke (2017), “Romantic Relationships and Relationship Satisfaction Among Adults With Asperger Syndrome and High-Functioning Autism,” Journal of Clinical Psychology 73(2):113–125

Dewinter, De Graaf & Begeer (2017), “Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity, and Romantic Relationships in Adolescents and Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder,” Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders

Dewinter, Vermeiren, Vanwesenbeeck et al. (2016), “Adolescent boys with autism spectrum disorder growing up: follow-up of self-reported sexual experience,” European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry 25(9):969–978
Roux, Shattuck, Rast, Rava & Anderson (2015), National Autism Indicators Report: Transition into Young Adulthood, A.J. Drexel Autism Institute

entries.title: The Gap Is Between Two People, and It Has Been Measured
entries.synopsis: In 2012 the sociologist Damian Milton published a four-page paper arguing that the standard account of autistic social difficulty had a hole in it. The dominant model held that autistic people struggled to model other minds. Milton pointed out that this was being tested in one direction only, and named the thing nobody was measuring: the double empathy problem.
aliases: Gap Is Between Two People, and It Has Been Measured
boundaryConditions: The diffusion-chain and thin-slice results describe mixed-neurotype pairings under laboratory conditions and predict nothing about how one particular pair will get on.
commonMisreadings: Autistic people cannot read other minds, which is why conversations with them break down.

sourceLinks.label: Milton (2012), “On the ontological status of autism: the ‘double empathy problem’,” Disability & Society 27(6):883–887
Crompton, Ropar, Evans-Williams, Flynn & Fletcher-Watson (2020), “Autistic peer-to-peer information transfer is highly effective,” Autism 24(7):1704–1712
Sasson, Faso, Nugent, Lovell, Kennedy & Grossman (2017), “Neurotypical Peers are Less Willing to Interact with Those with Autism based on Thin Slice Judgments,” Scientific Reports 7:40700
Sheppard, Pillai, Wong, Ropar & Mitchell (2016), “How Easy is it to Read the Minds of People with Autism Spectrum Disorder?” Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 46(4):1247–1254

entries.title: The Mask Works, Which Is Exactly the Problem
entries.synopsis: The standard workaround for the gap in the last section is performance: suppress the stims, rehearse the small talk, run a continuous background process that monitors your own face. The research calls it camouflaging or masking. It is worth being precise about why it is such a stubborn strategy.
aliases: Mask Works, Which Is Exactly the Problem
boundaryConditions: Camouflaging's costs are measured by association, including one momentary-assessment design; no study cited establishes that masking causes the outcomes it travels with.
commonMisreadings: Masking is a social skill worth practising until it runs by itself.

sourceLinks.label: Hull, Petrides, Allison, Smith, Baron-Cohen, Lai & Mandy (2017), “‘Putting on My Best Normal’: Social Camouflaging in Adults with Autism Spectrum Conditions,” Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 47(8):2519–2534
Cage & Troxell-Whitman (2019), “Understanding the Reasons, Contexts and Costs of Camouflaging for Autistic Adults,” Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 49:1899–1911
Scheeren, Nieuwenhuis, Crane, Roke & Begeer (2025), “Masking, social context and perceived stress in autistic adults: An ecological momentary assessment study,” Autism 29:3002–3013
Cassidy, Bradley, Shaw & Baron-Cohen (2018), “Risk markers for suicidality in autistic adults,” Molecular Autism 9:42
Ridgway, Cooke, Demmer, Hooley, Westrupp & Stokes (2025), “Camouflaging Autism in Pursuit of Friendship and Intimate Relationships: A Systematic Review,” Autism in Adulthood 7(5):543–557

Bargiela, Steward & Mandy (2016), “The Experiences of Late-diagnosed Women with Autism Spectrum Conditions: An Investigation of the Female Autism Phenotype,” Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 46(10):3281–3294

entries.title: Reading the Ask, and the Cost of Vagueness
entries.synopsis: Courtship in most of the anglophone world runs on deniability.
